title: Transitioning to yardstick for Calculation of Model Metrics
description:
The `ModelMetrics` package is currently used within the `caret` package to calculate model evaluation metrics. However, `ModelMetrics` is no longer actively maintained on CRAN (last updated: 2020-03-17). In highly regulated industries such as Pharma, use of well-validated and actively supported packages is often a requirement. At present, `ModelMetrics` is not part of the Atorus OpenVal validated packages. In contrast, the `yardstick` package from the `tidymodels` framework is actively maintained and has been included in the OpenVal packages:
https://www.atorusresearch.com/openval/openval-packages/

Currently, `caret` uses `ModelMetrics::auc` and `ModelMetrics::mlogLoss` to compute model metrics. These functions can be directly replaced by `yardstick::roc_auc_vec` and `yardstick::mn_log_loss_vec`, respectively.  Below are two examples demonstrating how to substitute the `ModelMetrics` functions with their `yardstick` equivalents.

### ModelMetrics::auc vs yardstick::roc_auc_vec

```r
testDF <- ModelMetrics::testDF

glmModel <- glm(y ~ ., data = testDF, family = "binomial")
Preds <- predict(glmModel, type = 'response')

ModelMetrics::auc(
    actual = testDF$y, 
    predicted = Preds
) # 0.9872666

yardstick::roc_auc_vec(
    truth = factor(testDF$y), 
    estimate = Preds, 
    event_level = "second"
) # 0.9872666
```

### ModelMetrics::mlogLoss vs yardstick::mn_log_loss_vec

```r
two_class_example <- yardstick::two_class_example

ModelMetrics::mlogLoss(
  actual = two_class_example[, "truth"],
  predicted = two_class_example[, c("Class1", "Class2")]
) # 0.3283096

yardstick::mn_log_loss_vec(
  truth = two_class_example[, "truth"], 
  estimate = two_class_example[, "Class1"]
) # 0.3283096
```

title: thresholder() is about 4x slower after moving metrics to yardstick
description:
Moving caret's metrics to yardstick (branch `modelmetrics-to-yardstick`) made `thresholder()` about 4x slower.

## Timing

`glm` fit to `twoClassSim(500)` with 10-fold CV and `savePredictions = "final"`, then `thresholder(fit, threshold = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01))`:

| Version | Elapsed (s) |
|---|---|
| before the transition (cf7bf44c) | 0.78 |
| Accuracy/Kappa in `confusionMatrix()` from yardstick | 3.07 |
| all by-class statistics from yardstick | 3.21 |

## Cause

`thresholder()` calls `confusionMatrix()` once per resample, tuning parameter combination, and threshold (990 calls here), inside two `plyr::ddply()` passes (one to recode the predicted classes and one to compute the statistics). Each `confusionMatrix()` call now makes about nine yardstick table-method calls, and each returns a tibble, so the fixed overhead per call is much larger than the arithmetic. Profiling shows `confusionMatrix()` takes about 88% of the time, and the yardstick `accuracy()`/`kap()` table methods alone account for most of the increase.

## Possible fixes

- **Compute the statistics from counts, all at once.** For each resample (and tuning parameter combination), sort the event probabilities once and use cumulative sums to get TP, FP, FN, and TN for every threshold. All of the statistics `thresholder()` reports (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, precision, recall, F1, prevalence, detection rate/prevalence, balanced accuracy, accuracy, Kappa, J, distance) are simple vectorized functions of those four counts. This would likely be faster than the original code, but it means caret computes these statistics itself again instead of using yardstick.
- **Use yardstick once per group instead of `confusionMatrix()`.** Build the recoded predictions for all thresholds (as `expand_preds()` does now), group by resample, parameters, and threshold, and call a single `yardstick::metric_set()` on the grouped data. This keeps yardstick as the source of the statistics, with one call per statistic instead of one per group. The few statistics yardstick doesn't have (e.g. detection rate, `Dist`) would be added from the same grouped counts.
- In either case, drop the two `ddply()` passes over the expanded predictions (`nrow(pred) * length(threshold)` rows).

The output (column names, `NA` handling, and the warning about removed missing values) should stay the same, and tests should compare the results with the current implementation.

title: upkeep plan for summer 2026
description:
We have a paid intern this year who is interested in helping modernize caret to make support and upkeep easier. The current overall plan of no new features is still in place. We just want to make the repository saner and easier to work with. 

This issue is to help refine a short-term plan to start moving in this direction. It's a working document so please add your thoughts about what would improve the current repository without affecting reverse dependencies. 

# Initial plan (through the end of summer)

1. Restructure the repo [DONE]:
	- Move the actual package to the top level
	- Fix links (eg. GHA, model file location change)
	- Archive files that we probably don't need anymore, like the regression tests or the RHTML docs
	- Move a number of directories to `inst` and add them to `.Rbuildignore`

2. Update GitHub Actions [DONE]. Only 6mo behind, so this shouldn't be a big deal. Will probably add actions for java install etc [DONE]. 

3. PR triage: We don't want to create more work than required so I'll work through a fair number of PRs with a focus on PRs for unit tests [DONE]. 

4. `air format` [DONE]

5. Overhaul _existing_ tests [DONE]

	- Move to edition 3 of testthat
	- Helper files
	- No data/code outside of tests
	- Remove noise (e.g. logging, pkg load notifications) in tests
	- Snapshot tests
	- "NoSuggests" tests

6. Increase code coverage: We want to get the unit test coverage as good as possible, not only because it is a good idea, but also so that we can avoid Claude making mistakes later when we get help for refactoring [DONE]. 

# Code refactoring

After these steps, there is a laundry list of things to improve (in no particular order): 

- Move away from older technologies (plyr, etc)
- Code consolidation to reduce redundancy
- Refactoring and redocumenting
- _Perhaps_ moving to better logging of messages, warnings, and errors (to cli, if at all)
- Assess model list for archived or otherwise difficult dependencies. It'll be a high bar to remove them. 
- Convert bookdown docs to Quarto (mostly done) and maybe automate deployment. 

Again, the goal is to keep the interface the same and minimize reverse-dependency issues down the line. There will be some breakages because I'm continually surprised by the "off-label use" of dependencies. However, assuming we don't have to submit to "safely retain [our] package on CRAN", we should have time to submit PRs to other repos to deal with any changes.

title: Remove resampleWrapper(): exported, uncalled, and broken since before 2014
description:
`resampleWrapper()` is exported but cannot run, and nothing in the package calls it.

```r
library(caret)
df <- data.frame(a = rnorm(20), b = rnorm(20), .outcome = rnorm(20))
x <- list(data = df, method = getModelInfo("lm", regex = FALSE)[[1]])
caret:::resampleWrapper(x, 1:15)
#> Error in do.call(createModel, x) : argument "x" is missing, with no default
```

The body builds its argument list around `x$data`:

```r
resampleWrapper <- function(x, ind) {
  out <- rep(NA, dim(x$data)[1])
  trainData <- x$data
  x$data <- x$data[ind, ]
  tmpModelFit <- do.call(createModel, x)
  ...
}
```

That matches a `createModel(data = ...)` signature which does not exist in this repository's history: at the first commit (caret 6.0-30, 2014) `pkg/caret/R/createModel.R` already defined `createModel2(x, y, wts, method, tuneValue, obsLevels, pp, last, classProbs, ...)`. So `data` lands in `...` while `x` and `y` are never supplied.

`grep -rn resampleWrapper R/` finds only the definition and the `@aliases` line in `createModel.Rd`; the only other reference is `export(resampleWrapper)` in NAMESPACE.

Since it is exported, it is grouped with the other dead exports for removal after a reverse-dependency check (as was done for `predict.PLS()` in #1512). Nothing can be calling it successfully, but the export is public API.

Found while raising test coverage: it is the only file left at 0%, and there is nothing meaningful to test.

title: Adaptive resampling with a recipe: the first resamples lose their tuning parameters, and drop the cell counts past five classes
description:
Found while raising test coverage (plan: `plans/2026-08-16-1545-100-percent-coverage.md`).

Two slips in the same block of `train_adapt_rec()` (`R/train_recipes.R`), the
phase that runs the resamples the race starts from before any candidate is
eliminated. Both are in the branch taken by models without sub-models.

**1. The saved predictions have no tuning parameters.** Every other phase merges
the loop row into `tmpPred`:

```r
tmpPred <- merge(tmpPred, new_info$loop[parm, , drop = FALSE], all = TRUE)
```

This one did not, so with `savePredictions = "all"` the rows from those
resamples come back with `NA` in the parameter columns and cannot be attributed
to a candidate. `adaptiveWorkflow()` (the x/y interface) already merges, so only
recipes were affected.

```r
cls <- iris[c(1:15, 51:65, 101:115), ]
fit <- train(
  recipes::recipe(Species ~ ., data = cls), data = cls, method = "knn",
  tuneGrid = data.frame(k = c(1, 30)),
  trControl = trainControl(
    method = "adaptive_cv", number = 6, savePredictions = "all",
    adaptive = list(min = 3, alpha = 0.05, method = "gls", complete = TRUE)
  )
)
table(fit$pred$k, useNA = "ifany")   # a third of the rows have k = NA
fit$results$Num_Resamples            # 6 and 3, so the resamples were run
```

**2. The confusion-matrix cells stop at five classes.** The threshold there was
`length(lev) <= 5`; the other seven places in the package that gate those counts
use `<= 50`. With six or more classes the resamples the race starts from carried
no cells while the racing and completion phases did, so `resampledCM` came back
with `NA` counts for them.

title: Adaptive resampling mislabels sub-model results in the completion resamples
description:
Found while raising test coverage (plan: `plans/2026-08-16-1545-100-percent-coverage.md`).

`trainControl(method = "adaptive_cv", adaptive = list(complete = TRUE))` runs the
remaining resamples for the candidates that survived the race. That completion
pass fits with the surviving loop (`new_info$loop[parm, ]`) and labels its
results with the surviving sub-models (`new_info$submodels[[parm]]`), but it
computed the predictions from `info$submodels[[parm]]` — the sub-models of the
grid the race *started* from.

`parm` indexes the narrowed loop, so the two lists are neither the same length
nor about the same candidates. The performance rows are then `cbind()`ed to the
parameter rows, which recycles when the counts divide (warning: `row names were
found from a short variable and have been discarded`) and errors otherwise. The
resampled performance from the completion resamples — and the saved predictions —
end up attached to the wrong tuning parameters.

Both interfaces are affected:

- `R/adaptive.R` lines 846, 848, 915, 957, 988 (`adaptiveWorkflow()`)
- `R/train_recipes.R` lines 1560, 1562 (`train_adapt_rec()`)

The burn-in phase already uses `new_info$submodels[[parm]]`
(`R/adaptive.R:421-424`, `R/train_recipes.R:1214-1217`), which is what the
completion pass should do too.

Reproducible with a sub-model model whose candidates each predict a distinct
constant: after the fix every saved prediction equals its own `shift`, before it
they do not. Covered by "the race labels sub-model results while finishing the
last resamples" in `tests/testthat/test-adaptive.R` and "the recipe race labels
sub-model results while finishing up" in `tests/testthat/test-train_recipes.R`.

title: print.train() reports trainControl(number) rather than the number of resamples actually used
description:
When the resampling index is supplied directly, `print.train()` reports the number of resamples from `trainControl(number = )` rather than from the index it actually used:

```r
library(caret)
dat <- iris[c(1:15, 51:65, 101:115), ]
folds <- createFolds(dat$Species, k = 3, returnTrain = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
fit <- train(Species ~ ., data = dat, method = "knn", tuneGrid = data.frame(k = 5),
             trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", index = folds))
fit
#> Resampling: Cross-Validated (10 fold)
#> Summary of sample sizes: 30, 30, 30
```

Three folds were used; the header says ten, because `resampName()` reads `x$control$number`, which keeps its default when only `index` is given. The line below it, built from `length(x$control$index)`, is right.

`length(x$control$index)` is available in the same function, so the header could use it (for `repeatedcv` the repeat count would still have to come from `control$repeats`).

Possibly intended — `number` is what the user nominally asked for — in which case this can be closed. Flagging it because the two adjacent lines disagree.

title: predict.preProcess(): untested imputation branch for inputs that are neither matrix nor data frame
print.preProcess() Yeo-Johnson "#NA" count is unreachable
description:
`print.preProcess()` reports how many Yeo-Johnson lambdas could not be estimated, but the count is always zero because the missing ones have already been dropped.

`R/preProcess.R`:

```r
  if (any(names(x$method) == "YeoJohnson")) {
    cat("Lambda estimates for Yeo-Johnson transformation:\n")
    lmbda <- get_yj_lambda(x$yj)
    if (length(lmbda) < 11) {
      naLmbda <- sum(is.na(lmbda))
      cat(paste(round(lmbda[!is.na(lmbda)], 2), collapse = ", "))
      if (naLmbda > 0) {
        cat(" (#NA: ", naLmbda, ")\n", sep = "")   # unreachable
      }
    }
```

`get_yj_lambda()` ends with `res[!is.na(res)]`, so `lmbda` never holds an `NA` and `naLmbda` is always 0. `preProcess.default()` also drops the columns whose estimate failed (`yj <- yj[!is.null(yj) & !is.na(yj)]`), so `x$yj` has none either.

Two ways to settle it, whichever matches the intent:

* the count is genuinely wanted, and `get_yj_lambda()` should stop filtering (the Box-Cox arm above prints the count from an unfiltered `x$bc`, so the two would then behave alike); or
* the transformation is simply not reported when it fails, and the `naLmbda` block plus the `!is.na()` guards can go.

Note the Box-Cox arm is asymmetric on purpose or by accident: `group_bc()` also strips the failures, so *its* count only fires for objects saved by an older caret. That is how it is currently covered by a test.

Found while raising test coverage; this is the one line in `R/preProcess.R` that cannot be reached.

title: optimism_boot and boot_all fail for pls: predict.plsda() cannot take duplicated row names
description:
`trainControl(method = "optimism_boot")` and `method = "boot_all"` error for `method = "pls"`:

```r
library(caret)
dat <- twoClassSim(60)
set.seed(1)
train(Class ~ ., data = dat, method = "pls", tuneGrid = data.frame(ncomp = 1:3),
      trControl = trainControl(method = "boot_all", number = 2))
#> Error: task 1 failed - "duplicate 'row.names' are not allowed"
```

`cv`, `boot` and `boot632` work with the same grid.

The cause is `predict.plsda()` (`R/plsda.R`), which copies row names from the data being predicted onto a data frame:

```r
rownames(out) <- rownames(newdata)
```

These two resampling schemes score the resampled training set itself, so the data being predicted contains the same row several times. A data frame cannot hold duplicated row names, so the assignment both warns ("non-unique values when setting 'row.names'") and then errors. Nothing about `optimism_xy()` or the sub-model shortcut is involved — a single-row `tuneGrid` fails the same way, and other models are unaffected only because they do not make this assignment.

`predict.bagFDA()` (`R/bagFDA.R`) has the identical line and the identical problem.

Fix: only copy the row names over when they are unique. With that change, both methods work for `pls` with a one-row grid and with a multi-row grid, and for the sub-model models (`rpart`, `gbm`) too.

title: Document the model-object element names that createModel() reserves
description:
`createModel()` (`R/createModel.R`, lines 84-92) writes five elements onto whatever a custom model's `fit` function returns:

```r
modelFit$xNames      <- colnames(x)
modelFit$problemType <- "Classification" / "Regression"
modelFit$tuneValue   <- tuneValue
modelFit$obsLevels   <- obsLevels
modelFit$param       <- list(...)
```

Two consequences are easy to trip over when writing a custom model, and neither is documented in the "Using Your Own Model" material:

1. Those five names are effectively reserved. A `fit` function that stores its own state under any of them has it silently overwritten.
2. `modelFit$param` is **not** the tuning parameters — it is the extra `...` passed to `train()`. The tuning values are in `modelFit$tuneValue`. The `param` argument *to* `fit` does hold the tuning values, so the same name means two different things either side of the call.

Storing tuning values under `param` in a custom `fit` therefore yields an empty list at predict time, a zero-length prediction, and — because caret treats that as a failed prediction and fills it via `fill_failed_pred()` — a zero-level factor and a downstream "Something is wrong; all the RMSE metric values are missing" error, with nothing pointing at the real cause.

A short note in the custom-model documentation listing the reserved names and clarifying `param` vs `tuneValue` would save that debugging.

title: Consolidate package helpers
description:
See #1422 

Pre-tidyvers/r-lib caret made a few choices that we should revisit: 

1. All of the `@importFrom` and `@import` directives for roxygen2 were added next to the code that used them. This makes a bit of sense, but there is so much of it around the package that it defeats the purpose of defining it next to where it is used. 
2. Similarly, there are _a lot_ of calls to `utils::globalVariables()`. This was added to R after caret was developed. Prior to this function, we had to initialize a variable that was flagged as a false positive during `R CMD check`, typically with a pattern like `var_name <- NULL`. The current `aaa.R` enumerates this and also tries to describe _why_ they are false positives. This has become such a regular thing that it should just be consolidated. 

## Action

The package should be changed so that: 

1. The unique set of  `@importFrom` and `@import` directives should be determined. This reduced list should be added to `caret-package.R`. This should respect the line widths, so multiple entries might be needed if we import a lot of functions from the same package. 
2. Encase these import directives between `## usethis namespace: start` and `## usethis namespace: end`.
3. Find the minimal unique set of names referenced with `utils::globalVariables()`. Sort them and assign them to a vector called `global_false_positives`. Make sure that the list obeys the standard column width limits. Also, in the line just prior to the definition of that vector, add  `# fmt: skip`
4. Place the new call to `utils::globalVariables()`  also inside `caret-package.R`. Use a code comment header of `# nocov start` and, afterward, `# nocov end`. Make sure that the long 

Redocument and run a full `R CMD check` (not as CRAN) to make sure everything works.

title: jarl analysis
description:
[jarl](https://jarl.etiennebacher.com/) is a linter for R. I wanted to get a sense of what we can have it fix in the codebase. 

```
> jarl check R/*.R tests/testthat/*.R --statistics
  145 [*] numeric_leading_zero
  135 [ ] vector_logic
  106 [*] seq
   37 [ ] implicit_assignment
   31 [*] any_is_na
   27 [*] outer_negation
   27 [ ] unused_function
   25 [*] matrix_apply
   16 [ ] internal_function
   14 [*] length_levels
   13 [ ] all_equal
    8 [ ] true_false_symbol
    8 [*] redundant_ifelse
    2 [*] comparison_negation
    1 [ ] duplicated_function_definition
    1 [ ] duplicated_arguments
    1 [*] sort
    1 [ ] unreachable_code

Rules with `[*]` have an automatic fix.
```

Some examples: 

```
warning: any_is_na
  --> R/BoxCoxTrans.R:86:16
   |
86 |   if(na.rm && (any(is.na(y)) | any(is.na(x)))) {
   |                ------------- `any(is.na(...))` is inefficient.
   |
   = help: Use `anyNA(...)` instead.
```

```
warning: vector_logic
  --> R/BoxCoxTrans.R:91:6
   |
91 |   if(!is.numeric(y) | is.factor(y) | is.character(y)) stop("y must be numeric")
   |      ----------------------------------------------- `|` in `if()` statements can be inefficient.
   |
```

```
warning: seq
  --> R/adaptive.R:34:20
   |
34 |     foreach(parm = 1:nrow(info$loop),
   |                    ----------------- `1:nrow(...)` can be wrong if the RHS is 0.
   |
   = help: Use `seq_len(nrow((...))` instead.
```

```
warning: numeric_leading_zero
   --> R/adaptive.R:488:37
    |
488 | ...                   cutoff = .001,
    |                                ---- Include the leading zero for fractional numeric constants.
    |

```

```
warning: any_is_na
   --> R/adaptive.R:926:8
    |
926 |     if(any(is.na(keepers))) keepers[is.na(keepers)] <- TRUE
    |        ------------------- `any(is.na(...))` is inefficient.
    |
    = help: Use `anyNA(...)` instead.
```

```
warning: implicit_assignment
   --> R/avNNet.R:249:20
    |
249 |       if (!is.null(cl <- attr(Terms, "dataClasses"))) {
    |                    -------------------------------- Avoid implicit assignments in `if()` statements.
    |

```

```
warning: matrix_apply
   --> R/avNNet.R:220:14
    |
220 |       return(apply(out, 1, mean))
    |              ------------------- `apply(x, 1, mean)` is inefficient.
    |
    = help: Use `rowMeans(x)` instead.
```

title: Forensic analysis of caret
description:
This package was initially developed in 2005. This was before things like

 - namespaces (added in R 2.14.0, Oct 2011)
 - imports (kind of gradual but also around 2014)
 - LazyData/LazyLoad of data within packages
 - `utils::globalVariables()`
 - `paste0()` (2012!)
 - roxygen and cli for documentation and printing
 - devtools, testthat, or rlang for tooling and modern R infrastructure
 - linters and formatters for R
 - etc etc

How did we live like this? /s

A colleague suggested enumerating old patterns in this package that appear to be "wtf?" but made sense at the time and have remained due to a lack of time for upkeep.

title: Deduplicate the two copies of `train` validation logic
description:
`train.default`'s validation/setup logic (tuning-grid checks, metric defaulting, pre-processing checks, error messages) is duplicated between the formula/xy path (~[train.default.R:337](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/train.default.R#L337)–675) and the recipe path (~[train.default.R:1005](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/train.default.R#L1005)–1264). Most `train` error messages therefore exist twice (e.g. tuning-grid error at [train.default.R:502](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/train.default.R#L502) and [train.default.R:1185](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/train.default.R#L1185)).

Factor shared validation into internal helpers so each check/message lives once. Pairs with #1440

title: Deduplicate the safs/gafs/rfe/selectByFilter resampling-setup block (largest)
description:
The `.default` and `.recipe` methods of `safs`/`gafs`, and the workflow paths of `rfe`/`selectByFilter`, each contain a near-identical ~30-line block that builds `$index` via `switch(tolower(method), ...)`, names it with `prettySeq`, derives `$indexOut`, validates/generates `$seeds`, and builds a fake `testOutput` to probe the summary function. title: Recompose long `paste()`/`paste0()` message strings with `glue::glue()`
description:
Keep `stop()`/`warning()`/`message()`/`cat()` as the delivery mechanism. Only replace the hand-built `paste(..., sep = "")` concatenation inside them with `glue::glue()` for readability. **Each rewrite must reproduce the exact string** (whitespace, `sep`, `collapse`, trailing `\n`).

Watch-outs:

- `cat('\n', paste(...))` inserts a space (cat default `sep = " "`) — preserve it.
- `paste(x, collapse = ", ")` → `glue::glue_collapse(x, sep = ", ")`, not `glue()`.
- `glue()` errors on length-mismatch where `paste()` recycles — check vectorized cases.

Candidates (scalar, clean conversions):

- [splsda.R:114](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/splsda.R#L114), [splsda.R:120](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/splsda.R#L120), [splsda.R:123](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/splsda.R#L123), [splsda.R:130](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/05c9943b45ac5a2fea2dd2a85ad9d66df88ce1e6/R/splsda.R#L130) — four print lines

title: Contrast predictions between default type and type "prob" in binary plsRglm model
description:
In general, we expect the predicted class is the type with greater probability. But I got contrast predicted results with "plsRglm" model. This affects the AUC calculation. Could someone help me to handle it?
This is my code:
```R
library(caret)
library(plsRglm)

# optVars is the vector of my variables

# fit plsRglm model
trControl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                          number = 10,
                          repeats = 3,
                          p = 0.7,
                          classProbs = T,
                          verboseIter = TRUE,
                          summaryFunction = twoClassSummary, # support for ROC-AUC calculation
                          search = "random")

fit <- train(label ~ ., data = train_data[, c("label", optVars)],
             method = "plsRglm",
             metric = "ROC",
             tuneLength = 15,

title: Possible Bug in findCorrelation_exact: Incorrect comparison logic for variable removal
description:
https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/c98cc1a3ba5f0b087d51f5c4362a3b751515e243/pkg/caret/R/findCorrelation.R#L66C9-L71C64

There appears to be a logical error in the `findCorrelation_exact` function when comparing variables for removal in findCorrelation.R file. 

```r
mn1 <- mean(x2[i,], na.rm = TRUE)
mn2 <- mean(x2[-j,], na.rm = TRUE)  # <- Issue here
```

The comparison is between:

mn1: Mean correlation of variable i with all other variables
mn2: Mean of the entire correlation matrix excluding row j (but still including row i)

I’m not sure whether this is correct, or if the algorithm should instead compare the mean correlations of the two highly correlated variables directly in order to decide which one to remove.

```r
mn1 <- mean(x2[i,], na.rm = TRUE)
mn2 <- mean(x2[j,], na.rm = TRUE) 
```

Could someone confirm if this is the intended behavior or if it should be corrected?

title: Inconsistent NA handling in createDataPartition
description:
https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/c98cc1a3ba5f0b087d51f5c4362a3b751515e243/pkg/caret/R/createDataPartition.R#L122

As I'm finding in work towards #1382, missing inputs are handled a bit inconsistently by `createDataPartition()`:

```r
library(withr)

# y is numeric, missing --> error
createDataPartition(c(NA, 1))
# Error in quantile.default(y, probs = seq(0, 1, length = groups)) : 
#   missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE

# y is character, level with only one observation --> warning
with_seed(78458, createDataPartition(c("a", "b", "b")))
# $Resample1
# [1] 1 3
# Warning message:
# In createDataPartition(c("a", "b", "b")) :
#   Some classes have a single record ( a ) and these will be selected for the sample

# y is character, missing level has only one observation --> no warning
with_seed(78458, createDataPartition(c(NA, "b", "b")))
# $Resample1
# [1] 1 3
```

What is the proper handling of missing `y`? Should we just error if `y` has any missing observations? That would certainly make the migration away from `dlply()` simpler (c.f. 5805d30a4032c1973345cb5b928192fb3068d212).

title: Support for Hierarchical Constraints in glmStepAIC within caret::train
description:
When using caret::train with method = "glmStepAIC" for stepwise regression, the underlying MASS::stepAIC function can remove main effects involved in interaction terms (e.g., dropping PredictorVariable1 while retaining PredictorVariable1:PredictorVariable2). This violates the hierarchical principle in regression 

> Hierarchical testing in multiple regression ensures higher-order interactions are evaluated only when lower-order interactions and main effects are included, prioritizing additive relationships over multiplicative ones. While excluding lower-order terms may improve estimation precision in some cases, their inclusion is critical when variables are measured at the interval level to maintain theoretical and interpretive consistency - Allison PD. Testing for Interaction in Multiple Regression. Am J Sociol 1977; 83: 144–153.

, which requires main effects to be retained when their interactions are included, especially for interpretability with interval-level variables. There’s no built-in way to enforce this constraint while preserving caret’s resampling framework (e.g., repeated cross-validation via trControl).

Reproducible Example:  
```
library(caret)
set.seed(123)
dataset <- data.frame(
  OUTCOME = rnorm(100),
  PredictorVariable1 = rnorm(100),
  PredictorVariable2 = rnorm(100),
  PredictorVariable3 = rnorm(100)
)
splitRule <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 5)

model <- train(
  Outcome ~ PredictorVariable1 + PredictorVariable2 + PredictorVariable3 + 
            PredictorVariable1 * PredictorVariable2,
  data = dataset,
  trControl = splitRule,
  method = "glmStepAIC",
  direction = "both"
)
summary(model$finalModel)  # May drop main effects like PredictorVariable1
```

I’d expect an option (e.g., a parameter or custom method) to enforce hierarchical constraints, ensuring main effects aren’t removed if their interactions remain, without losing integration with trControl’s resampling. Instead, glmStepAIC freely drops main effects, breaking hierarchy, and there’s no straightforward way to adjust this within caret::train. Running stepAIC separately loses the resampling benefits. I tried a custom model, but it resulted in "all RMSE metric values are missing," suggesting compatibility issues with caret’s internals.

title: Flaky test on dummyVars
description:
This test is flaky:

https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/5f4bd2069bf486ae92240979f9d65b5c138ca8d4/pkg/caret/tests/testthat/test_Dummies.R#L122-L139C3

It fails whenever some entry from `1:15` is missing from `sample.int(15, size = 100, replace = TRUE, prob = rep(1 / 15, 15))`.

That happens about (probably exactly? too lazy to do the math) 1.5% of the time:

```r
mean(replicate(1e6, all(1:15 %in% sample.int(15, size = 100, replace = TRUE, prob = rep(1 / 15, 15)))))
# [1] [1] 0.984922
```

Observe:

```r
# get an entry missing one of 1:15
repeat {
  entry <- sample.int(15, size = 100, replace = TRUE, prob = rep(1 / 15, 15))
  if (!all(1:15 %in% entry)) break
}

# now finish the test
data = data.frame(matrix(rep(as.factor(entry), 15), ncol = 15), stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
essai_dummyVars = caret::dummyVars(stats::as.formula(paste0("~ ", colnames(data), collapse = "+")), data)

exp_names_lvls <- apply(expand.grid(paste0("X",1:15), paste0(".",1:15)), 1, paste, collapse="")
res_names_lvls <- colnames(predict(essai_dummyVars, data))
all(exp_names_lvls %in% res_names_lvls)
# [1] FALSE
```

title: Wrong accuracy value for logit boost model
description:
**Summary**
While using the caret package to compare machine learning models, we observed that the accuracy of Logit Boost (LogitBoost) models might be overestimated. This issue arises because observations where predictions are not made are excluded from the confusion matrix and subsequent performance metric calculations.

**Description**
We recently conducted a model comparison study using AI methods to attribute cases of human salmonellosis to various animal-based food sources (e.g., pig, bovine, poultry). We employed the caret package in R to compare Random Forest (RF), Logit Boost (LB), and Support Vector Machines (SVM) models. The train function was used, both with and without cross-validation, to train the models.

During the prediction phase on the test dataset (with a known response variable), we observed the following behavior:

1) All models predicted the food source for each observation, except Logit Boost.
2) For Logit Boost, when two or more predicted probabilities were identical for a given observation, the model appropriately failed to make a prediction, returning NA instead.

However, the issue arises during accuracy calculation:

1) Non-predicted observations (NA values) were excluded from the confusion matrix.
2) This exclusion potentially inflates the reported accuracy of Logit Boost, as it only considers successfully predicted observations.

In our opinion the model performance evaluation could account for the missing predictions to ensure a more accurate comparison.


Below is an example illustrating the discrepancy between RF and LB predictions (without cross-validation), using an artificial dataset. The confusion matrix and accuracy for RF include all observations, while for LB, they exclude cases with NA predictions.

#################################################################################################      
###### -----------------------  Example code ---------------------------------------------- #
library(caret)
# --------------------- DATASET
set.seed(123)
n=500

# Y variable
response <- factor(sample(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), n, replace = TRUE))

# X variables: qualitative and quantitative
predictor <- factor(sample(c("X", "Y", "Z"), n, replace = TRUE))
quant_var1 <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)   
quant_var2 <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 100)  

dataset<- data.frame(Species = response,
                     Predictor = predictor,
                     Quantitative1 = quant_var1,
                     Quantitative2 = quant_var2)


# ---------------------- TRAIN AND TEST WITHOUT CROSS VALIDATION

set.seed(839)
id=sample(1:NROW(dataset), 0.70*NROW(dataset))
data_train=dataset[id,]
data_test= dataset[-id,]
data_test2<-data_test

#---- Logit Boost -------------------------------------------------------------------- #
set.seed(839)
model_logitboost=train(Species ~ .,   
                       data = data_train,  
                       method = "LogitBoost",  metric="Accuracy",
                       trControl = trainControl(method = "none"))
model_logitboost

predictions_logitboost=predict(model_logitboost, data_test)
conf_matrix_logitboost=confusionMatrix(predictions_logitboost,data_test$Species)
conf_matrix_logitboost

#Accuracy
accuracy<-conf_matrix_logitboost$overall[1]
accuracy
#0.2545455

probability<-predict(model_logitboost, data_test, type="prob")
probability2=cbind(probability, predictions_logitboost)

#N of observations included in confusion matrix
sum(table(predictions_logitboost)) #55
dim(data_test)[1] #150
#% predicted
sum(table(predictions_logitboost))/dim(data_test)[1] #0.37
#% did not predicted
1-sum(table(predictions_logitboost))/dim(data_test)[1] #0.63


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

# ------------------------------------- Random Forest ------------------------------------- #

set.seed(839)
model_rf=train(Species~ .,   
               data = data_train,  
               method = "rf", metric="Accuracy",        
               trControl = trainControl(method = "none"))

model_rf
model_rf$finalModel         

predictions_rf=predict(model_rf, data_test)
conf_matrix_rf=confusionMatrix(predictions_rf, data_test$Species)
conf_matrix_rf  

sum(table(predictions_rf)) #150
dim(data_test)[1] #150
#% predicted
sum(table(predictions_rf))/dim(data_test)[1] #1
#% not predicted
1-sum(table(predictions_rf))/dim(data_test)[1] #0

#Accuracy
accuracy<-conf_matrix_rf$overall[1]
accuracy
#0.2866667 

probability<-predict(model_rf, data_test, type="prob")
probability2=cbind(probability, predictions_rf)

#N of observations included in confusion matrix
sum(table(predictions_rf)) #150
dim(data_test)[1] #150
#% predicted
sum(table(predictions_rf))/dim(data_test)[1] #1
#% did not predicted
1-sum(table(predictions_rf))/dim(data_test)[1] #0

title: Incorrect Mean Absolute Calculation in findCorrelation_exact
description:
Since the commit `f2ad13509ba3d6ab28069840c9631a66a9e7ecc8`, the function `findCorrelation_exact` on row 38 computes the incorrect mean absolute correlation for `mn2`. The function calculates the mean of the matrix without the variable `j`, instead of calculating the mean of variable `j` against the other variables. There are two possible solutions:

1 - Remove the minus sign from `j`, thereby comparing two different rows of the matrix. However, when `verbose = TRUE`, the output prints: "Compare row i and column j with corr...". Despite the mirroring of the row and column (being the same), this text is incorrect.

2 - Remove the minus sign and change `j` to the column position.

``` r
#before the commit
(mean(x[i, -i]) > mean(x[-j, j]) #compare the mean of two vectors
#after the commit
mn1 <- mean(x2[i,], na.rm = TRUE) #return the mean of a vector
mn2 <- mean(x2[-j,], na.rm = TRUE) #return the mean of a matrix
#possible solution 1
mn2 <- mean(x2[j,], na.rm = TRUE) #return the mean of the row 
#possible solution2
mn2 <- mean(x2[, j], na.rm = TRUE) #return the mean of the column
```

### Minimal dataset:

```{R}

                       -0.117569784133002, 1, -0.42844010433054, -0.366125932536439, 
                       0.871753775886583, -0.42844010433054, 1, 0.962865431402796, 0.817941126271576, 
                       -0.366125932536439, 0.962865431402796, 1), dim = c(4L, 4L), dimnames = list(
                         c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"
                         ), c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"
                         )))
```

``` r

title: caret 6.0-86: Function groupKFold does not return the requested number of folds
description:
The function groupKFold in caret 6.0-86 does not return the requested number of folds, even though it is possible according to the number of groups. caret version 6.0-84 returns the correct number of folds.

Example:

R Version 4.0.1
Caret Version 6.0-86

require(caret)
set.seed(1)

Vector with 10 groups
group <- as.factor(sort(rep(seq(1, 10), 10)))

folds <- caret::groupKFold(group, k = 10)

Number of folds I expected: 10 folds with 1 group missing in each
Number of folds I got: 7

length(folds)


Caret Version 6.0-84

require(caret)
set.seed(1)

Vector with 10 groups

group <- as.factor(sort(rep(seq(1, 10), 10)))

folds <- caret::groupKFold(group, k = 10)

Number of folds I expected: 10 folds with 1 group missing in each
Number of folds I got: 10

length(folds)

title: Allow summary functions for RFE variability estimation
description:
Currently (`v6.0-94`), only internal  `MeanSD` function is supported in RFE to compute the variability of the (repeated) CV metrics. As long as one assumes (repeated) CV samples coming from a normal distribution, this is perfectly fine. But in case this assumption is not taken, then reporting only the SD is very limiting. 

A simple addition would be to allow the user to specify an e.g. "`summarySD`" function in `caret::rfeControl(functions)`, which can point to `MeanSD` by default. A very quick and dirty implementation one can find [here](https://github.com/DavorJ/caret/compare/master...fixes#diff-75c813a5cbf6f6be5523aa71d2d78c290b7bfedc3a4335b6f312e63c9c16c22eR728). This would allow much more flexibility for custom implementations of `selectSize` RFE functions since one could pass extra information and not only the SD.

title: Zero features model in RFE
description:
Is there any reason why zero feature model (i.e. intercept/mean only model) is not allowed within caret RFE? I am referring to `caret::rfe(sizes)` argument.

Why is this important? Because the intercept only model might actually be the best possible model. Here is a performance profile (from corrected caret) where you see the 0 features model is the best model, and adding extra features simply overfits:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/47a602d5-0f52-416f-9df3-5053ae69fbbe)

Currently, specifying `sizes = 0:200` in caret is no different than `sizes = 1:200`. Caret will always take at least 1 feature, so in this case 0 and 1 features would be the same. See [here](https://github.com/DavorJ/caret/compare/master...fixes#diff-daccc6a07442a82a603ecbe972df9b3a9546171e9195f96c5dcc7240110851ffR509-R519) for the adjustments in caret code required to make zero features models possible in RFE.
 
Hence I would either allow zero feature models like in the adjustment above, or check and throw an error if `0 %in% sizes` to point to the user that 0 features is not supported.

PS I am aware that there are metrics that might suggest that the zero features model is the best one, but RMSE, which may be an ideal metric for performance analysis in some cases, is not one of them. So I don't think that "use an other performance metric" is a valid argument for disallowing zero feature models.

```
   TwoFactor1 TwoFactor2 Linear1 Linear2 Nonlinear1 lp.false lp.true
1           1          2      10      20        100      132      42
2           1          2      10      20        100      132      42

4           1          2      10      20        100      132      42

9           1          2      10      20        100      132      42
10          1          2      10      20        100      132      42
```

For simplicity, I changed the all variables to be deterministic. The `lp` is defined as `4 * tmpData$TwoFactor1 + 4 * tmpData$TwoFactor2`, and when `linearVars > 0`:

- `lp <-  lp + tmpData[, i + 3] `; which is stored as `lp.false`
- `lp <- lp + tmpData[, i + 2]`; which is stored as `lp.true`

It should be clear, now, that `lp <-  lp + tmpData[, i + 3] ` produces results that are inconsistent with the documentation, as the correct `lp` should be `4 * 1 + 4*2 + 10 + 20 = 42` and not `4 * 1 + 4*2  + 20 + 100 = 132`

title: bug in createFolds where it fails when y is numeric but all values of y are the same
description:
- [x] Start a new R session
- [x] Install the latest version of caret: `update.packages(oldPkgs="caret", ask=FALSE)`
- [x] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [x] **Do not** use parallel processing in the code (unless you are certain that the issue is about parallel processing).
- [x] run `sessionInfo()`

### Minimal, reproducible example:

```{R}
custommethod <- 
  list(library = NULL, type = "Regression", prob = NULL,
       fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev = NULL, last, weights, classprobs, ...) {return(stats::runmed(x = y, k = param$k))},
       parameters = data.frame(parameter = "k", class = "numeric", label = "k"),
       grid = function(x, y, len, search) {return(data.frame(k = seq(from = 1, by = 2, length.out = len)))},
       predict = function(modelFit, newdata, preProc = NULL, submodels = NULL) {return(rep(NA, length(newdata)))})

library(caret)
set.seed(1)
data <- data.frame(x = 1:100, y = rep(0.05, 100))
train(x = data.frame(x = data$x), y = data$y, method = custommethod, trControl = trainControl(method = "cv"))

Error in cut.default(y, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE) : 
  invalid number of intervals
```

It appears this issue is because of this section of `createFolds`

```{R}
if(is.numeric(y)) {
      cuts <- floor(length(y)/k)
      if(cuts < 2) cuts <- 2
      if(cuts > 5) cuts <- 5
      breaks <- unique(quantile(y, probs = seq(0, 1, length = cuts)))
      y <- cut(y, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
    }
```

When `y` is numeric, but has no variation, `breaks` will be the single value of y. However, `cut` will interpret this single value not as the value where a cut should be made, but as the **number** of breaks to make. When the y value is an integer, this will likely lead to an unexpected result where the number of breaks made is the y value, rather than the value of cuts. When the y value is not an integer, this will return an error because breaks can only be an integer.

title: Improve clarity of tuneGrid error messages
description:
Let's say I want to fit a random forest model.
```{R}
library(caret)
set.seed(1)
example <- data.frame(replicate(10,sample(0:10,1000,rep=TRUE)))
```
I then decide to make a tuning grid, without going to read the documentation.

```{R}
cv <- trainControl(
  method = "repeatedcv",
  number = 10,
  repeats = 5,
  savePredictions = "final"
)

tune_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry = c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2),
  min.node.size = c(2, 4, 6),
  splitrule = c("variance", "extratrees"),
  num.trees = c(50, 100, 150, 200),
  max.depth = 1:11
)

model_class <- train(
  X1 ~ ., 
  example, 
  metric='RMSE',
  method = "ranger",
  trControl= cv,
  tuneGrid = tune_grid
)
```

If you run this, you get this error message:

```
Error: The tuning parameter grid should have columns mtry, splitrule, min.node.size
```

Now, if you see this error message, you might think to yourself "wait, don't I have mtry, splitrule, and min.node.size in my tuning parameter grid?". This is confusing. Really we want the user to see something like:

```
Error: The tuning parameter grid for a 'ranger' model should only have columns mtry, splitrule, min.node.size. 
```
Or perhaps even something like:

```
Error: The tuning parameter grid has invalid columns for the specified model type! Please refer to the documentation for your model at https://topepo.github.io/caret/available-models.html
```

title: dummyVars ignores sep argument for character variables
description:
Hey,

I spotted a potential issue with dummyVars: When a character variable (instead of a factor variable) is included in the RHS of the formula the sep argument is ignored for these variables (ie the separators between variable name and levels are not inserted).

It's a minor issue but took me some time to figure out the reason. Is this expected behaviour? If not I'm happy to invest some time into finding a fix.

Cheers

### Minimal, reproducible example:

``` r

library(earth)
library(tidyverse)
library(magrittr)
library(caret)

data(etitanic)

#  this works fine giving the correct separators between variable name and level
dummies <- dummyVars(survived ~ ., data = etitanic,sep=".")
head(predict(dummies, newdata = etitanic))
#>   pclass.1st pclass.2nd pclass.3rd sex.female sex.male     age sibsp parch
#> 1          1          0          0          1        0 29.0000     0     0
#> 2          1          0          0          0        1  0.9167     1     2
#> 3          1          0          0          1        0  2.0000     1     2
#> 4          1          0          0          0        1 30.0000     1     2
#> 5          1          0          0          1        0 25.0000     1     2
#> 6          1          0          0          0        1 48.0000     0     0

#  after converting a variable to character dummyVars fails to insert the separator character
etitanic %<>% mutate(pclass = as.character(pclass))
dummies <- dummyVars(survived ~ ., data = etitanic,sep=".")
head(predict(dummies, newdata = etitanic))
#>   pclass1st pclass2nd pclass3rd sex.female sex.male     age sibsp parch
#> 1         1         0         0          1        0 29.0000     0     0
#> 2         1         0         0          0        1  0.9167     1     2
#> 3         1         0         0          1        0  2.0000     1     2

title: [Feature Request]: Progress Bar...
description:
Except for some particular models ( `ranger` or `randomForest` among others) it is quite difficult to know in which step of the processing is function `train()`. Most of the time, one is completely blind about how far is the model to finish. Even when parameter `verboseIter = TRUE`

For those models that can verbose its status, it happens when most of the process finished, when `train()` collects the results from the different samplings.

This feature is already available in `H2O`, and although it is in text format, it is quite informative about giving a clear indication of where the process is.

There are some packages in `R` already available for this, although I do not know if they are the adequate for `caret` structure:
- https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/progress/
- http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/r.utils/docs/ProgressBar

Thanks,
Carlos.

title: In silico Negative Control Testing Results in AUCs Significantly Less than 0.5
description: I have a question that is likely not a bug, but perhaps a technical feature of cross-validation by caret. In the minimal example below, I demonstrate (using mtcars) that identical data submitted with two different labels (A,B) in a single dataframe results in Cross-Validated Model Scores that are substantially higher in the Control label (A) compared to the Case Label (B). I had hoped that for this negative control experiment that the AUC would approximately be 0.5. Is there a reason for this behavior? This bias toward AUC < 0.5 is observed when using other approaches such as logistic regression. It is also observed when randomizing the input data to training and when significantly adding identical data to the negative control dataset. It is also observed when using `loocv` or `boot`. Adding a small amount of noise to the data does not change the outcome much either. However, adding a small signal to distinguish B from A correctly generate AUCs above > 0.5, and CV Scores with appropriate directionality. The results make me think that there is some type of tie mechanism in place in the absence of signal to choose the Control label (A). Thank you for your time. ### Minimal, reproducible example: #### Minimal dataset: ```{R} library(caret) library(pROC) library(randomForest) set.seed(12345) # ---- # input ml data is mtcars repeated exactly twice # and given A and B labels for CV training mlInputData = rbind(mtcars,mtcars) mlInputData$varOfInterest = c(rep("A",nrow(mtcars)), rep("B",nrow(mtcars))) ``` #### Minimal, runnable code: ```{R} trainControlSettings <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 5, verboseIter = FALSE, savePredictions = TRUE, classProbs = TRUE, summaryFunction = twoClassSummary, allowParallel = FALSE) thisMLTrainedModel <- train(varOfInterest ~ ., data = mlInputData, method = "rf", metric = "ROC", trControl = trainControlSettings, tuneGrid = expand.grid(.mtry=floor(sqrt(ncol(mlInputData)-1))), importance = TRUE, trace = FALSE) # plot 1 cvScoresPlots <- ggplot(thisMLTrainedModel$pred, aes(x=obs, y=B)) + geom_boxplot(aes(color=obs), alpha=0.8) + geom_point(aes(color=obs), alpha=0.65) + xlab("True Status") + ylab("Model Score [Predicting B Status]") # plot 2 rocOutput <- roc(obs ~ B, data = thisMLTrainedModel$pred, ci = TRUE, direction = "<", plot=TRUE, boot.n=100, ci.alpha=0.6, stratified=FALSE, auc.polygon=FALSE, print.auc=TRUE) sens.ci <- ci.se(rocOutput, specificities=seq(0, 1, .01)) plot(sens.ci, type="shape", col="lightblue") ``` Plot 1: ![plot1](https://github.com/topepo/caret/assets/143096549/0303f189-7a4e-470a-89d5-0a8069da6ca1) Plot 2: ``` sessionInfo() R version 4.1.1 (2021-08-10) Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin17.0 (64-bit) Running under: macOS Monterey 12.0.1 Matrix products: default BLAS: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.1/Resources/lib/libRblas.0.dylib LAPACK: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.1/Resources/lib/libRlapack.dylib locale: [1] en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8 attached base packages: [1] stats graphics grDevices utils datasets methods base other attached packages: [1] randomForest_4.7-1 pROC_1.18.0 caret_6.0-90 lattice_0.20-45 ggplot2_3.3.6 ```

description:
Hi,

I've encountered the "Something is wrong; all the Accuracy metric values are missing:" error when one of my columns is a factor. However, the help function did not specify any limitation for the data structure. I think I managed to get around it, but I just wanted to understand if the "workaround" is not changing the data analysis by any means.

Here is a toy data set:
```{R}
library(caret)

set.seed(2023)
x_train <- data.frame(feat1 = rnorm(80, 0, 2),
                      feat2 = rnorm(80, 0, 2),
                      feat3 = rnorm(80, 0, 2),
                      feat4 = rnorm(80, 0, 2),
                      feat5 = rnorm(80, 0, 2),
                      Male = factor(rbinom(n = 80, size = 1, prob = 0.5)))

set.seed(123)
y_target <- factor(rbinom(n = 80, size = 1, prob = 0.5))

```

If I run the train function using x_train and y_target as inputs, I get the error:
```
elaNet_model <- caret::train(x_train, y_target, method = "glmnet")

Something is wrong; all the Accuracy metric values are missing:

Error: Stopping
In addition: There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50)
```

However, I saw somewhere else that using the formula input could solve the problem, so I tested it:
```
test_df <- cbind(y_target, x_train)

elaNet_model <- caret::train(y_target ~.,
                             data = test_df,
                             method = "glmnet")
```

Indeed no error message is displayed, and I get the full model. The factor feature is still a factor:

```

I am testing a bunch of models, and I see the same pattern with "xgbTree", "svmLinear", "svmRadial", and "nb".

Therefore, it seems to me that at some point, Caret is changing the data structure when using the formula input. Is it the case? Or does it simply mean that Caret can only handle factors properly when using the formula input?

title: test "Good names for dummies with reocurring patterns" fails sometimes
GLMNET predict when test data features are in different order
description:
# The problem
Other issues in caret (https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/968) have highlighted how predict()with glmnet models requires all features in the training to be present in the testing data for prediction. However, I have noticed decreased performance on models trained with a change of the order of the training features. The training and testing data is from the same larger dataset, but feature selection that changed the order of the training features was performed on the training data before a glmnet model was trained. I imagine we see this because glmnet selects by column number, not column name? As such, I imagine it is a requirement for features in the testing data to be a similar order of the training data features when using glmnet in caret?

It seems that similar issues identified in tidymodels (https://github.com/tidymodels/parsnip/issues/273) and glmnet (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/18420586/can-i-do-predict-glmnet-on-test-data-with-different-number-of-predictor-variable) have answered my questions. This issue has been rectified in tidymodels and should be rectified in caret as it is still a popular method for ML in R.

# Reproducible example
```# training data
library(caret)
set.seed(1)
dat <- twoClassSim(100, noiseVars = 5)

# feature selection that changes order of training features
set.seed(1)
featureSelection <- sample(1:ncol(dat)-1, 10)
X <- dat[,featureSelection]
y <- dat[["Class"]]

# fit glmnet model
set.seed(1)
glm_fit <- train(
  X, y, 
  metric='ROC',
  method = 'glmnet',
  preProcess =  c("center", "scale"),
  trControl=trainControl(
    method="cv", 
    number=5,
    classProbs=TRUE, 
    summaryFunction=twoClassSummary,
    savePredictions="final")
)

# predictions with the full original dataset
table(predict(glm_fit, dat) == y) # FALSE 44 TRUE 56

# predictions with feature selection applied to the full original dataset
table(predict(glm_fit, dat[,featureSelection]) == y) # FALSE 28 TRUE 72

# predictions when feature selection applied but in a different order
table(predict(glm_fit, dat[,sort(featureSelection)]) == y) # FALSE 44 TRUE 56

# feature selection in a similar order of the training features
X <- dat[,sort(featureSelection)]

# fit glmnet model
set.seed(1)
glm_fit <- train(
  X, y, 
  metric='ROC',
  method = 'glmnet',
  preProcess =  c("center", "scale"),
  trControl=trainControl(
    method="cv", 
    number=5,
    classProbs=TRUE, 
    summaryFunction=twoClassSummary,
    savePredictions="final")
)

# predictions with the full original dataset
table(predict(glm_fit, dat) == y) # FALSE 28 TRUE 72

# predictions with feature selection applied to the full original dataset
table(predict(glm_fit, dat[,featureSelection]) == y) # FALSE 28 TRUE 72

# predictions when feature selection applied but in a different order
table(predict(glm_fit, dat[,sort(featureSelection)]) == y) # FALSE 28 TRUE 72

title: Imputing mixed numeric/categorical data within train preProc?
description:
Is it possible to impute mixed numeric/categorical data within `train`'s `preProc` argument?  I want to impute within `train`'s cross validation, thereby accounting for how uncertainty in imputations affects estimation of generalization error.

The `?preProcess` help page suggests it is not possible to impute categorical variables:

> x : a matrix or data frame. Non-numeric predictors are allowed but will be ignored.

However, the `bagImpute` method can handle mixed data, in theory.  The following code runs, but I am not sure if it is actually imputing the missing factor or simply removing patients with missing factor values:

``` r
library(caret);
#> Loading required package: ggplot2

nrow(iris);

    Sepal.Length ~ .,

title: rqPen changes in version 3.1.x - `rqPen::rq.lasso.fit()` and `rqPen::rq.nc.fit()` should be `rqPen::rq.pen()`
description:
Error sources:

- [https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/5f4bd2069bf486ae92240979f9d65b5c138ca8d4/models/files/rqlasso.R#L17](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/5f4bd2069bf486ae92240979f9d65b5c138ca8d4/models/files/rqlasso.R#L17)
- [https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/5f4bd2069bf486ae92240979f9d65b5c138ca8d4/models/files/rqnc.R#L19](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/5f4bd2069bf486ae92240979f9d65b5c138ca8d4/models/files/rqnc.R#L19)

Error description: 

The current `fit` functions for models using the `rqPen` package ("rqlasso" and "rqnc" are using the `rqPen` 3.0 fitting method:

```{r}
# From rqlasso.R
fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
  rqPen::rq.lasso.fit(as.matrix(x), y, lambda = param$lambda, ...)
}
```

```{r}
# From rqnc.R
fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
  rqPen::rq.nc.fit(as.matrix(x), y,
                          lambda = param$lambda,
                          penalty = as.character(param$penalty), ...)
}
```

[(From `rqPen` NEWS, 2023-02-20)](https://github.com/cran/rqPen/blob/2205062cef07bfa201fd678de3015be42662ecfa/NEWS#L23):
Older functions that were deprecated in `rqPen` 3.0 are no longer exported. Big changes are `rq.pen()` should be used instead of `rq.lasso.fit()` or `rq.nc.fit()`. Similarly `rq.group.pen()` should be used instead of `rq.group.fit()`. Finally `rq.pen.cv()` and `rq.group.pen.cv()` should be used instead of `cv.rq.pen()` and `cv.rq.group.pen()`.

Reproducible Example:

```{r}

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility

# Create data
n <- 100 # number of observations
p <- 5 # number of predictors

# Generate predictors
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p)
colnames(X) <- paste0("X", 1:p)

# Generate response variable
beta <- rnorm(p)
y <- X %*% beta + rnorm(n)

# Combine predictors and response into a data.frame
df <- data.frame(y = y, X)

# Fit using quantile regression with LASSO regularization 
fit <- caret::train(
    y ~ ., 
    data = df, 
    method = "rqlasso", # Also "rqnc", which also uses `rqPen::rq.pen`
    trControl = caret::trainControl(method="cv", number=5),
    preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
    metric = "RMSE"
)

## 1: `rq.lasso.fit()` was deprecated in rqPen 3.0.
## ℹ Please use `rq.pen()` instead.

```

}
```

title: confusionMatrix: Precision == Positive Predictive Value and Recall == Sensitivity
description:
Hi, thanks for the great work on this package!

I noticed that the `confusionMatrix()` returns the Precision and the Positive Predictive Value, these are actually the same (and should be). Same goes for the Recall and the Sensitivity (True Positive Rate), those are identical as well. So I guess those values could be removed from the calculation.

On the other hand, I would like some additional derivations that are mentioned here: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confusion_matrix>, like the False Negative Rate (FNR), the False Positive Rate (FPR), the False Discovery Rate (FDR) and the False Omission Rate (FOR). Could that be easily added? I could create a PR if you like.

title: Add ability to optimize probability thresholds for class imbalances without having to create a custom model
description:
I am interested in binary classification on an extremely unbalanced dataset. As is often the case with such data, the default probability threshold of 0.5 is inappropriate, and results in a lack of sensitivity to predict the rarer class.
I was pleased to see that this issue has been addressed through the use of custom models as described here: http://topepo.github.io/caret/custom_models.html#Illustration5
However, I have not been able to get this method working with the method I'd like to use (gbm), no doubt due to my lack of programming ability. I have seen questions on StackOverflow suggesting that other caret users have been having similar difficulties. 

Would it then be possible to include functionality in caret making it easier for the user to optimize the probability threshold, without having to create a custom model?

Thanks.

train, preProcess
**Bug**? Categorical variables preprocessed differently inside train vs. outside train.
**Bug**? Does not preprocess inside train despite saying it does.
**Enhancement**: Make preProcess transform response inside train
Thanks for caret and tidy models!

``` r
library(caret)
#> Loading required package: ggplot2
#> Loading required package: lattice

df <- mtcars[c("mpg", "wt", "am")]
# Change am to factor ("0" or "1")
df$am <- factor(df$am)
df[c(1, 4), ]

# preProcess only transforms predictors inside train, not response.

preProcValues <- caret::preProcess(df[c("wt", "am")], method = c("center", "scale"))

title: Calculation of Optimism-Corrected Performance
description:
I am currently working on the topic "Calculation of Optimism-Corrected Performance". Caret provides this function via trainControl(method="optimism_boot"). I took the liberty to have a look at the code. In doing so, I noticed the following here:

caret/R/workflows.R
line 316
final_estimate <- out[ , paste0(perfName, "Apparent")] + optimism

That should be:
final_estimate <- out[ , paste0(perfName, "Apparent")] - optimism

Excerpt from the book "Clinical Prediction Models" by Ewout Steyerberg, page 107, chapter 5.3.4 "Calculation of Optimism-Corrected Performance".

ptimism-corrected performance is calculated as
Optimism-corrected performance = Apparent performance in original sample **-** Optimism;
where
Optimism = Bootstrap performance  **-**  Test performance:

Or?

title: Heldout predictions are different
description: Hello, I am training a regression model with ridge regression and self-defined samples. The same heldout data are used twice, so each model is outputting the predictions for each data twice. I would expect that the predictions obtained for the same heldout data to be the same, yet they are slightly different. Below you have a screenshoot, where the same rowIndex refer to the same heldout data, and the corresponding predictions. In the manual, I found the following: > "For particular model, a grid of parameters (if any) is created and the model is trained on **slightly different data** for each candidate combination of tuning parameters. " I suspect that the observed slightly different predictions may be related to this. My question here is do you modify the data before training/prediction? If so, what is the purpose?

title: custom holdout indexes: train reports wrong samples, calculations are fine
description:
When specifying the holdout samples `indexOut` for cross-validation myself, the `index` values reported in the train object are wrong. They are are created as if `indexOut` was not provided at all.

``` r
library(caret)
data <- data.frame(response = c("a","b"), x = rnorm(10), y = rnorm(10))
out  <- list(c(1:4), c(5:10))
set.seed(1)
m <- train(response~.,data = data, trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 2, indexOut = out, savePredictions = "final"))
m$control$index      # --> wrong, should be 5:10 and 1:4 respectively
#> $Fold1
#> [1]  1  2  5  8 10
#> 
#> $Fold2
#> [1] 3 4 6 7 9

m$control$indexOut  # --> is correct
#> $Resample1
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
#> 
#> $Resample2
#> [1]  5  6  7  8  9 10
```

title: Timeslice with longitudinal data
description:

I originally have a balanced panel data set with 22 years and 37,442 unique cross-sectional observations. Here is an example data set to exemplify the structure of the data

```
dat <- data.frame( id = sort( rep( c( "A", "B", "C" ), 22 )), 
                    t = rep( 2000:2021, 3 ), 
                    y = round( runif( 66, 10, 200 ), 0 ), 
                   x1 = rnorm( 66 ), 
                   x2 = rbinom( 66, 3, 0.3 ))
```
I tried to use 'train' to run a simple random forest model on the data with a fixed time window of 5 years and a horizon of 2 years:

```
library( caret )
library( ranger )

model <- train( 
             y ~ ., 
             tuneLength = 5, 
             data = dat, 
             method = "ranger", 
             trControl = trainControl(

                              allowParallel = TRUE,

title: Why caret train function always return one .outcome when the model can have more than one dependent variable?
description:
This is something very tricky and is related with other questions I did in StackOverflow ([1][1], [2][2], [3][3]). The data to use is in [1][1].

Basically, I am comparing two neural network trainings:

1. One using directly the function `neuralnet()` from the `neuralnet` package.
2. One using the function `train()` from the `caret` package, and including `method = "neuralnet"`.

#### The same formula in both models

In both cases, in the arguments to introduce the formula:

* `f <- as.formula(paste("DC1 + DC2 + DC3 ~", paste(n[!n %in% c("DC1","DC2","DC3")], collapse = " + ")))`

If we see its structure, you can see that there are three DEPENDENT VARIABLES (`DC1`, `DC2`, `DC3`)

```
str(f)
Class 'formula'  language DC1 + DC2 + DC3 ~ DC4 + DC5 + DC6 + DC7 + DC8 + DC9 + DC10
  ..- attr(*, ".Environment")=<environment: R_GlobalEnv> 
```

## Using `neuralnet()` (neuralnet)

This is the code

```
BestModel <- neuralnet(formula = f, 
                 data = train_df,  # available in one of the links above
                 hidden = c(3,2,4) # random neurons per layer     
                 learningrate = 0.01, 
                 threshold = 0.01,   
                 stepmax = 50000       
                 
)
```
## Using `train()` (caret)

This is the code (all the parameters are available in [this question][1]):

```
model <- train(f, data = predict(pre_mdl_df, train_df), 
               method = "neuralnet", 
               tuneGrid = tune.grid.neuralnet,
               metric = "RMSE",
               stepmax = 100000,
               learningrate = 0.01,  
               threshold = 0.01,
               act.fct = softplus,
               trControl = caret::trainControl (
                 method = "repeatedcv", 
                 number = 2,               # Number of folds of the cv
                 repeats = 1,              # Number of cv repetitions
                 verboseIter = TRUE,
                 savePredictions = TRUE,
                 allowParallel = TRUE))
```

Here, we store as `finalModel` the final and best model obtained in the training:

```
finalModel <- model$finalModel
```

## Comparison of the outputs from `neuralnet()` and `train()`

#### Different structures

* `neuralnet()`: `str(BestModel)` is a List of 14.
* `train()`: `str(FinalModel)` is a List of 19

#### Different responses:

As you can see, the response from `neuralnet()` is having `chr [1:3] "DC1" "DC2" "DC3"`, whereas from `train()` has `chr ".outcome"`. I guess this will impact the results later, because the prediction will return different quantity of results.

```
# neuralnet()
str(BestModel$response)
 num [1:26, 1:3] 4 5 6 8 11 11 11 6 8 5 ...
 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  ..$ : chr [1:26] "165" "167" "168" "172" ...
  ..$ : chr [1:3] "DC1" "DC2" "DC3"

# train()
str(finalModel$response)
 num [1:26, 1] 0.83 0.509 1.199 1.353 1.55 ...
 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  ..$ : chr [1:26] "X165" "X167" "X168" "X172" ...
  ..$ : chr ".outcome"
```

#### Different model lists

```
# neuralnet()
str(BestModel$model.list)
List of 2
 $ response : chr [1:3] "DC1" "DC2" "DC3"
 $ variables: chr [1:7] "DC4" "DC5" "DC6" "DC7" ...

# train()
str(finalModel$model.list)
List of 2
 $ response : chr ".outcome"
 $ variables: chr [1:7] "DC4" "DC5" "DC6" "DC7" ...
```

#### Different plots

* From `neuralnet()`: as expected, with three outputs representing the three dependent variables (`DC1`, `DC2`, `DC3`).

[![enter image description here][4]][4]

* From `train()`: only one output, `.outcome`.

[![enter image description here][5]][5]

#### Different prediction variables

I expect to predict the three variables simultaneously, as it happens with `neuralnet()` but not with `train()`, that returns only one.

```
# neuralnet()
head(predict(BestModel, train_df))
        [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
165 9.384303 10.38448 10.07678
167 9.384303 10.38448 10.07678
168 9.384303 10.38448 10.07678
172 9.384303 10.38448 10.07678
174 9.384303 10.38448 10.07678
176 9.384303 10.38448 10.07678

# train()
head(predict(finalModel, train_df))
         [,1]
165 0.8641611
167 1.3874627
168 0.8641579
172 1.1318320
174 0.8639903
176 1.7193986
```

## Key questions

After comparing both models, which were supposed to behave similarly, several questions come to my mind:

* How can I make `train()` to work similarly as `neuralnet()`? This includes the plots and predictions.
* Is there any way to modify the code from `train()`?
* Is there a bug in `train()`?
* How can I change `.outcome` to have the three dependent variables?

Please, I need help!

  [1]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74869752/questions-regarding-saving-loading-carettrain-models-using-neuralnet-package
  [2]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74876146/predict-multiple-dependent-variables-in-r-linear-model-as-example
  [3]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74878552/predict-multiple-dependent-variables-in-a-neural-network-in-r-caret-train-neu
  [4]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/4CjoT.png
  [5]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/BK2W3.png

description:
## Generate test data

```
library(mgcv, quietly = TRUE)
library(caret, quietly = TRUE)
dat <- gamSim(3, n=400, scale=2, verbose=FALSE)
head(dat)

## 5 -0.9480075 0.20614605 0.012163713 0.015923858
## 6  1.6789991 0.52966272 0.014891997 0.028424794
```
## Create custom `modelInfo` from gam.R

Goal is to fit: `y ~ s(x1) + s(x2, by = f)`

```
modelInfo <- list(label = "Generalized Additive Model using Splines",
                  library = "mgcv",
                  loop = NULL,
                  type = c('Regression', 'Classification'),
                  parameters = data.frame(parameter = c('select', 'method'),
                                          class = c('logical', 'character'),
                                          label = c('Feature Selection', 'Method')),
                  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
                    if(search == "grid") {
                      out <- expand.grid(select = c(TRUE, FALSE), method = "GCV.Cp")
                    } else {
                      out <- data.frame(select = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = len, replace = TRUE),
                                        method = sample(c("GCV.Cp", "ML"), size = len, replace = TRUE))
                    }
                    out[!duplicated(out),]
                  },
                  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) { 
                    dat <- if(is.data.frame(x)) x else as.data.frame(x)

                    ## Ignored original code
                    #modForm <- caret:::smootherFormula(x)
                    #if(is.factor(y)) {
                    #  dat$.outcome <- ifelse(y == lev[1], 0, 1)
                    #  dist <- binomial()
                    #} else {
                    #  dat$.outcome <- y
                    #  dist <- gaussian()
                    #}

                    ## New code
                    modForm <- y ~ s(x1) + s(x2, by = f)
                    dist <- gaussian()

                    ## Resume original code
                    modelArgs <- list(formula = modForm,
                                      data = dat,
                                      select = param$select, 
                                      method = as.character(param$method))
                    ## Intercept family if passed in
                    theDots <- list(...)
                    if(!any(names(theDots) == "family")) modelArgs$family <- dist
                    modelArgs <- c(modelArgs, theDots)

                    out <- do.call(getFromNamespace("gam", "mgcv"), modelArgs)
                    out

                  },
                  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
                    if(!is.data.frame(newdata)) newdata <- as.data.frame(newdata)
                    if(modelFit$problemType == "Classification") {
                      probs <-  predict(modelFit, newdata, type = "response")
                      out <- ifelse(probs < .5,
                                    modelFit$obsLevel[1],
                                    modelFit$obsLevel[2])
                    } else {
                      out <- predict(modelFit, newdata, type = "response")
                    }
                    out
                  },
                  prob = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL){
                    if(!is.data.frame(newdata)) newdata <- as.data.frame(newdata)
                    out <- predict(modelFit, newdata, type = "response")
                    out <- cbind(1-out, out)
                    ## glm models the second factor level, we treat the first as the
                    ## event of interest. See Details in ?glm
                    colnames(out) <-  modelFit$obsLevels
                    out
                  },
                  predictors = function(x, ...) {
                    predictors(x$terms)
                  },
                  levels = function(x) x$obsLevels,
                  varImp = function(object, ...) {
                    smoothed <- summary(object)$s.table[, "p-value", drop = FALSE]
                    linear <- summary(object)$p.table
                    linear <- linear[, grepl("^Pr", colnames(linear)), drop = FALSE] 
                    gams <- rbind(smoothed, linear)
                    gams <- gams[rownames(gams) != "(Intercept)",,drop = FALSE]
                    rownames(gams) <- gsub("^s\\(", "", rownames(gams))
                    rownames(gams) <- gsub("\\)$", "", rownames(gams))
                    colnames(gams)[1] <- "Overall"
                    gams <- as.data.frame(gams)
                    gams$Overall <- -log10(gams$Overall)
                    allPreds <- colnames(attr(object$terms,"factors"))
                    extras <- allPreds[!(allPreds %in% rownames(gams))]
                    if(any(extras)) {
                      tmp <- data.frame(Overall = rep(NA, length(extras)))
                      rownames(tmp) <- extras
                      gams <- rbind(gams, tmp)
                    }
                    gams
                  },
                  notes = "Which terms enter the model in a nonlinear manner is determined by the number of unique values for the predictor. For example, if a predictor only has four unique values, most basis expansion method will fail because there are not enough granularity in the data. By default, a predictor must have at least 10 unique values to be used in a nonlinear basis expansion.",
                  tags = c("Generalized Linear Model", "Generalized Additive Model"),
                  sort = function(x) x)
```

title: feature request: support for classprobs with bstSm
description:
The method `bstSm` does not appear to support classProbs=TRUE. I'm requesting that the method support probability predictions. Here's a reprex that shows the error when class probabilities are requested for `bstSm`.

```r
library(caret)

## data

set.seed(1)

x <- rnorm(1000)

z <- -2 + 2*x + rnorm(1000)

y <- rbinom(1000, 1, boot::inv.logit(z))

df <- data.frame(y=y, x=x)

summary(df)

## response

df$label <- factor(ifelse(df$y == 1, "yes", "no"),
                   levels=c("yes","no"))

summary(df)

## control

fcstHorizon <- 100
initWindow <- 800
param_skip <- fcstHorizon - 1

fitControl_oneSE <- trainControl(method = "timeslice",
                                 initialWindow=initWindow,
                                 horizon=fcstHorizon,
                                 fixedWindow=FALSE,
                                 skip=param_skip,
                                 ## Estimate class probabilities
                                 classProbs = TRUE,
                                 ## Evaluate performance using 
                                 ## the following function
                                 summaryFunction = mnLogLoss,
                                 selectionFunction="oneSE")

## gamboost

set.seed(1)

gam_mod <- train(
  label ~ x,
  data = df,
  method = "gamboost",
  trControl = fitControl_oneSE,
  metric = "logLoss",
  dfbase =3
)

plot(gam_mod)

## bstSm (errors out)

set.seed(1)

bst_mod <- train(
  label ~ x,
  data = df,
  method = "bstSm",
  trControl = fitControl_oneSE,
  metric = "logLoss"
)

plot(bst_mod)

```
