title: [Feature?] leapSeq intercept tuning
description:
It is currently impossible to create a model without intercept for various linear regression models. I noticed this (for example) for lmStepAIC, leapSeq, leapForward, leapBackward. I have managed to create my own modelInfo for leapSeq that works (?) (shown below, it's the same as the generic one but with intercept/int set to F), but it would be nice if this could be done in a better way. 

No hurry, just an idea!

```
modelInfo <- list(label = "Linear Regression with Stepwise Selection",
                  library = "leaps",
                  type = "Regression",
                  parameters = data.frame(parameter = 'nvmax',
                                          class = "numeric",
                                          label = 'Maximum Number of Predictors'),
                  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid"){
                    if(search == "grid") {
                      out <- data.frame(nvmax = 2:(len+1))
                    } else {
                      out <- data.frame(nvmax = sort(unique(sample(2:(ncol(x) - 1), size = len, replace = TRUE))))
                    }
                    out
                  },
                  loop = function(grid) {   
                    grid <- grid[order(grid$nvmax, decreasing = TRUE),, drop = FALSE]
                    loop <- grid[1,,drop = FALSE]
                    submodels <- list(grid[-1,,drop = FALSE])
                    list(loop = loop, submodels = submodels)
                  },
                  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {   
                    theDots <- list(...)
                    if(any(names(theDots) == "nbest")) stop("'nbest' should not be specified")
                    if(any(names(theDots) == "method")) stop("'method' should not be specified")
                    if(any(names(theDots) == "nvmax")) stop("'nvmax' should not be specified")
                    
                    leaps::regsubsets(as.matrix(x), y,
                                      weights = if(!is.null(wts)) wts else rep(1, length(y)),
                                      nbest = 1, nvmax = param$nvmax, method = "seqrep", 
                                      intercept = F,
                                      int = F, ...)
                  },
                  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
                    newdata <- as.matrix(newdata)
                    foo <- function(b, x) x[,names(b),drop = FALSE] %*% b
                    
                    path <- 1:(modelFit$nvmax - 1)
                    betas <- coef(modelFit, id = 1:(modelFit$nvmax - 1))
                    
                    newdata <- cbind(rep(1, nrow(newdata)), as.matrix(newdata))
                    colnames(newdata)[1] <- "(Intercept)"
                    
                    out <- foo(betas[[length(betas)]], newdata)[,1]
                    
                    if(!is.null(submodels))
                    {
                      numTerms <- unlist(lapply(betas, length))
                      if(any(names(betas[[length(betas)]]) == "(Intercept)")) numTerms <- numTerms - 1
                      ## Need to find the elements of betas that 
                      ## correspond to the values of submodels$nvmax
                      
                      keepers <- which(numTerms %in% submodels$nvmax)
                      if(length(keepers) != length(submodels$nvmax))
                        stop("Some values of 'nvmax' are not in the model sequence.")
                      
                      ## The grid code sorted from largest to smallest, so 
                      ## to match them, reverse the order
                      keepers <- rev(keepers)
                      preds <- lapply(betas[keepers], foo, x= newdata)
                      preds <- do.call("cbind", preds)
                      
                      out <- as.data.frame(cbind(out, preds))
                      out <- as.list(out)
                    }
                    
                    out
                  },
                  tags = c("Linear Regression", "Feature Selection Wrapper"),
                  prob = NULL,
                  sort = function(x) x[order(x[,1]),])
```

title: Use of internal functions and foreach
description:
So, this is really more of an FYI and a probably bug in foreach.

Several caret functions call  non-namespace exported functions within the body of foreach expressions, see for instance `nominalTrainWorkflow` https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/master/pkg/caret/R/workflows.R#L86 and elsewhere.  Unfortunately, foreach currently does not automatically discover the namespace context of these internal function calls and fails.

Currently, foreach resolves required symbols with a function called `getexports`, which itself in turn optionally relies on the `getGlobalsAndPackages` function from the futures package.  That approach does a nice job of exporting objects in the calling environment to the foreach workers, but fails to identify package namespace objects.  This is just the situation in caret.

Consider the following `example.r` file:


```{r}
library(doMPI)
library(caret)
cl = startMPIcluster()
registerDoMPI(cl)
data(BloodBrain)
ans = train(bbbDescr, logBBB, "knn", trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", verboseIter=TRUE))
closeCluster(cl)
mpi.quit()
```
invoked with

```
mpirun -np 3 R --slave -f example.r
```

This fails with the error
```
task 2 failed - "object 'requireNamespaceQuietStop' not found"
```

It seems that many of the changes to the `workflows.R` file attempted to deal with this deficiency in foreach in one form or another. In my opinion, this is ultimately a weakness of foreach and the long-term solution lies there (in the `getexports` function).

But in the short term, one possible fix for this is to change, for example, line https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/master/pkg/caret/R/workflows.R#L57 from `loadNamespace("caret")` to something like
`attach(environment(caret::train))`.

Making that change fixes the above example. Prudence advises making this change in every incantation of foreach (parallel) within caret.

Again, this is just a suggestion. Long-term I think the right approach is to fix foreach, which I will try to do!

title: add noise variable var to tunable parameters for kernlab's gaussianpr
description:
Hi,

I'm using caret with kernlab's gaussianpr using a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel (in caret, method = 'gaussprRadial'). The only tuning parameter available is sigma, which controls the bandwidth of the RBF kernel. Would it be possible to add var as another tuning parameters? See the documentation for gausspr in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kernlab/kernlab.pdf. 

The parameter var controls the noise level in the likelihood, and it is equivalent to the regularization strength. It appears that it is very important to be able to tune not just the rbf kernel, but also the regularization strength. Currently I have to write an outer loop to tune this parameter, and it's quite messy and painful.

Could we please add var as another tuning parameter for gaussprRadial?

Thanks!

title: Adapt train for survival models
description:
Some things that would have to change:
- `train` has a component called `modelType` that is currently either "Regression" or "Classification". Another option, "Survivial" would need to be added and a search should be made for any error traps or checks on this value.
- `is.Surv` should be added to make sure the outcome is correct
- Documentation will need to be added
- Test cases for specific models
- New models based on this change that should be considered: [superpc](http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/superpc/index.html) (add this model type), [randomForestSRC](http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/randomForestSRC/index.html), [bujar](http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bujar/index.html), [randomSurvivalForest](http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/randomSurvivalForest/index.html) and probably others

description:
I noticed that the results in my models obtained from caret:train , as in

fitCtrl<-trainControl(method='repeatedcv',num=10,repeats=5,savePredictions=TRUE,classProbs=TRUE,summaryFunction=BalAc)
model<-train(Y~.,data=data1,metric='OptBalAcc',method='qda',trControl=fitCtrl)
model$results

are much more optimistic than what I get from

confusionMatrix(model$pred$pred,model$pred$obs)

, where I had expected these to be the same. Or at least for the latter (which I thought were the predictions made by the best model when it is applied again to all of the folds together?) to be at least as good as the former (which I thought is the mean of the holdout performances for each fold/repeat and thus a little less subject to overfitting due to being held out each time when the fit takes place?)

So I'm trying to understand how its possible that Confusionmatrix is always the more pessimistic one, when it is just the training error made when the same best model is used to predict all the data? Or is this not the case? Thanks

title: Breaking Backward Compatibility
description:
Not an issue but a running list of things that we might change in a single release that would break backward compatibility (which I have almost always avoided). 

Suggestions and comments are welcome...
- change how `preProcess` options are passed from `train` (via the `preProcess` argument to `train` as opposed to being in `trainControl`)
- move `metric` argument in `sbf`, `rfe` and other feature selection routines to their control objects
- add a parameter range module to each model. Right now this is baked into the `grid` module
- move function modules out of list and into an environment? 
- pass `...` to the `grid` function
- refactor options in control to lists of arguments? For example, for resampling there are options 

``` r
trainControl(method, number, repeats, p, initialWindow, horizon, fixedWindow, ...)
```

It might be cleaner to change this to something like:

``` r
trainControl(resample = list(method, number, repeats, p, initialWindow, horizon, fixedWindow))
```

Overall, it would like like:

``` r
trainControl(resample = list(method = "boot", 
                             number = ifelse(grepl("cv", method), 10, 25),
                             repeats = ifelse(grepl("cv", method), 1, number), 
                             p = 0.75, 
                             initialWindow = NULL,
                             horizon = 1,
                             fixedWindow = TRUE, 
                             verboseIter = FALSE, 
                             returnData = TRUE),
             search = "grid",
             returnResamp = "final", 
             savePredictions = FALSE, 
             classProbs = FALSE,
             functions = list(summary= defaultSummary, 
                              selection = "best"),
             preProcOptions = list(thresh = 0.95, 
                                   ICAcomp = 3, 
                                   k = 5), 
             sampling = NULL,
             index = list(model = NULL, holdout = NULL, final = NULL), 
             timingSamps = 0,
             predictionBounds = rep(FALSE, 2), 
             seeds = NA, 
             adaptive = list(min = 5,
                             alpha = 0.05, 
                             method = "gls",
```

title: mixed models toys for lme4 model inclusion
description:
It would be great if caret could handle mixed models, given the importance at times of modeling observation groups and/or to determine if partial pooling would benefit a model. 

To help this happen, I've created two toy data sets, both based on the high-scoring 1998 season in baseball.  Both are designed to be used with the widely-accepted "lme4" package, although they should work with any mixed-modeling package. These data sets use "batter" and "pitcher" as random effects, although the same approach could be used with observation groups, cities, schools, etc.  So, I feel these are representative and useful.

The first data set is designed for a linear mixed model with crossed and unbalanced random effects.  It contains two acceptable fixed effects: one categorical (stadium) and one continuous (game time temperature, a/k/a "temp_log"); and two categorical random effects (batter and pitcher).  The output, "lwts", is continuous, and refers to the average linear weight of each batting event (a single, a home run, an out, etc.)

The recommended model specification, under the package lme4, is:
lmer(lwts ~ stadium + temp_log + (1|batter) + (1|pitcher))

The second data set is similar except it has a binomial output and thus is a generalized linear mixed model.  To provide the binomial output, this data set focuses on home runs, with "1" being a home run and "0" being a plate appearance with some other outcome.  The recommended specification is:

glmer(HR ~ stadium + temp_log + (1|batter) + (1|pitcher), family=binomial(link='probit'), nAGQ=0).

The standard logit link works fine as well, but in my opinion, the probit link tends to be a better choice for generalized mixed models.  I would suggest supporting both.  

Both toys are in a Zip file entitled "mixed.model.toys.zip" and can be found here: http://1drv.ms/1PdmxDN 

Both data sets are also large, ~ 180k observations.  For ease of modeling, a random subset of half or even less of each file would probably be sufficient.

For those interested, the data sets and models are an outgrowth of our mixed model work at Baseball Prospectus on catcher framing (http://www.baseballprospectus.com/article.php?articleid=25514) and pitcher modeling (http://www.baseballprospectus.com/article.php?articleid=26195).

title: How to create data partitions using multiple categorical and numerical columns?
description:
My problem is that I'd like to split a dataset while maintaining the relative proportions of multiple columns. If there was a single column, I could use `createDataPartition`. With multiple categorical columns, I could pass `paste(data$column1, data$column2, ...)` as the `y` in `createDataPartition` and everything would be fine. With multiple numerical columns passing `data$num1 * data$num2 ...` should be enough, but I couldn't find how to do the same when I have multiple categorical and numerical columns.

I asked [this question on StackOverflow](http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/166337/how-to-create-a-data-partition-in-r-using-categorical-and-numerical-columns) a few days ago, but had no answers. I ended up solving it by writing a `createGroups` function that converts the numerical data to categorical using quantiles and paste them all together, returning something like:

```
"[-3.54,-0.634](0.724,3.06]Class2"
"(0.715,2.86](0.724,3.06]Class1"
"(-0.634,-0.0055][-3.21,-0.677]Class1"
...
```

This could then be used with `createDataPartition`. The full code and explanation is in [the StackOverflow page](http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/166337/how-to-create-a-data-partition-in-r-using-categorical-and-numerical-columns)

I'm posting it here to double check if this problem was solved somewhere in caret I can't find and, if not, if it would be useful to add to caret. If that's the case, I would be happy to clean the code and submit a pull request in a few weeks.

title: Use data.tables internally to store data?
description:
Hi Max,

I was thinking we might consider using data.tables internally to save memory in `caret::train`.  In particular the `pred` object can get pretty huge when `savePredictions=TRUE` (especially for GBMs and glmnets).  I often find myself trying to run caretEnsemble on caret models with pred objects that take up 16-20 GB of RAM.  The out-of-sample predictions are essential for ensembling, but a 20GB data.frame is unbearably slow to work with.  (A 20GB data.table is workable).

These models also take a really long time to train, because every re-sample has to append data to a really large pred object.

If this seems like a good idea to you, I think it could save a TON of RAM when training large models.  I could start investigating this weekend.

Thanks,

Zach

title: Getting Confidence & Prediction Intervals from predict.train
description:
It is not currently possible with `predict.train` to request confidence or prediction intervals via the underlying `predict` functions of models (for those methods that support it). Calling the `predict` method on the `finalModel` is not straightforward because the predictors need to be pre-processesed and in the form of a design matrix.

Supporting intervals via `predict.train` would require the following:
1. Modify `extractPrediction`, `predictionFunction`, pass `...` arguments down to the `predict` function in the model definitions
2. Modify `extractPrediction` to handle prediction results with multiple columns
3. Modify `trimPredictions` to handle 2-dimensional data
4. Modify `predict.train` to return those extra columns when present
5. Modify all model definitions to pass `...` on to the model's `predict` function

I have completed 1-4 [on my fork](https://github.com/wmurphyrd/caret/tree/PredictionIntervals) and am working my way through 5. Additional effects of these changes are that other optional arguments to the model's `predict` method can be specified and the `param` argument to `predictionFunction` can now be passed to the higher level functions in order to successfully retrieve sub-model predictions (not sure if this is valuable to end users). 

Concerns: 
- Not all model's `predict` methods utilize optional arguments, but it seems easier just to add the dots to all of them (since no harm will be done) than to look up each specification to check
- Some model's caret definitions retrieve specific variables or columns from the predict function result, so requested intervals would not make it back to the user (unsure if any of these actually support intervals; may be moot)
- Requesting both sub-models and intervals would result in 3-dimensional data that is not supported by the modified `extractPrediction`; I haven't identified any model methods that actually support both options, but planning to add checking and error message just in case

Alternative: Could add a `prepareOnly` optional argument to `predict.train` that would return the prepared `newdata` instead of the predictions so that the user could then call `predict` on `finalModel` with whichever arguments were desired. It would be a simpler update, but less user-friendly experience

Let me know if this is something you'd be interested in pulling, and I'll finish the model definition updates and add unit tests

title: preProcess doesn't find and remove correlated features
description:
I have stumbled upon a bug in the preProcess function which in the current version cannot find highly correlated features and remove them. The seperate findCorrelation function works fine and as intended, but it seems its integration in preProcess has a bug related to how methods are executed.

The following code executes preprocessing with correlation cutoff set to 0.9 using the current version 6.0.86.

```{R}
library(caret)
data("longley")
```

title: Feature request: Add 'blocking' to createFolds()
description:
Hi, 

To prevent data leaking between K-folds, there is a technique called blocking. Where the instances from the same block are not split between folds. For example if you wish to predict customer behaviour using K-fold cross-validation for parameter optimisation. You don't want the same customer appearing in the training and validation set.

I hope the blocking feature can be added to `createFolds()` where the block ids are given as a parameter. Maybe something like this:

`createFolds(y, k = 10, list = TRUE, returnTrain = FALSE, block = customer_ids)`

where customer_ids is a vector of customer IDs.

This should also preserver stratification as well to keep the class proportions uniform between folds.

`mlr` already has this handy feature, please see [Resampling](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/reference/Resampling.html#grouping-blocking) docs.

Thank you.

title: Improve error message when unsupported tuning parameters are passed for a method
description:
Caret gives a confusing error message the `tuneGrid` passed to `train` contains a tuning parameter not supported by passed `method`.  As a simple example consider what happens when `mtry` is including in the `tuneGrid` for `gbm` (note `mtry` is not a tuning parameter of `gbm`).

```
library(caret)
mtry <- round(sqrt(18), 0)
gbmGrid <- expand.grid(
    interaction.depth = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
    , n.trees = seq(10, 10000, by = 100)
    , shrinkage = 0.01
    , n.minobsinnode = c(5, 10, 20, 30)
    , distribution = 'gaussian'
    , method = 'gbm'
    , mtry = mtry
)
fitControl <- trainControl(
    method = "repeatedcv"
    , number = 2
    , repeats = 3
)
gbmFit1 <- train(
    Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width
    , data = iris
    , trControl = fitControl
    , tuneGrid = gbmGrid
    , verbose = FALSE
)
# Error: The tuning parameter grid should have columns mtry
```

The current message says the parameter grid should include `mtry` despite the facts that:

1. `mtry` is already within the tuning parameter grid
2. `mtry` is not tuning parameter of `gbm`

I was digging into why it was giving such a strange error message and realized an improved error message would be a straightforward code change.  I will be opening a pull request for this issue that adds 5 lines of code and in the above case would now show the error message.
```
# Error: The tuning parameter grid should not have columns mtry
```

By simply adding a **NOT** to the message for this circumstance, the error message now becomes much more helpful.

The current error message has certainly tripped me up in the past and apparently [others as well](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52832898/caret-the-tuning-parameter-grid-should-have-columns-mtry).

title: XGBoost parallelization fails when twoClassSummary is the first summaryFunc used
description:
### Overview

When using caret to train an XGBoost model with parallelization at the resample level, execution continues indefinitely (or at least, for more than several hours in my tests), when the first `summaryFunc` used is of type `twoClassSummary`.

For the same code, if a call is first made to `train()` on any arbitrary data, however, the executions proceeds as expected, and in the case of the example below, finishes in seconds.

This effect does not appear to depend on the parallelization back-end used; tested with:

- doParallel/PSOCK
- doMC
- doFuture

It also occurs if the `twoClassSummary` is used along-side of other summary functions as part of a yardstick `metric_set()`.

Based on this behavior, I'm guessing there is some kind of initialization of the interface with the parallelization back-end that normally occurs during the first invocation to `train()` which is not taking place as-expected, in the case below.

### Minimal, reproducible example:

To see the behavior in action, first run the code below _as-is_, and (at least in the linux environment I'm testing it in), it will likely continue running for a long time.

Next, uncomment the commented first call to `train()` and re-run the script. It will execute in parallel and finish quickly as expected.

```r
library(caret)
set.seed(1)

# create fake data
test_dat <- twoClassSim(20)

library("doFuture")
registerDoFuture()
plan(multiprocess, workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1)

# fast, when the lines below are uncommented...
# mod <- train(Class ~ ., data = test_dat, method = "xgbTree",
#              tuneLength = 1, nthread = 1,
#              trControl = trainControl(search = "random"))
# message("warm-up done...")

train_control <- trainControl(search = 'random',
                              classProbs = TRUE,
                              summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)

t1 <- Sys.time()
mod <- train(Class ~ ., data = test_dat, method = "xgbTree", tuneLength = 10,
             nthreads = 1, trControl = train_control,
             metric = 'ROC')
t2 <- Sys.time()
t2 - t1

# with warm-up: ~2 seconds
# without warm-up: > 3hrs
```

title: Parallel seeds with ranger
description:
I'm running into an issue with setting seeds to reproduce `ranger` models in parallel processing. Following is a minimal reproducible example in which I set seeds in 3 ways: first with `set.seed()` before calling `train()`, then passing a seed to `train()` which it passes to `ranger()`, then passing a list of seeds inside `trainControl()`. I use these seeds to perform two identical training runs. However, as you can see below, the resampled performance measures are different between the two runs. I'm pretty sure the issue lies in how `train` generates the resamples (possibly around https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/master/pkg/caret/R/train.default.R#L436-L439 ?), since I can eliminate the following alternative explanations:

- It's not happening within the call to `ranger()` since variable importance is identical between the runs. Moreover, if I take out the seed passed to `ranger()`, variable importance changes between runs. So it's not `ranger()` or the fact that `ranger()` calls C++ code.

- It's not the issue reported [here](https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/248); in my example, `seedList` is identical to `seedList %>% lapply(as.vector)`, so the suggested fix doesn't work.

- It *is* something to do with parallel proceessing, since if I use `lapply()` rather than `mclapply()` to loop over the parameters, this issue goes away.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
#> Loading required package: lattice
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'caret'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:purrr':
#> 
#>     lift
library(ranger)
library(parallel)
tuneNumFolds <- c(4, 6)
set.seed(302302)
seedList <- list(
  `4` = c(map(1:4, sample.int, n=10000, size=6), sample.int(n=10000, size=1)),
  `6` = c(map(1:6, sample.int, n=5000, size=6), sample.int(n=5000, size=1))
)
set.seed(302302)
fstList1 <-
  mclapply(tuneNumFolds,
           mc.cores=2,
           FUN = function(tuneNmFld) {
             train(Species ~ .,
                   data=iris,
                   method="ranger",
                   importance="impurity",
                   num.trees=100,
                   seed=70707,
                   trControl=trainControl(method="cv", 
                                          number=tuneNmFld,
                                          seeds=seedList[[as.character(tuneNmFld)]],
                                          returnResamp="all"),
                   tuneGrid=data.frame(mtry=2, splitrule="gini", min.node.size=1))
           }) %>% 
  set_names(tuneNumFolds)
set.seed(302302)
fstList2 <-
  mclapply(tuneNumFolds,
           mc.cores=2,
           FUN = function(tuneNmFld) {
             train(Species ~ .,
                   data=iris,
                   method="ranger",
                   importance="impurity",
                   num.trees=100,
                   seed=70707,
                   trControl=trainControl(method="cv", 
                                          number=tuneNmFld,
                                          seeds=seedList[[as.character(tuneNmFld)]],
```

title: if(!all.equal(...  is not appropriate code
description:
Hello, 

 In confusionMatrix.R, I see

```
  if(!all.equal(nrow(data), ncol(data))) stop("the table must nrow = ncol")
  if(!all.equal(rownames(data), colnames(data))) stop("the table must the same classes in the same order")
```

This code is not appropriate. `all.equal` does not return `FALSE` is the condition is not fulfilled:

```
> all.equal(2, "a")
[1] "Modes: numeric, character"               "target is numeric, current is character"
```
Then the error messages never appear.

The code should be

```
  if(nrow(data) != ncol(data)) stop("the table must nrow = ncol")
  if(!isTRUE(all.equal(rownames(data), colnames(data)))) stop("the table must the same classes in the same order")
```

title: Uninformative error message generated for logical response with train(x = recipe, ...)
description:
### Overview

When attempting to use a recipe to build a classification model (in this case, glm) for a training set with a logical response variable, `train` fails with an error along the lines of:

```
# Error in .subset(x, j) : invalid subscript type 'list'                                       
# Calls: train -> train.recipe -> evalSummaryFunction -> t -> apply -> [ -> [.data.frame
```

On the other hand, if the same data is given to `train` in a more "traditional" form without using a recipe, the response type is checked and a helpful message is printed out:

```{R}
library(caret)
```

title: Speed up groupKFold
description:
Hello. The function `groupKFold` is very important in practical applications. However, it is extremely slow. 

Demo code:

```{R}
X <- data.frame(group = sample(1:1e6, size = 3e6, replace = TRUE))
system.time(out <- caret::groupKFold(X$group, k = 5)) # 53 Seconds
```

Here is a fast version (with slightly different output structure):
```{R}
fastGroupKFold <- function(group, k) {
  g_unique <- unique(group)
  stopifnot(k <= length(g_unique))
  g_folds <- sample(k, size = length(g_unique), replace = TRUE)
  split(seq_along(group), g_folds[match(group, g_unique)])
}
system.time(out <- fastGroupKFold(X$group, k = 5)) # 0.6 Seconds
```

It would be fantastic if you could speed up the current implementation of `groupKFold`.

title: vglmCumulative error in caret for partial proportional odds model
description:
I am trying to run my vgam/vglm "partial proportional odds" model in caret, as I ultimately want to use this model for prediction on a subset of my data. As long as I run a "proportional odds" (method = "vglmCumulative"; and expand.grid(parallel = TRUE)) or a "non-proportional odds" (method = "vglmCumulative"; and expand.grid(parallel = FALSE)) model, this works perfectly fine. Yet, when I try to run my "partial proportional odds" model (method = "vglmCumulative"; and expand.grid(parallel = TRUE ~ -1 + predictor_with_parallel_slopes)), which runs fine in vglm/vgam, this does not run any longer in caret. I get the following error : 

> Error in vector(type, length) :  vector: cannot make a vector of mode 'language'.

In the reproducible example below (i.e. fabricated data) you can see what I want to do and where it goes wrong. Please apologize that the model brings up a lot of warnings, this is result of the poorly fabricated data, but the error in the "partial proportional odds" model is the same as in my own data.

## libraries, data and model
```{r}
library("caret")
library("VGAM")
d.AD <- data.frame(treatment = gl(3, 120),outcome = gl(3, 1, 9),counts = c(18,17,15,20,10,20,25,13,12,19,15,16,18,13,17,28,10,7))
d.AD$outcome <- gsub("1","alow", d.AD$outcome)
d.AD$outcome <- gsub("2","bmoderate", d.AD$outcome)
d.AD$outcome <- gsub("3","chigh", d.AD$outcome)
formula <-  outcome ~ counts + treatment
```

## model in vgam
NB: works the same if vgam is replaced with vglm.
```{r}
#proportional odds model - all predictors need to have a parallel slope 
fit <- vgam(formula, data = d.AD, cumulative(link = "logitlink", parallel = TRUE, reverse = FALSE))
coef(summary(fit))

#non-proportional odds model - none of predictors needs to have a parallel slope 
fit <- vgam(formula, data = d.AD, cumulative(link = "logitlink", parallel = FALSE, reverse = FALSE))
coef(summary(fit))

#partial-proportional odds model - only counts needs to have a parallel slope 
fit <- vgam(formula, data = d.AD, cumulative(link = "logitlink", parallel = TRUE ~ -1 + counts, reverse = FALSE))
coef(summary(fit))
```

## model translated to caret 
I ignore for the moment train/test splitting, as well as CV or bootstrapping.
```{r}
#proportional odds model - all predictors need to have a parallel slope 
grid <- expand.grid(parallel = TRUE, link = c("logit", "probit"))
seeds <- set.seed(100)
fit_II <- train(formula,
                data = d.AD,
                method = "vglmCumulative",
                trControl = trainControl(classProbs = TRUE,
                                         seeds=seeds,
                                         summaryFunction = multiClassSummary),
                tuneGrid =  grid,
                metric = "ROC"); fit_II$finalModel

#non-proportional odds model - none of predictors needs to have a parallel slope 
grid <- expand.grid(parallel = FALSE, link = c("logit", "probit"))
seeds <- set.seed(100)
fit_II <- train(formula,
                data = d.AD,
                method = "vglmCumulative",
                trControl = trainControl(classProbs = TRUE,
                                         seeds=seeds,
                                         summaryFunction = multiClassSummary),
                tuneGrid =  grid,
                metric = "ROC"); fit_II$finalModel

#partial-proportional odds model - only counts needs to have a parallel slope 
#NB: here it goes wrong and I get the error!
grid <- expand.grid(parallel = TRUE ~ -1 + counts, link = c("logit", "probit"))
seeds <- set.seed(100)
fit_II <- train(formula,
                data = d.AD,
                method = "vglmCumulative",
                trControl = trainControl(classProbs = TRUE,
                                         seeds=seeds,
                                         summaryFunction = multiClassSummary),
                tuneGrid =  grid,
                metric = "ROC"); fit_II$finalModel
```
I was wondering whether the error is result of me mis-specifying the code, or whether this simply is not possible (yet) in caret? I have tried a couple of things, but everything results in this error. If the "partial proportional odds" option (expand.grid(parallel = TRUE ~ -1 + predictor_with_parallel_slopes)) is not possible in caret, is there a way around it (e.g. to specify it in another way) to still be able to use caret in conjunction with my vgam model? This would be fantastic, as it would ease the prediction process notably. Or would you advice not to use caret in this particular case?

I am looking forward to your advice,

Jess

title: Interpretation of sensitivity and specificity in bwplot resamples function
description:
Hello,

This question is more related to interpretation than coding.

When we are comparing different models using resamples function we can plot the models via bwplot and compare their ROC, Sensitivty and Specificity. Here is example:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35683078/66806728-ea4e9d00-ef30-11e9-8fb6-caa12dbed936.png)
https://topepo.github.io/caret/model-training-and-tuning.html

While there are no questions regards the ROC but how can we interpret the results of sensitivity and specificity? 

1. First of all, which is which? We know that sensitivity shows the ability of a test to correctly identify events (TP / (TP + FN)), that is, proportion of actual positives which are identified as such. In a 2-class classification modelling, there are possible two outcomes, which may be outcome A and outcome B. How can I know whether bwplot has identified outcome A as positive, not negative, or vice verse?
2. Usually, sensitivity and specificity are measured with particular cutoff where it is clear what is TP and TN rate. In this case, no particular cutoff is given, therefore, the question is how does caret's resamples bwplot functions deals with it?

Thanks in advance.

title: confusionMatrix Feature Request: Marginal Map Proportion (weighting by base population)
description:
Recently, I started adapting `caret::confusionMatrix` to fit state-of-the-art accuracy assessment for sampled land cover data to estimate marginal map area proportions as described in [Olofsson et al. (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2012.10.031) and [Stehman & Foody (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.05.018). 
Basically, the concept does rely on weighing the stratum in the error matrix by the proportion of each class in the the whole data set (in case you use stratified random sampling). 

This would involve adding a new parameter (`NULL` by default) holding the number of occurrences of each class in the parent population. If this vector is provided and fulfills the necessary properties, weighting by marginal proportion is conducted and the estimated confusion matrix as well as estimated overall and class accuracies are returned. 

Before I go all the way of filing a pull request, I wanted to know if there is any use for that outside of the remote sensing community. Perhaps this might be called somehow different, though. 
If you think this is of any value for the `caret` user base, I would be happy to create a PR. 

Let me know. I am looking forward to a fruitful discussion.

title: Bug: imputation does not work in train
description:
For data with missing values, imputing with either `knnImpute`, `bagImpute`, or `medianImpute` (in the `preProcess` argument of `train`) just results in omitting the rows with missing data, or failing with an error due to them. i.e. imputation is not done.

Using the `preProcess()` function outside of `train` works as expected to impute missing data and not drop rows. However, doing this preprocessing outside of repeated cross validation loops doesn't seem conceptually correct, as it would be like having access to "future" data to figure out the imputed values. 

This bug seems to be years old, and a number of StackOverflow questions have addressed this. Eg:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/20054906/carettrain-values-not-imputed

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/39619913/missing-value-error-when-using-bagimpute-preprocessing-within-carettrain-funct

Is there a workaround? Any chance of getting a bug fix?

title: Question on LGOCV
description:
My first impression of the term 'leave group out CV" would be that the resampling population consists of some level of grouping which can be used as the basis for resampling.  For example, a population consisting of a single species may consist of several genus level groups, in which case it may make sense in some scenario to leave each group out in order to infer performance.  It seems that LGOCV within the context of caret actually refers to Monte Carlo CV though.

Anyway, I'm wondering if you have any thoughts on achieving the former with caret.  Perhaps by writing a wrapper around manual split selection?

title: fit function for rpart1SE is wrong (weights)
description:
The fit function for rpart1SE is wrong (weights)...


```
mdi <- getModelInfo("rpart1SE",regex=FALSE)[[1]]
mdi$fit

function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) { 

                    dat <- if(is.data.frame(x)) x else as.data.frame(x)
                    dat$.outcome <- y
                    
                    ## check to see if weights were passed in (and availible)

                    if(!is.null(wts)) { **# if wts is set we don't use it?**

                       out <- rpart::rpart(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, ...)

                     } else { **# if wts=NULL we post that to rpart?**
 
                       out <- rpart::rpart(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, weights = wts, ...)

                    }
                    out           
}
```


correct:

```
function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) { 

                    dat <- if(is.data.frame(x)) x else as.data.frame(x)
                    dat$.outcome <- y
                    
                    ## check to see if weights were passed in (and availible)
                    if(is.null(wts)) { # <--- if no wts / weights 
                      out <- rpart::rpart(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, ...)
                    } else { # if wts is set
                      out <- rpart::rpart(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, weights = wts, ...)
                    }
                    out           
                  }
```
shorter:
```
function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) { 
                    dat <- if(is.data.frame(x)) x else as.data.frame(x)
                    dat$.outcome <- y                    
                    out <- rpart::rpart(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, weights = wts, ...)
                    out           
                  }
```

title: ranger now accepts weights
description:
Hi Max,

I have seen that package `ranger` now accepts weights using parameter `case.weights`. It is included in CRAN [version 0.4](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/NEWS). 
.

If I use `case.weights` inside `train` dots, it gives me an error. I created a custom function like the one below and it seems to work fine. If no `case.weights`, ranger expects `NULL` as in `train`, this is why I include `wts` directly to ranger.

```
rangerWeight <- getModelInfo("ranger")$ranger

rangerWeight$fit <- function (x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) 
{
  if (!is.data.frame(x)) 
    x <- as.data.frame(x)
  x$.outcome <- y
  out <- ranger(.outcome ~ ., data = x, mtry = param$mtry, 
                write.forest = TRUE, probability = classProbs, case.weights = wts, ...)
  if (!last) 
    out$y <- y
  out
}
```

Not sure if this is a feature requesting weights in `ranger` or a bug when I use them inside dots.

If you need a reproducible example of the error or a pull request to method ranger I'll be happy to provide them.

Thank you very much,

title: predict.train gives different predictions for a data.frame versus a tibble for data with factors
description:
I have a suspicion that this issue is related to the one I just opened for the recipes package: https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/376

I am getting highly different predictions from predict.train when I simply do nothing more than convert my data to a tibble.  But, this seems to only be an issue when the data set contains factors. Reproducible example is below. I suspect that for the issue linked above, when tune preps/bakes the recipe, the resulting data used for prediction is a tibble and that leads to the issue I show below.

```{R}
library(caret)
library(gbm)
library(dplyr)

data(cars)

# use x,y, format
traindata <- cars[,-1]
trainresponse <- cars$Price

# run gbm within caret
tune <- train(traindata, trainresponse, 
              method = "gbm",
              bag.fraction = .5,
              distribution = "gaussian",
              metric = "RMSE",
              verbose = FALSE)

# make predictions with the final model 
caret_pred <- predict(tune, cars)
cars_tibble <- as_tibble(cars)
caret_pred2 <- predict(tune, cars_tibble) # using a tibble here will result in the same results (cars has no factors)
plot(caret_pred, caret_pred2)


# add a factor variable
cars$color <- as.factor(sample(c("green", "black", "red", "white", "orange"), size = 804, replace = TRUE))

# use x,y, format
traindata <- cars[,-1]
trainresponse <- cars$Price

# run gbm within caret
tune <- train(traindata, trainresponse, 
              method = "gbm",
              bag.fraction = .5,
              distribution = "gaussian",
              metric = "RMSE",
              verbose = FALSE)

# make predictions with the final model 
caret_pred <- predict(tune, cars)
cars_tibble <- as_tibble(cars)
caret_pred2 <- predict(tune, cars_tibble) # using a tibble here will result in different results (cars has a factor)
plot(caret_pred, caret_pred2)

# both the data.frame and the tibble have the factor as factor class
lapply(cars, class)
lapply(cars_tibble, class)

# for another dataset from the DALEX package, the issue is even more pronounced
library(DALEX)
# use x,y, format
traindata <- apartments[,-1]
trainresponse <- apartments$m2.price

# run gbm within caret
tune <- train(traindata, trainresponse, 
              method = "gbm",
              bag.fraction = .5,
              distribution = "gaussian",
              metric = "RMSE",
              verbose = FALSE)

# make predictions with the final model 
caret_pred <- predict(tune, apartments)
apartments_tibble <- as_tibble(apartments)
caret_pred2 <- predict(tune, apartments_tibble) # using a tibble here will result in very different results (apartments has factor)
plot(caret_pred, caret_pred2)

# if I remove the factor variable, the two predictions are the same
apartments <- apartments[,-6]

# use x,y, format
traindata <- apartments[,-1]
trainresponse <- apartments$m2.price

# run gbm within caret
tune <- train(traindata, trainresponse, 
              method = "gbm",
              bag.fraction = .5,
              distribution = "gaussian",
              metric = "RMSE",
              verbose = FALSE)

# make predictions with the final model 
caret_pred <- predict(tune, apartments)
apartments_tibble <- as_tibble(apartments)
caret_pred2 <- predict(tune, apartments_tibble) # using a tibble here will result in the same results (apartments has no factors)
plot(caret_pred, caret_pred2)
```

title: Performance of gbm using sub-model trick
description:
I have been experiencing very slow run times using `method = "gbm"` when grid tuning and checking anything more than a few values for `n.trees` less than my maximum number of trees.

According to [this description](https://topepo.github.io/caret/parallel-processing.html) of the sub-model trick: "in most implementations of boosted models, a model trained on B boosting iterations can produce predictions for models for iterations less than B."

My understanding from this is that to find the "best" number of trees <= 5,000 I need to train only one model with 5,000 trees. While I expected that training a model with 5,000 trees with `caret` would be slightly slower than training the same model with `gbm` directly, I did not expect that checking several values < 5,000 (`expand.grid(n.trees = (1:50)*100, ...)`) would be significantly slower than checking all values < 5,000 (`expand.grid(n.trees = 1:5000, ...)`).

This is quick to do in `gbm` using `gbm.perf()`. If this were the only parameter I cared about tuning I would do this in `gbm` directly, but since I am looking for a full grid tune, that won't work. I understand that including other parameters in my grid will require building separate models and will quickly increase runtime, but given my experience with `gbm` and knowing of `caret`'s submodel trick I didn't expect tuning the `n.trees` parameter to add much time.

So:
- Am I misunderstanding the "submodel trick"?

- Is this increase in time expected?


### Minimal, reproducible example:
``` r
# Data --------------------------------------------------------------------
library(caret)
#> Loading required package: lattice
#> Loading required package: ggplot2
library(gbm)
#> Loaded gbm 2.1.5

set.seed(1)
dat <- twoClassSim(2000)
dat_numeric <- dat
dat_numeric$Class <- ifelse(dat_numeric$Class == "Class1", 1, 0)

# GBM ---------------------------------------------------------------------
system.time(
  gbm_model <- gbm(Class ~ .,
                   data = dat_numeric,
                   distribution = "bernoulli",
                   n.trees = 5000,
                   interaction.depth = 2,
                   n.minobsinnode = 10,
                   shrinkage = 0.002,
                   cv.folds = 5,
                   class.stratify.cv = TRUE)
)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    7.50    0.12   19.03

system.time(
  gbm_best_trees <- gbm.perf(gbm_model, plot.it = FALSE, method = "cv")
)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>       0       0       0

# Caret -------------------------------------------------------------------
train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv",
                              number = 5,
                              returnResamp = "final",
                              classProbs = TRUE)

more_trees_grid <- expand.grid(n.trees = 1:5000,
                               interaction.depth = 2,
                               n.minobsinnode = 10,
                               shrinkage = 0.002)

more_trees_model <- train(Class ~.,
                          data = dat,
                          method = "gbm",
                          distribution = "bernoulli",
                          trControl = train_control,
                          tuneGrid = more_trees_grid,
                          verbose = FALSE)

fewer_trees_grid <- expand.grid(n.trees = (1:50)*100,
                                interaction.depth = 2,
                                n.minobsinnode = 10,
                                shrinkage = 0.002)

fewer_trees_model <- train(Class ~.,
                           data = dat,
                           method = "gbm",
                           distribution = "bernoulli",

                           tuneGrid = fewer_trees_grid,
```

title: Citation generated from DESCRIPTION is not bibtex friendly
description:
The citation created by R is not latex friendly and the result is quite unfair to Max Kuhn.

The DESCRIPTION contains:

```
Author: Max Kuhn. Contributions from Jed Wing, Steve Weston, Andre
    Williams, Chris Keefer, Allan Engelhardt, Tony Cooper, Zachary Mayer,
    Brenton Kenkel, the R Core Team, Michael Benesty, Reynald Lescarbeau,
    Andrew Ziem, Luca Scrucca, Yuan Tang, Can Candan, and Tyler Hunt.
```

Using the raw output of `citation("caret")` in a bib/tex document, it becomes quite a mouthful and doesn't even cite Max properly:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10772583/56027793-aaeb8d80-5d0e-11e9-8556-003fa335e580.png)

title: require R-3.5.0
description:
If you are filing a bug, make sure these boxes are checked before submitting your issue— thank you!

- [ ] Start a new R session
- [ ] Install the latest version of caret: `update.packages(oldPkgs="caret", ask=FALSE)`
- [x] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [x] **Do not** use parallel processing in the code (unless you are certain that the issue is about parallel processing).
- [ ] run `sessionInfo()`

### Minimal, reproducible example:

Something `caret` does uses `utils::warnErrList`, which did not appear in R until R-3.5.0.

In a version of R before 3.5:

```r
> library(caret)
Error: package or namespace load failed for ‘caret’:
 object ‘warnErrList’ is not exported by 'namespace:utils'
```

I apologize for the incomplete question, I am posting the issue on behalf of a StackOverflow question: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56367701. From my answer there:

> You can back this up by looking at the list of exported functions for [`utils` in R-3.5.0](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/utils/versions/3.5.0) and you can find `warnErrList`, whereas [`utils` in R-3.4.3](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/utils/versions/3.4.3) (the previous release of R), the function cannot be found.

(I've requested the SO/OP to add the results from `sessionInfo()` and `traceback()` to see what package is ultimately also under-requiring R. I don't have the older versions available, but if there is something else going on, my apologies.)

title: failing in a Latin-1 locale
description:
> This concerns packages 
> 
> CHNOSZ SARP.moodle caret dplyr fpeek fs gestalt hyphenatr incadata 
> jpndistrict lobstr lucr pillar postGIStools rbison rchie rcmdcheck 
> rcrossref rdatacite rerddap rgbif rplos skimr snakecase styler svglite 
> swirl swirlify taxize testthat textTinyR traitdataform units urltools 
> 
> which are failing their checks in a strict Latin-1 locale: see the 
> debian-clang results. (Several of these seem to stem from vcr.) 
> 
> On Linux, such a locale can be ensured via LC_CTYPE=en_US (which may 
> need installing for distros that micro-package). AFAWK it cannot be 
> done on Windows. 
> 
> 1) The character in don't is an (ASCII) apostrophe, not a right quote: 
> 
> don’t 
> 
> (with a right quote) is used in packages CHNOSZ dplyr ptstem skimr 
> styler text2vec textTinyR (and others not failing). 
> 
> 2) **en and em dashes are not portable**, found in packages 
> CHNOSZ SARP.moodle **caret** dplyr gestalt ptstem quanteda rchie rcrossref 
> rdatacite rerddap rgbif rplos taxize textTinyR traitdataform units . 
> 
> 3) Using \uxxxx coding for non-ASCII chars in R character strings should 
> help in some cases (see 'Writing R Extensions'). 
> 
> Please correct before May 10 to safely retain the package on CRAN. 
> 
> -- 
> Brian D. Ripley, ripley@stats.ox.ac.uk 
> Emeritus Professor of Applied Statistics, University of Oxford

title: Adaptive Resampling for sub-model-trick methods
description:
Debut post so please ask for further information if this isn't self-explanatory.

I'm noticing that when running adaptive resampling methods for models that are able to use the sub-model-trick I'm not seeing any improvement in speed.

Let's say we have a 10x10 grid of sub-model-trick hyperparameters, we only need to train 10 models. If we have 10 folds that's 100x single model train time to cross validate 100 parameter combinations.

Compare this to the adaptive random case where even after knocking out 50% of our parameter pairs we still need to train 50 models on the next fold. After 2 folds we have already used 150x single model training time.

Max refers to this in e.g. https://www.academia.edu/7960048/Adaptive_Sampling_in_Predictive_Analysis

I don't see any reason why the adaptive method couldn't be adapted to take advantage of the powerful sub-model-trick?

title: train with recipes breaks if any roles are NA
description:
Alright Davis, time to tell me what I'm doing wrong :P . 

train() is breaking if there are any roles in the recipe that are NA. Looks like it happens when it checks for case weights (case weights are not being specified here).  

(Also just noticed a bunch of warnings about using newdata instead of new_data in bake, which I'll delete the duplicates of in the reprex so it's not so cluttered.)

``` r
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressMessages(library(recipes))
suppressMessages(library(caret))


rec <- recipes::recipe(head(iris)) %>%
  update_role(Sepal.Width, new_role = "predictor") %>%
  update_role(Sepal.Length, new_role = "outcome")
rec %>% prep() %>% summary()
#> # A tibble: 5 x 4
#>   variable     type    role      source  
#>   <chr>        <chr>   <chr>     <chr>   
#> 1 Sepal.Length numeric outcome   original
#> 2 Sepal.Width  numeric predictor original
#> 3 Petal.Length numeric <NA>      original
#> 4 Petal.Width  numeric <NA>      original
#> 5 Species      nominal <NA>      original

tc <- caret::trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)
set.seed(1234)
caret::train(rec, iris, method = "lm", trControl = tc, metric = "RMSE")
#> Error in if (any(is_weight)) {: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

``` r
# bascially replicating what train.recipe does when checking for case weights ---
```

``` r
roles <- rec %>% prep() %>% summary() %>%
  purrr::pluck("role")
is_weight <- roles == "case weight"
any(is_weight)
#> [1] NA

if(any(is_weight)) print("not gonna happen")
#> Error in if (any(is_weight)) print("not gonna happen"): missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

``` r
# work around by assigning all other variables to a role so there are no NAs ---
```

``` r
rec_removeNA <- rec %>%
  update_role(-contains("Sepal"), new_role = "other")
rec_removeNA %>% prep() %>% summary()
```

title: Validation set approach as method in trainControl?
description:
When learning resampling methods, students are often first exposed to what is often called the validation set approach (see for example chapter 5 of "An introduction to statistical learning"). In this approach, one simply splits the data at random in two parts, fits the model on one part and evaluates on the held-out part. 

It would be nice, primarily for teaching purposes, to have an easy way to use the validation set approach in caret. This could also serve as a first introduction to the caret package.

My impression is that such functionality currently does not exist.

I am aware of the possibility of combining `createDataPartition` function with  the  `index` argument of `trainControl` , to implement this (I wrote it up as a blog post).

However, this is not really suitable as a first introduction to caret. When using the `index` argument, the `method` argument is ignored, which is confusing for beginners. It also creates stratified samples, that adds further complexity that is unwanted in a teaching setting. 

So i am proposing creating a new method = "validation" that creates random samples (not stratified) and performs the validation set approach (this is not the same as 2-fold cv). 
 
I could write a pull request if the maintainers of caret will allow such and extension.

title: ggplot.resamples and plot.resamples when results constant
description:
Using the function _plot_ or _ggplot_ for an object of class _resamples_ will not visualize data points for a model in which _data$model$values_ are constant or near constant.
The problem seems to be in these lines of code of the _ggplot.resamples_ function (line 982):

```r
results <- lapply(
      plotData,
      function(x, cl) {
        ttest <- try(t.test(x$value, conf.level = cl),
                     silent = TRUE)
        if (class(ttest)[1] == "htest") {
          out <- c(ttest$conf.int, ttest$estimate)
          names(out) <-
            c("LowerLimit", "UpperLimit", "Estimate")
        } else
          out <- rep(NA, 3)
        out
      }
```

In particular the t.test function will fail to report confidence intervals or **means.** An example:

```r
t.test(rep(1,10), conf.level = 0.95)

Error in t.test.default(rep(1, 10), conf.level = 0.095) : data are essentially constant 
```

and thus also the mean alone will not be plotted and the _out_ will be vector of NA.

I suppose that a model with results nearly constant is a rare occurrence, but I realized this because it happened to me. :)

Claudio

title: Adjusting the intercept after downsampling
description:
I've had good results with easing the estimation process for binary classification by using the downsampling routine outlined [in the book](https://topepo.github.io/caret/subsampling-for-class-imbalances.html#subsampling-during-resampling). The issue that I've come up against is that while using the `predict()` method for a test data set on the resulting `train` objects, I get a much higher general predicted base rate than if I hadn't downsampled.

My suspicion is that, in essence, the intercept term needs to be adjusted in account for the downsampling, but there may well be something else that I'm missing.

### Reproducible example:

The following is unfortunately not exactly a minimal example (it takes several minutes to run on my machine), but it was selected because it extends the example provided in the book. We compare the predicted expected value of the total number of cases over the test data set for the downsampled model (`down_inside`) and a non-downsampled model (`vanilla` - this is the one that takes awhile to run).

FWIW, my actual use-case is getting good predictions out of a lasso logistic model fit with `glmnet`.

``` r
library(caret)

set.seed(2969)
imbal_train <- twoClassSim(10000, intercept = -20, linearVars = 20)
imbal_test  <- twoClassSim(10000, intercept = -20, linearVars = 20)

ctrl_down <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
                     sampling = "down")

set.seed(5627)
down_inside <- train(Class ~ ., data = imbal_train,
                     method = "treebag",
                     nbagg = 50,
                     metric = "ROC",
                     trControl = ctrl_down)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)

set.seed(5627)
vanilla <- train(Class ~ ., data = imbal_train,
                     method = "treebag",
                     nbagg = 50,
                     metric = "ROC",
                     trControl = ctrl)

p_down    <- predict(down_inside, imbal_test, type = "prob")$Class2
p_vanilla <- predict(vanilla, imbal_test, type = "prob")$Class2
sum(p_down)
#> [1] 2378.74
sum(p_vanilla)
#> [1] 567.28
```

title: predict.train vs predict using recipe objects
description:
After specifiying a recipe to use in caret::train I am trying to predict new samples. I have a couple of questions around this as I can not find in caret/recipes documentation.

Should I use `predict()` or `predict.train()`? Whats the difference?
Should I bake the test data with the prepared recipe first before using predict? When using `preProcess` directly in `train()` you are advised not to `preProcess` new data as the train object will automatically do that. Is this the same when using recipes?

Below is a reproducible example illustrating my process and the difference in predictions when using predict vs predict.train.

```
library(recipes)
library(caret)
# Data ----
data("credit_data")

credit_train <- credit_data[1:3500,]
credit_test <- credit_data[-(1:3500),]

# Set up recipe ----

set.seed(0)
Rec.Obj = recipe(Status ~ ., data = credit_train) %>%
    step_knnimpute(all_predictors()) %>% 
    step_center(all_numeric())%>%
    step_scale(all_numeric())

# Control parameters ----
set.seed(0)
TC = trainControl("cv",number = 10, savePredictions = "final", classProbs = TRUE, returnResamp = "final")

set.seed(0)
Model.Output = train(Rec.Obj,
                     credit_train,
                     trControl = TC,
                     tuneLength = 1,
                     metric = "Accuracy",
                     method = "glm")

# Preped recipe ----
set.seed(0)
prep.rec <- 
    prep(Rec.Obj, newdata = credit_train)

# Baked data for observation ----
set.seed(0)
bake.train <- bake(prep.rec, new_data = credit_train)
bake.test <- bake(prep.rec, new_data = credit_test)

# investigation of prediction methods ----

# no application of recipe to newdata
set.seed(0)
predict.norm = predict(Model.Output, credit_test, type = "raw")
predict.train = predict.train(Model.Output, credit_test,  type = "raw")

identical(predict.norm,predict.train)
# evaluates to FALSE

# Apply recipe to new data (bake.test)
predict.norm.baked = predict(Model.Output, bake.test, type = "raw")
predict.train.baked = predict.train(Model.Output, bake.test, type = "raw")

identical(predict.norm.baked, predict.train.baked)
# evaluates to FALSE

# Comparison of both predict() funcs
identical(predict.norm, predict.norm.baked)
# evaluates to FALSE
`
```

description:
I raised a question on [SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54957458/pls-da-prediction-of-a-single-row-of-data-returns-multiple-predictions) which is similar to a bug issue raised [previously](https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/345)

predict() returns an incorrect number of predictions for single records for type = "prob" and type = "class". It works fine for type = "raw". I assume it is a similar bug related to the one raised previously

```
library(caret)

trainLow <- as.data.frame(matrix(data = rnorm(533*32), nrow = 32, ncol = 533))

low_plsda_model <- plsda(trainLow, 
                         trainLowClass,
                         probMethod = "Bayes",
                         ncomp = 4,
)

#Works as expected
predict(low_plsda_model, trainLow, ncomp = 2)
predict(low_plsda_model, trainLow[1:2,], ncomp = 2)

#Returns multiple predictions
predict(low_plsda_model, trainLow[1,], ncomp = 2)
```

title: caret::dummyVars reoccurring pattern in column name causes errors in dummy variable names
description:
I noticed that dummyVars is producing erroneous variable names when creating (predicting) dummy variables if one of the column names in the original dataset matches the start of the name string of a subsequent column name. For these cases, the new dummy variable names get split in the wrong place. Part of the column names of the partly matching subsequent column name is put with the factor level name.
As far as I can tell the function still delivers the right result, just with a confusing name.
#### Minimal dataset:

``` R
data <- data.frame('id' = seq(1,30,1),
                   'fooFactor' = factor(c(rep(1,10), rep(2,10), rep(3,10))),
                   'fooFactorBar' = factor(c(rep(4,10), rep(5,10), rep(6,10))),
                   'fooBarFactor' = factor(c(rep(7,10), rep(8,10), rep(9,10))))
```
#### Minimal, runnable code:

``` R
library(caret)
library(dplyr)
#make some data
data <- data.frame('id' = seq(1,30,1),
                   'fooFactor' = factor(c(rep(1,10), rep(2,10), rep(3,10))),
                   'fooFactorBar' = factor(c(rep(4,10), rep(5,10), rep(6,10))),
                   'fooBarFactor' = factor(c(rep(7,10), rep(8,10), rep(9,10))))
#dummify the data
dummies <- dummyVars(formula = id ~., 
                     data = data,
                     sep = '-') %>%
  predict(data)

#check the names
colnames(dummies)
#will return:
# [1] "fooFactor-1"    "fooFactor-2"    "fooFactor-3"    "fooFactor-Bar4" "fooFactor-Bar5"
# [6] "fooFactor-Bar6" "fooBarFactor-7" "fooBarFactor-8" "fooBarFactor-9"

#notice how 'fooFactor' and 'fooBarFactor' are both fine,
#but 'fooFactorBar' gets turned into 'fooFactor-Bar4' etc.
```

The same is true when using 'levelsOnly = TRUE' by the way. With this option, dummy variable names become 1, 2, 3, Bar4, Bar5, Bar6, 7, 8, 9.

This is my first bug report on github. Please point out anything that is missing or should be done better. Thanks for all the effort that went into this fantastic and super helpful package!

title: Where is tuneScheme() function?
description:
Hi everyone,

I'm developing an experimental classification method and I would be interested in not fitting the model for all the rows of the grid parameter. I want to keep all its possible combinations though. 

This is because the real stuff happens in the prediction. Just imagine we were talking about knn with a grid with different values for the k, the distances from the instances of the testing set to the instances of the training set would be the same for all the possible values of k, only the output would change based on the number of instances being considered. Well, my method is not knn and the equivalent step of calculating distances is too time consuming, so it would be a great advantage avoid it when possible.

In the comments of the`train.default` function in https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/master/pkg/caret/R/train.default.R it says that:

    ## trainInfo will hold the information about how we should loop to train the model and what types
    ## of parameters are used.

    ## There are two types of methods to build the models: "basic" means that each tuning parameter
    ## combination requires it's own model fit and "seq" where a single model fit can be used to
    ## get predictions for multiple tuning parameters.

    ## The tuneScheme() function is in miscr.R and it helps define the following:
    ##   - A data frame called "loop" with columns for parameters and a row for each model to be fit.
    ##     For "basic" models, this is the same as the tuning grid. For "seq" models, it is only
    ##     the subset of parameters that need to be fit
    ##   - A list called "submodels". If "basic", it is NULL. For "seq" models, it is a list. Each list
    ##     item is a data frame of the parameters that need to be varied for the corresponding row of
    ##     the loop object.

But I'm not able to find this function anywhere, nor an explanation about where I should use it. Does anyone knows how could I solve this?

Thank you in advance :)

Noelia

title: `method = "knn"` fails when you supply a recipe
description:
`method = "knn"` works just fine when supplying the formula or XY to `train()` in a traditional manner but fails when you supply it via a recipe. # works

```{R}
  Sale_Price ~ ., 
  data = ames, 
  method = "knn"
  )
```

title: Problem using the glmnet logistic regression model trained in Caret but with only the features selected predictor variables
description:
I have trained a glmnet binary logistic regression model in caret by tuning over a grid of lambda at alpha 0.5 and selecting for the sparsest model within oneSE of the best trained performance. It has selected features. Predict.train in caret automatically applies my preprocessing (as specified during training) to my new test data. However, it requires the same columns as the train data. 

I would like to be able to input only the feature selected predictor variables into the model and get a prediction. 

I tried to do this manually by extracting the final model coefficients at the optimally tuned lambda, manually standardising the predictor variables and calculating the logit then probability for my outcome. 

However, I get a different probability for my outcome compared to using predict.train function. I am not really sure where I am going wrong.

I will outline my problem with the following example using the Titanic dataset:

    #load required libraries
    library(plyr)
    library(caret)
    library(pROC)
    
    #Dummy Session with Titanic data
    titanicDF = read.csv('http://math.ucdenver.edu/RTutorial/titanic.txt',sep='\t')
    #Get the title
    titanicDF$Title = ifelse(grepl('Mr ',titanicDF$Name),'Mr',ifelse(grepl('Mrs ',titanicDF$Name),'Mrs',ifelse(grepl('Miss',titanicDF$Name),'Miss','Nothing'))) 
    #remove name and reorder
    titanicDF <- titanicDF[c('PClass', 'Age',    'Sex',   'Title', 'Survived')]

    print(str(titanicDF))
    #change to factors where needed, caret will automatically dummy code categorical variables
    titanicDF$Title = as.factor(titanicDF$Title)
    titanicDF$Survived = as.factor(titanicDF$Survived)
    #remap to Yes No with Plyr
    titanicDF$Survived = revalue(titanicDF$Survived, c("0"="No","1"="Yes"))

    #split train test
    set.seed(987)
    splitIndex <- createDataPartition(titanicDF[,"Survived"], p = .75, list = FALSE, times = 1)
    trainDF <- titanicDF[ splitIndex,]
    testDF  <- titanicDF[-splitIndex,]

    #set traincontrol - choose sparsest model within oneSE
    control <- trainControl(method="repeatedcv", number=10, repeats=10, classProbs=TRUE, summaryFunction=twoClassSummary, selectionFunction ="oneSE")

    #optimise over alpha 0.5 but range of lambda values
    tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha=0.5, lambda = 10 ^ seq(-0.3, -5, length = 100))

    #preprocess will remove zv and nzv variables, impute missing data in age column (no other missing data in dataset) and centre/scale training data
    set.seed(987)
    titanicMod = train(Survived ~ ., data=trainDF, method="glmnet", metric="ROC", tuneGrid = tuneGrid, preProc = c("nzv","zv","center", "scale","knnImpute"), trControl=control, na.action = na.pass)
    #test the model with predict
    titanicResult = predict(titanicMod, testDF, type = "prob", na.action = na.pass)
    #get the roc auc to show model works (not required for this example)
    titanicROC = roc(predictor = titanicResult$Yes, response = testDF$Survived=="Yes")
    titanicROC$auc
    plot(titanicROC)

    #extract the best model coefficients - model has selected features
    coef(titanicMod$finalModel, titanicMod$bestTune$lambda)
    #OUTPUTS
    #8 x 1 sparse Matrix of class "dgCMatrix"
    #                   1
    #(Intercept)  -0.86345
    #PClass2nd    -0.11079
    #PClass3rd    -0.74226
    #Age          -0.15205
    #Sexmale      -0.53578
    #TitleMr      -0.48990
    #TitleMrs      0.12372
    #TitleNothing  .      

    #extract the information for standardisations of new test data
    titanicMod$preProcess$mean
    #OUTPUTS
    #PClass2nd    PClass3rd          Age      Sexmale      TitleMr     TitleMrs TitleNothing 
    #0.20994      0.54361     30.25872      0.65822      0.57911      0.14706      0.10142 

    titanicMod$preProcess$std
    #OUTPUTS
    #PClass2nd    PClass3rd          Age      Sexmale      TitleMr     TitleMrs TitleNothing 
    #0.40747      0.49835     14.37039      0.47455      0.49395      0.35434      0.30204 

    #compare predict to manually calculating the prob by just predicting first row of test data
    predict(titanicMod, testDF[1,], type = "prob", na.action = na.pass)
    #This gives a probability of survival as 0.78292

    #function to input untransformed predictor variables (those that were featured selected) for standardisation, calculation of logit and then output probability
    probSurvival = function(x_PClass2nd,x_PClass3rd,x_Age,x_Sexmale,x_TitleMr,x_TitleMrs){
  
      #Define the beta coefficients from above
      B_intercept = -0.86345
      B_PClass2nd = -0.11079
      B_PClass3rd = -0.74226
      B_Age = -0.15205
      B_Sexmale = -0.53578
      B_TitleMr =  -0.48990
      B_TitleMrs = 0.12372
  
      #standardise the predictor variables from above information for standardisation
      z_PClass2nd = (x_PClass2nd-0.20994)/0.40747
      z_PClass3rd = (x_PClass3rd-0.54361)/0.49835
      z_Age = (x_Age-30.25872)/14.37039
      z_Sexmale = (x_Sexmale-0.65822)/0.47455
      z_TitleMr = (x_TitleMr-0.57911)/0.49395 
      z_TitleMrs = (x_TitleMrs-0.14706)/0.35434
  
      #calculate logit survival
      logitSurvival = B_intercept + (B_PClass2nd * z_PClass2nd) + (B_PClass3rd * z_PClass3rd) + (B_Age * z_Age) + (B_Sexmale * z_Sexmale) + (B_TitleMr * z_TitleMr) + (B_TitleMrs * z_TitleMrs)
      #convert logit to probability
      probSurvival = 1/(1+exp(-logitSurvival))
  
      return(probSurvival)
    }

    #Testing the first row of testDF manually should give same probability of survival
    testDF[1,]
    #OUTPUTS
    #  PClass Age    Sex Title Survived
    #1    1st  29 female  Miss      Yes
    
    #Enter the values manually 
    probSurvival(0,0,29,0,0,0)
    #Gives a probability of 0.50416 which is not the same as predict!

Potential problems with caret/nnet
description:
Dear all, 
There might be two problems with caret/nnet. Or I might have misunderstood
something. Regards, Bernard

Potential problem no. 1: the manual calculation of the RMSECV of a LOOCV does not match
the output of caret and nnet, if size and decay values are to be optimized in a grid.
However, the manual calculation matches the output of caret and nnet, if size and decay
are not optimized in a grid.

Potential problem no. 2: set.seed() works fine with caret and kernlab: I get the 
same optimal results including the correct RMSECV from caret, independent, whether a grid search is done or the optimal values from the grid search are taken afterwards. In contrast: with caret and nnet this
is not the case (see below).

If you are filing a bug, make sure these boxes are checked before submitting your issue— thank you!

- [x ] Start a new R session
- [x ] Install the latest version of caret: `update.packages(oldPkgs="caret", ask=FALSE)`
- [x ] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [x ] run `sessionInfo()`

### Minimal, reproducible example:
``` r
require(pls) # taking gasoline data as input
#> Lade nötiges Paket: pls
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'pls'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     loadings
require(caret)
#> Lade nötiges Paket: caret
#> Lade nötiges Paket: lattice
#> Lade nötiges Paket: ggplot2
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'caret'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:pls':
#> 
#>     R2
require(nnet)
#> Lade nötiges Paket: nnet


# calculating the scores which will be the predictors for nnet
# only the units with odd numbers will be taken in the cross-validation
odd <- seq(1,nrow(gasoline$NIR),by=2);odd[c(1:4,length(odd))]
#> [1]  1  3  5  7 59
X <- scale(gasoline$NIR, scale=F, center = colMeans(gasoline$NIR[odd,]))
Xodd.svd <- svd(X[odd,])
Xodd.scores <- Xodd.svd$u %*% diag(Xodd.svd$d)

# preparing the data frame: 1st column: response variable
# other columns: predictors
ann_cali <- data.frame(gasoline$octane[odd],Xodd.scores)

net_grid <- expand.grid(size = seq(from = 1, to = 10, by = 1),           
                        decay = seq(from = 0, to = 1, by = 0.1))         

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "LOOCV", savePred=T)

set.seed(77)

mod <- train(gasoline.octane.odd. ~ ., data = ann_cali, linout=T,trace=F,
             method = "nnet", tuneGrid = net_grid,trControl = ctrl)

# optimum size and decay
mod$bestTune$size
#> [1] 9
mod$bestTune$decay
#> [1] 0.1

# manual calculation of the sum of squares of residuals by extracting
# the measured and modelled values from the object calculated by caret
# with the optimum size and decay
sum_of_squares_cv <- sum((mod$pred[mod$pred$size==mod$bestTune$size& 
                                     mod$results$decay==mod$bestTune$decay,2]-  
                            mod$pred[mod$pred$size==mod$bestTune$size& 
                                       mod$results$decay==mod$bestTune$decay,1])^2)

# manual calculation of the rmsecv from the sum of squares
rmse_cv <- sqrt(sum_of_squares_cv/length(mod$pred[mod$pred$size==mod$bestTune$size& 
                                                    mod$results$decay==mod$bestTune$decay,2]))
rmse_cv
#> [1] 1.274447

# caret gets a different result of the rmsecv for the optimum size and decay
rmse_cv_caret <- mod$results[mod$results$size==mod$bestTune$size & 
                               mod$results$decay==mod$bestTune$decay,]$RMSE
rmse_cv_caret
#> [1] 0.3933177

# my rmse_cv calculated manually is also in the rmse result object of caret but with
# a different size and decay
mod$results[which(mod$results$RMSE == rmse_cv),] 
#>    size decay     RMSE  Rsquared      MAE
#> 96    9   0.7 1.274447 0.2930981 1.074333

# rmse_cv_caret and size and decay according to caret

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "LOOCV", savePred=T)

set.seed(77)
```
