title: Bug when using `ranger` with factors in regression mode
description:
I've found a possible bug when using the `ranger` method in regression mode AND some of the predictors are factors:

First, we add a random factor to `mtcars`:

```
data(mtcars)
mtcars$rand_fact <- sample(LETTERS[1:3], size = nrow(mtcars), replace = TRUE)
head(mtcars)
```

Then we build two models: a "reference" model using the `ranger` library, and another one using the `caret` API: 

```
library(caret)
library(ranger)

fit_rg <- ranger(
  formula = mpg ~ ., 
  data = mtcars,
  mtry = 3,
  min.node.size = 3,
  splitrule = "variance",
  importance = "impurity"
)

fit_ct <- caret::train(
  form = mpg ~ .,
  data = mtcars,
  trControl = caret::trainControl(
    returnData = TRUE,
    method = "cv",
    number = 5
  ),
  method = "ranger"
)
```

When trying to run `predict` directly on the resulting object, it fails for `caret`:

```
> predict(fit_rg, data = mtcars)
Ranger prediction

Type:                             Regression 
Sample size:                      32 
Number of independent variables:  11 

> predict(fit_ct, data = mtcars)
 Error in `[.data.frame`(data, , forest$independent.variable.names, drop = FALSE) : 
  undefined columns selected 
```

It can be track down to discrepancies in the model object, in particular it seems one column of data is generated for each factor level:

```
> fit_rg$forest$dependent.varID
[1] 0
> fit_ct$finalModel$forest$dependent.varID
[1] 12
```

and

```
> fit_rg$forest$independent.variable.names
 [1] "cyl"       "disp"      "hp"        "drat"      "wt"        "qsec"      "vs"        "am"       
 [9] "gear"      "carb"      "rand_fact"
> fit_ct$finalModel$forest$independent.variable.names
 [1] "cyl"        "disp"       "hp"         "drat"       "wt"         "qsec"       "vs"        
 [8] "am"         "gear"       "carb"       "rand_factB" "rand_factC"
> 
```

The latter seems to explain the `undefined columns selected` when trying to run `predict`.

title: Possible bug for learing_curve_dat() when using a multiclass classification problem with MXNET
description:
I am trying to plot a learning curve using learing_curve_dat() for a multiclass classification problem (with 10 classes) using the neural network option 'mxnet'. Although the learning curve function seems to work for binary mxnet problems, it looks like it fails with multiclass problems.

Below is a reproducible example using the Iris dataset (multiclass with 3 classes), which fails when using 'mxnet' (or "lda").  

```{R}
library(caret)
library(mxnet)
data(iris)

set.seed(2345)

trctrl <- trainControl(method='none', verboseIter=TRUE, returnData=TRUE, classProbs=TRUE, summaryFunction=multiClassSummary)

nnet.grid <- expand.grid(layer1=30, layer2=6, layer3=3, learning.rate = 0.1, momentum = 0, dropout=0, activation='tanh')

learn_data <- learing_curve_dat(dat = iris, 
                              outcome = "Species",
                              test_prop = 0.2,
                              verbose=TRUE,
                              ## `train` arguments:
                              method = "mxnet", 
                              metric = "ROC",
                              tuneGrid = nnet.grid,
                              trControl = trctrl)

ggplot(learn_data, aes(x = Training_Size, y = Accuracy, color = Data)) + 
  geom_smooth(method = loess, span = .8) + 
  theme_bw()

```
However this stops running with the following error: 

```{R}
Error in `$<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, "Training_Size", value = 12L) : 
  replacement has 1 row, data has 0
```

Here is another example to show that the learning curve function works when using mxnet with a binary problem.  

```{R}
set.seed(2345)

class_dat <- twoClassSim(1000)

nnet.grid <- expand.grid(layer1=30, layer2=6, layer3=10, learning.rate = 0.1, momentum = 0, dropout=0, activation='tanh')

binary_data <- learing_curve_dat(dat = class_dat, 
                              outcome = "Class",
                              test_prop = 0.2, 
                              ## `train` arguments:
                              method = "mxnet", 
                              metric = "ROC",
                              tuneGrid = nnet.grid,
                              trControl = trainControl(classProbs = TRUE, 
                                                       summaryFunction = twoClassSummary))

ggplot(binary_data, aes(x = Training_Size, y = ROC, color = Data)) + 
  geom_smooth(method = loess, span = .8) + 
  theme_bw()

title: update.train making .weights an independent variable when method = 'ranger'
description:
As the title says. I am trying to override the train object $bestTune to get a different $finalModel for prediction. I am not entirely sure if this should be placed here or with ranger. Thanks.

### Minimal, reproducible example:
```{R}
library(caret)

grid <- expand.grid(mtry = 1:2,
                    min.node.size = c(5, 10, 15),
                    splitrule = "variance" )

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv",
                     number = 5)

## define response for model
response <- iris$Sepal.Length / iris$Sepal.Width
## define case.weights for ranger
wgt <- iris$Sepal.Width

## fit initial train using ranger
trn.ranger <- train( y = response,
                     x = iris[, 3:5],
                     weights = wgt,
                     method = "ranger",
                     tuneGrid = grid,
                     verbose = F,
                     trControl = ctrl,
                     num.trees = 20,
                     importance = "impurity")

varImp(trn.ranger) ## 3 features in model
trn.ranger$bestTune ##bestTune is mtry=1, min.node.size = 10

## update to choose different bestTune
trn.ranger.update <- update(trn.ranger, param = list(mtry = 2, 
                                                     splitrule = "variance", 
                                                     min.node.size = 15))
varImp(trn.ranger.update) ## new 4th feature is .weights

## error due to .weights column does not exist in newdata
predict(trn.ranger.update, newdata = iris)

title: recipe returned by train != recipe trained for finalModel when indexFinal is specified
description:
(First - thanks for caret, recipes, and the whole list of fun toys coming down the pipe. I use your tools every day!)

I'm a heavy user of custom resampling setups, specified in `trainControl` with `index`, `indexOut`, and `indexFinal`. I've switched most of my feature engineering logic to `recipes` run through train in (what I think is) the recommended way. Here's the issue I stumbled on:

`train` returns a `recipe` object. I have always expected that object to be a prepped recipe, with prep done using the same training dataset as `finalModel`, so that you can use this for baking new data. This is true generally, but I think there's an exception when an `indexFinal` is specified in `trainControl`. It looks like ([line 1003 in caret/train.default.R](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/fa5817ca52420ec807830e19a173b6a91dff0fe4/pkg/caret/R/train.default.R#L1003)) the recipe train is done directly on the `data` input, so it bypasses the `indexFinal` subsetting. 

The consequence is that `predict.train.recipe` fails whenever (by coincidence) the recipe prepped on full data has a different set of terms than the recipe prepped on the `indexFinal` subset (which are the terms `finalModel` knew about). The consequence is invisible, unless the difference grows large enough that it leads to different terms being retained (like, which PC components fall above/below the retained variance threshold). I've looked back at prior code and found differences in the returned prepped recipe and what finalModel would have seen, and only when an indexFinal was specified, but it was only last night that I saw the difference grow large enough to cause a mismatch in terms.

As far as I can tell, everything is correct in the recipe prep and training for `finalModel`. The reprex below demonstrates both of these cases.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(caret)
library(ranger)
library(recipes)
data(iris)

devtools::session_info()

# Setup: we're going to use a ranger model through caret::train, where we
# specify an indexFinal in the trainControl that is a much smaller number of rows than
# the full dataset we passed in. (This example is contrived for illustration.)
# After model train, we'll show that (a) the recipe returned in the train object
# has a different set of predictors from a recipe manually prepped on the data
# that our indexFinal setting would have yielded; and (b) we see an error thrown
# when we try to predict from the train object normally, but not when we predict
# using ranger's own generic and the manually-prepped data.

# Make many rows of randomly-sampled-with-replacement/randomly-ordered iris rows.
# Then add random noise to everything. The goal is to increase the number of 
# PCs we can work with in a step_pca, because it's easiest to see this issue
# when the recipe returned by train and finalModel have different predictors.

sample_nrow <- 1000 # how many extra rows we're creating from iris for training
indexFinal_nrow <- 50 # how many rows of the full set go to indexFinal

set.seed(1234)
iris_noisy <- iris %>%
  dplyr::sample_n(size = sample_nrow, replace = TRUE) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(starts_with("Sepal"), starts_with("Petal")),
            funs(plusrand_1 = . + rnorm(n = sample_nrow, mean = 0, sd = 10),
                 plusrand_2 = . + rnorm(n = sample_nrow, mean = 0, sd = 100),
                 plusrand_3 = . + rnorm(n = sample_nrow, mean = 0, sd = 1000)))

iris_recipe <- recipe(Species ~ .,
                      data = iris_noisy) %>%
  step_center(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_scale(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_pca(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.7)

iris_rf <- train(iris_recipe, 
                 data = iris_noisy,
                 method = "ranger", 
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "boot",
                                          number = 10,
                                          indexFinal = c(1:indexFinal_nrow)))

# > # This fails with error 'undefined columns selected'
# > predict(iris_rf, newdata = iris_noisy)
#  Show Traceback
#  
#  Rerun with Debug
#  Error in `[.data.frame`(data.selected, , (forest$dependent.varID + 1):ncol(data.selected)) : 
#   undefined columns selected 
# 
# > caret:::predict.train.recipe(iris_rf, newdata = iris_noisy)
#  Show Traceback
#  
#  Rerun with Debug
#  Error in `[.data.frame`(data.selected, , (forest$dependent.varID + 1):ncol(data.selected)) : 
#   undefined columns selected 

# NEXT: 
# Manually prep a recipe on the data specified in indexFinal, then
# predict through ranger on the baked full dataset
manually_prepped_recipe <- prep(iris_recipe, 
                                training = iris_noisy[1:indexFinal_nrow, ])

ranger:::predict.ranger(iris_rf$finalModel, 
                        data = bake(manually_prepped_recipe, 
                                    newdata = iris_noisy))
# ranger:::predict.ranger works just fine

# > manually_prepped_recipe <- prep(iris_recipe, 
# +                                 training = iris_noisy[1:indexFinal_nrow, ])
# > ranger:::predict.ranger(iris_rf$finalModel, 
# +                         data = bake(manually_prepped_recipe, 
# +                                     newdata = iris_noisy))
# Ranger prediction
# 
# Type:                             Classification 
# Sample size:                      1000 
# Number of independent variables:  7 
# > 

# NEXT
# Here, let's look at the variables that are in the prepped recipe from iris_rf
# and the recipe we prepped manually.
iris_rf$recipe$term_info$variable
manually_prepped_recipe$term_info$variable
# > iris_rf$recipe$term_info$variable
#  [1] "Species" "PC1"     "PC2"     "PC3"     "PC4"     "PC5"     "PC6"     "PC7"     "PC8"     "PC9"    
# > manually_prepped_recipe$term_info$variable
# [1] "Species" "PC1"     "PC2"     "PC3"     "PC4"     "PC5"     "PC6"     "PC7"    

# Pretty clear what happened - iris_rf$recipe has 9 PCs under 70% cumvar threshold
# while the manually prepped recipe (fewer rows, less variation) has 7 PCs

all.equal(iris_rf$recipe,
          manually_prepped_recipe)

# Check for equality of recipe prepped on full data and in iris_rf$recipe
manually_prepped_recipe_fulldata <- prep(iris_recipe, 
                                         training = iris_noisy, 
                                         retain = TRUE)

all.equal(iris_rf$recipe, manually_prepped_recipe_fulldata)

# > manually_prepped_recipe_fulldata <- prep(iris_recipe, 
# +                                          training = iris_noisy, 
# +                                          retain = TRUE)
# > all.equal(iris_rf$recipe,
# +           manually_prepped_recipe_fulldata)
# [1] TRUE

```

title: recipes and all_outcomes
description:
Hi,

I'm currently using the very useful package recipes to define data transformations.  If I make transformations on the outcome variables, the predict function returns the prediction of the transformed response.

Example:
```
library(caret); library(recipes)
data(cox2)
cox2 <- cox2Descr
cox2$potency <- cox2IC50

cox2_recipe <- recipe(potency ~ ., data = cox2) %>%
  step_log(potency, base = 10) %>%
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_pca(contains("VSA"), prefix = "surf_area_", 
    threshold = .95) %>%
  step_corr(all_predictors(), -starts_with("surf_area_"), 
    threshold = .90) %>%
  step_center(all_predictors(), -starts_with("surf_area_")) %>%
  step_scale(all_predictors(), -starts_with("surf_area_"))

set.seed(888)
cox2_lm <- train(cox2_recipe, 
  data = cox2,
  method = "lm", 
  trControl = trainControl(method = "cv"))

predict(cox2_lm, newdata = cox2) # on the log scale
```
Am I using caret/recipes correctly?  If so, could the functionality to ~reserve~ (reverse?) the transformation be added to caret predict function?

Thank you for all your help, best wishes,

Oli

title: Predict using only features selected in a final model
description:
Hi, I have built a model using caret which I would like to distribute. The final model uses less features than the features inputted as training data. Ideally, users could input new data with only the subset of features used in the final model. This is desirable because the original number of features is many many times larger than the final features. However, I notice 'predict()' will require all training features to present in any new sample to be ran on. To this end, I fiddled around trying to extract the components of the modelFit object (e.g. modelFit$Finalmodel) for quite awhile, with no success. I hope it is ok to post this as an 'issue', but I would appreciate direction to the proper forum if this is not it.

Below I post the development of a glmnet model, and then the ideal code a user would have to execute to get predictions on data with only features used in the final model. 

```{R}
# training data
library(caret)
set.seed(1)
dat <- twoClassSim(100, noiseVars = 5)
X <- dat[,1:20]
y <- dat[["Class"]]

# fit glmnet model
glm_fit <- train(
  X, y, 
  metric='ROC',
  method = 'glmnet',
  trControl=trainControl(
    method="cv", 
    number=5,
    classProbs=TRUE, 
    summaryFunction=twoClassSummary,
    savePredictions="final")
)

length(predictors(glm_fit)) 
ncol(X) # 15 / 20 variables in final model

# predict on new samples, where only the 15 variables used in the final model are present
set.seed(2)
newDat <- twoClassSim(100, noiseVars = 5)
newDat_subset <- newDat[,predictors(glm_fit)] # subset out 15 final predictors
dim(newDat_subset) # 100 15

predict(glm_fit, newDat_subset) # error
```

title: variable importance for vanilla linear model?!
description:
Hi @topepo ,

I hope all is well. I was reading the docs about the variable importance in `caret` and found that for linear models you take the absolute value of the t-stat.

I wonder if there is some literature that supports that argument. Indeed, I thought that (assuming your variables are standardized), for the purpose of prediction it is the absolute size of the coefficient that matters. Also, with many many variables it is problematic to compare the t-stats, as many will be type -I errors. 

In essence, statistical inference and prediction/variable importance are often two different animals. But I know you are a stats PhD, so there must be some interesting insight here.

What do you think? Thanks!!

title: New parameters in custom prediction function
description:
Hi,
I'm trying to use caret for a special application in genetics. Thus I need to handle different input formats, that's why I can't provide you a reproducing example.
To do that,  I coded a custom fit and predict function. I entered these functions in caret like here:
```{r}
caretMeth<- list(library=c("qtl"),
                    type="Regression",
                    parameters=caretParam,
                    grid=caretGrid,
                    fit=custom_caretFit,
                    predict=custom_caretPredict,
                    prob=NULL,
                    sort=NULL)
```

The custom fit and predict function work fine alone but when I'm using `train` I got an error: `Error in { : task 1 failed`. I search where it comes from and I found that in `nominalTrainWorkflow` function, which is called in `train.default` function, at line 58, the function `predictionFunction` is called. 

I ran manually `train.default`, `nominalTrainWorkflow` and `predictionFunction` and I figured out that the new parameter (new_param), which is in `custom_caretPredict` was not called. I got the error : `Argument "new_param" is missing, with no default` or if I enter new_param as argument of `predictionFunction`, I get `unused argument (new_param)`.

 
###  predictionFunction 
```
predicted <- try(predictionFunction(method = method,
                      modelFit = mod$fit, newdata = caret:::subset_x(x, holdoutIndex),
                      preProc = mod$preProc, param = submod), silent = TRUE)
```
              
If I modify manually `predictionFunction` to introduce new_param as an argument in the function and inside the function, I get the prediction:

```
function (method, modelFit, newdata, preProc = NULL, param = NULL, new_param) 
{
  if (!is.null(newdata) && !is.null(preProc)) 
    newdata <- predict(preProc, newdata)
  out <- method$predict(modelFit = modelFit, newdata = newdata, 
                        new_param=new_param,
                        submodels = param)
  out
}
```
I already had to enter more parameters in `custom_caretFit` function and I had no problem with that.
I don't know if it's really the function `predictionFunction`which does not accept other parameters or if I coded `custom_caretPredict`or `train` functions in the wrong way (I put all parameters in train, no matter if there will be useful for `custom_caretFit` or `custom_caretPredict` function).


### custom_caretPredict function

```
custom_caretPredict <- function(modelFit,new_param, newdata, submodels=NULL) {
  newdata <- t(newdata)
  jm <- cbind(new_param, newdata)
  X <- rutilstimflutre::joinMap2designMatrix(jm=jm, rm.col.zeros = TRUE, verbose=0)
  X <- X[, -1] # remove intercept
  allelic.effects <- as.matrix(modelFit$allelic.effects$effect)
  rownames(allelic.effects) <- modelFit$allelic.effects$predictor
  
  stopifnot(dim(X)[2] == nrow(allelic.effects))
  out <- X %*% allelic.effects
  write(head(out[,1]), stderr())
  
  return(out[,1])
}
```

title: Horizons and Multi-Step Forecasts in a Time-Series Setting
description:
Hi, I've recently been using Caret to test various models in a time-series context. In doing so, I am a little unclear on the specific meaning of the horizon parameter. In the online documentation found at https://topepo.github.io/caret/data-splitting.html#data-splitting-for-time-series . it seems that I specify a training window size, and suppose I keep this fixed. Then, I specify a horizon, say 5 as in the example.

When I specify this horizon, am I correct in thinking this is not the same as a mulit-step forecast? My current thinking is, we train the model in the specified training window, and then forecast 1 step ahead. Without retraining the model, we give it data for the next step and again forecast 1 step ahead, repeating this until we have 5 forecasts, each of which were actually 1 step ahead from the data presented.

As far as I understand, the alternative would be that caret either: 
1) iteratively computes forecasts, however in the context of say regression, we would need to use the future values of the covariates to forecast.
2) trains k separate models, in this case 5, each of which is trained to forecast a single point, but trained on different horizons. 

If these truly are 5 1-step ahead forecasts, is the correct way to go about multi-step forecasts to alter my input matrix to directly align responses k minutes ahead with predictors at any given time?

Any clarification you can provide on this will be very useful, thanks in advance.

I traced back and found the error to be here:

https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/6546939345fe10649cefcbfee55d58fb682bc902/pkg/caret/R/workflows.R#L276-L279 

This is caused by this line 

https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/6546939345fe10649cefcbfee55d58fb682bc902/pkg/caret/R/workflows.R#L263

library(caret)

mccSummary <- function(data, lev = NULL, model = NULL) {

  # convert to one hot format
  oh <- dummyVars(~ obs, data = data)

  # get class probabilities, make sure they are in the same column order
  # as target labels, mcc cannot take data.frame so need matrix as input
  pred.probs <- as.matrix(data[, lvls])
  
  out <- ModelMetrics::mcc(actual = obs.oh, 
                           predicted =pred.probs,

title: offset in xgbtree poisson regression
description:
Hi!

I am piggybacking on this issue (https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/507) which asked questions about both offsets and early_stopping and the answer was that one would need to create a custom method.

I am re-opening this question, because it appears that offsets ("base_margins")  are used by caret when we feed caret::train a  "xgb.Dmatrix" object.  At least, the predictions are very affected by the offsets.

However, it appears that the offsets are not used when saving the  out-of-fold predictions generated using kfold.   

If that is correct, is there are way to extract them?  Maybe multiplying the result by offset/ mean(offset) ?

Here is an example code, widely inspired by the code at issue #507.

![80bd97f9-7d60-4479-bfa3-ad9fd248abe1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23444900/37616156-6cbd58ec-2b85-11e8-9b32-5fdae7ef754e.png)


```
library(xgboost)
library(dplyr)
library(caret)
library(insuranceData) # example dataset https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/insuranceData/insuranceData.pdf
library(pdp) # partial dependency plots
library(lime) # Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
library(gridExtra)
set.seed(123)
data(dataCar)
mydb <- dataCar %>% select(clm, exposure, veh_value, veh_body,
                           veh_age, gender, area, agecat)

label_var <- "clm"  
offset_var <- "exposure"
feature_vars <- mydb %>% 
  select(-one_of(c(label_var, offset_var))) %>% 
  colnames()


#preparing data for xgboost (one hot encoding of categorical (factor) data
myformula <- paste0( "~", paste0( feature_vars, collapse = " + ") ) %>% as.formula()
dummyFier <- caret::dummyVars(myformula, data=mydb, fullRank = TRUE)
dummyVars.df <- predict(dummyFier,newdata = mydb)
mydb_dummy <- cbind(mydb %>% select(one_of(c(label_var, offset_var))), 
                    dummyVars.df)
rm(myformula, dummyFier, dummyVars.df)



feature_vars_dummy <-  mydb_dummy  %>% select(-one_of(c(label_var, offset_var))) %>% colnames()

mydb_xgbmatrix <- xgb.DMatrix(
  data = mydb_dummy %>% select(feature_vars_dummy) %>% as.matrix, 
  label = mydb_dummy %>% pull(label_var),
  missing = "NAN")


#first issue with caret: specifying a base margin to the matrices
#base_margin: base margin is the base prediction Xgboost will boost from

title: train.default's predictions are not consistent with the returned model's predictions
description:

title: Predicting on left-out folds with recipes, rsample and step_downsample: discrepancies
description:
- [✓] Start a new R session
- [✓] Install the latest version of caret: `update.packages(oldPkgs="caret", ask=FALSE)`
- [✓] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [✓] run `sessionInfo()`

## Problem description

When downsampling is used as a step in a `recipe`, the predictions on the fold left out differs between that produced by `caret` and that produced just using `recipes` and `rsample` [as described in this vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rsample/vignettes/Recipes_and_rsample.html). 

The predictions are equal when the downsampling step is not used. The location of `step_downsample` in the order of steps appears not to matter. I have not investigated if any other `recipies::step_...` function results in similar discrepancies.

### Minimal, reproducible example:

#### Minimal dataset:
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
#> Loading required package: broom
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'rsample'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:tidyr':
#> 
#>     fill
library(recipes)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stringr':
#> 
#>     fixed
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
library(caret)
#> Loading required package: lattice
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'caret'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:purrr':
#> 
#>     lift

# Simulate data 
set.seed(1)
n_obs <- 100
df <- tibble(X1 = rnorm(n_obs), X2 = rnorm(n_obs),
             unbalanced_factor = ifelse(runif(n_obs) > 0.1, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  mutate(response = -0.1 - exp(X1) + X2^2)

```


#### Minimal, runnable code:
```{r}
# Extract training set and its cross-validation folds, and test set
df_split <- df %>% initial_split(prop = 0.8)

training_set <- training(df_split)
test_set <- testing(df_split)

cv_split <- vfold_cv(training_set, v = 5)

# Specify basic recipe
rec <- recipe(response ~ ., data = training_set) %>%
  step_center(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_scale(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_downsample(unbalanced_factor)

# Get fold indices to be used in calls to caret::train
cv_indices <- rsample2caret(cv_split)

# Fit linear model in caret
myControl <- trainControl(method = "cv", 
                          number = 5,
                          savePredictions = TRUE,
                          index = cv_indices$index,
                          indexOut = cv_indices$indexOut)

lm_trained <- train(rec, 
                    data = training_set, 
                    method = "lm",
                    trControl = myControl)

# Fit model model as described in the "Recipes and rsample" vignette

# Apply recipe to cross-validation splits
cv_split$recipes <- purrr::map(cv_split$splits, prepper, recipe = rec, 
                               retain = TRUE)

fit_lm <- function(rec_obj, ...) lm(..., data = juice(rec_obj, everything()))

cv_split$lm_mod <- map(cv_split$recipes, fit_lm, response ~ .)

pred_lm <- function(split_obj, rec_obj, model_obj, ...) {
  mod_data <- bake(
    rec_obj, 
    newdata = assessment(split_obj),
    all_predictors(),
    all_outcomes()
  ) 
  
  out <- mod_data %>% select(response)
  out$predicted <- predict(model_obj, newdata = mod_data %>% select(-response))
  out
}

# Make the predictions
cv_split$pred <- pmap(lst(split_obj = cv_split$splits, 
                          rec_obj = cv_split$recipes, 
                          model_obj = cv_split$lm_mod),
                      pred_lm)

rmse <- function(dat) sqrt(mean((dat$response - dat$predicted)^2))
cv_split$RMSE <- map_dbl(cv_split$pred, rmse)

# Compare caret's prediction to those made using rsample
(preds <- lm_trained$pred %>%
  group_by(Resample) %>%
  mutate(error_sq = (obs - pred)^2) %>%
  summarize(caret_RMSE = sqrt(mean(error_sq))) %>%
  mutate(resample_RMSE = cv_split$RMSE))
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   Resample caret_RMSE resample_RMSE
#>   <chr>         <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 Fold1          2.61          2.61
#> 2 Fold2          1.03          1.38
#> 3 Fold3          1.91          1.66
#> 4 Fold4          2.06          2.95
#> 5 Fold5          1.75          1.42

title: Sample size of each resample in the bootstrap
description:
I am calculating a performance metric based on the resamples obtained from cross-validation and bootstrap.

### Minimal, reproducible example:

library(caret)
library(tidyverse)
data(iris)
TrainData <- iris[,1:4]
TrainClasses <- iris[,5]

control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, 
                        returnResamp = "all",
                        savePredictions = TRUE, classProbs = TRUE,  
                        summaryFunction = multiClassSummary)

fit <- train(TrainData, TrainClasses,
             method = "glmnet",
             preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
             tuneGrid =  expand.grid(alpha = 1,
                                     lambda = seq(0.000, 0.3,by = 0.05)),
             trControl = control)
pred_cv <- as_data_frame(fit$pred) %>% 
  filter(lambda == fit$finalModel$lambdaOpt) %>% nest(-Resample)

control <- trainControl(method = "boot632", number = 10, 
                        returnResamp = "all",
                        savePredictions = TRUE, classProbs = TRUE,  
                        summaryFunction = multiClassSummary)

fit <- train(TrainData, TrainClasses,
             method = "glmnet",
             preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
             tuneGrid =  expand.grid(alpha = 1,
                                     lambda = seq(0.000, 0.3,by = 0.05)),
             trControl = control)
pred_boot <- as_data_frame(fit$pred) %>% 
  filter(lambda == fit$finalModel$lambdaOpt) %>% nest(-Resample)
pred_cv
pred_boot

```
The number of rows of each data frame in the two lists (pred_cv$data and pred_boot$data) above is the sample size for each resample. The sample size for each resample using Cross-Validation is always the same as expected and defined by the number of folds in the function trainControl. On the other hand, it is not the same using bootstrap, even though the same sample size is expected.

Is there any reason that the sample size is different for each resample? Is there any way to control it?

title: Bayesian Optimization of Machine Learning Models
Nested parallelism with xgboost
description:
Should `caret` and/or the parallel backend avoid nested parallelism?

As described in the [documentation](http://topepo.github.io/caret/parallel-processing.html), using certain functions in combination with using a parallel backend with P processors results in P^2 processes. I found out that xgboost (xgbLinear, xgbTree, etc) happens to be one of these functions.

This results in a P-core processor being overloaded by a factor of P, greatly increasing computation time (5x slowdown in one of my tests).

Workarounds:

- have xgboost use one thread (via `nthread=1` parameter in `caret::train`, or `tuneList=list(xgbLinear=caretModelSpec(method="xgbLinear", nthread=1))` in `caretEnsemble::caretList`) while using a parallel backend (`doMC`, `doFuture`, etc) and `allowParallel=TRUE`
- let xgboost parallelize which it does by default, and set caret's `allowParallel=FALSE` and/or don't use a parallel backend

It seems there may be some performance difference between the two options above, as indicated [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/39528392/parallel-processing-with-xgboost-and-caret).

I tried using the `doFuture` backend since @HenrikBengtsson mentioned in [another issue](https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/449) that it would automatically prevent this problem, but at least with xgboost I still counted P^2 processes in `htop`.

title: caret::train requires excessive amounts of memory with the xgbTree method
description:
This is a follow up to issue #870. `caret::train` is gobbling up memory to exhaustion with a 2 GB regression matrix, which I initially thought was cased by the number of sub-processes it triggers (taking up all of the available CPUs). After learning about the `nthread` argument I was able to control the number of CPUs used, however, the memory issues did not go away. Even with a single CPU `caret::train` exhausts the 26 GB of RAM in my workstation and is terminated by the OS.

I thus [sought help with the XGBoost community](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/xgboost-user/FFw9VpsEch8). The full enquiry:

> I am presently working with an R script that trains a model using the *xgbTree* method through the `caret::train` function. Something like:
> 
> `mXGB <- caret::train(theFormula, data=dfs, method="xgbTree", trControl=ctrl, tuneGrid=gb.tuneGrid, nthread=2) `
> 
> The dfs dataset takes up about 2 GB of RAM. However, as the training starts, those two processes start consuming memory up to exhaustion. This is in a workstation with 26 GB of RAM.
> 
> Why is this method taking up so much memory? Is there any way to manage memory with this method? 
> 
> The software I am using:
> R 3.4.4
> caret 6.0.79
> xgboost 0.6.4.1

The reply sheds some light into it:

> Don't use caret::train's formula interface in this case. Its internal 
> processing does not take advantage of XGBoost's data structures, so it's 
> making a separate data frames for each CV fold, then another copy for 
> each fold to construct an xgb.DMatrix etc., so e.g. in a 10-fold CV it 
> may make at least 20 copies of your data. That was the state of caret's 
> code last time I tried doing what you do, and I suspect this didn't 
> change if you're reporting it. I remember inspecting caret::train's code 
> and noting that making it work well would be quite a lot of work too. 
> 
> I think if you convert your data into an xgb.DMatrix and then call 
> `caret::train` using its the matrix interface, it might be fine. But I 
> remember having problems even with this approach. 
> 
> The R package of XGBoost has `xgb.cv` for cross-validation. It's simpler 
> than `caret::train`: you'll probably need to explicitly convert your 
> data frame into an `xgb.DMatrix` and perform preprocessing, a loop over 
> your parameter grid, etc. But then memory usage will be under control. 
> 
> I usually end up writing the whole process from scratch anyway, using 
> bare `xgb.train` or even calling the predict/update functions 
> explicitly. Somehow almost every time I use XGBoost models, some custom 
> need shows up demanding a non-trivial change to training or validation 
> schemes… 

This explains why `caret::train` is exhausting memory regardless of the number of sub-processes spawned by the `xgboost` routines.

My next step is to try the `xgb.DMatrix` data structure, but it seems to me that there is something wrong in requiring 40 GB of RAM to process a 2 GB dataset. If in fact `caret::train` is being used correctly.

title: XGBoost parameter tuning error (complaining missing columns while having them)
description:
Hi Max,

Thanks for providing such an awesome package, and supporting XGBoost.
I ran into the following problems when using caret for tuning XGBoost.
If you think this is an unfortunate bug, can you suggest any temporary work around please?
If not, can you tell what I did wrong?
Thanks!

---------------

### What I'm trying to do:
Using `caret` together with `XGBoost` to develop a binary classifier.

### What is happening:

Providing extra hyper-parameters to be tuned generates error with message
> Error: The tuning parameter grid should have columns nrounds, max_depth, eta, gamma, colsample_bytree, min_child_weight, subsample

In the following example, the parameter I'm trying to add is the second last parameter mentioned on [this page](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest//how_to/param_tuning.html) of XGBoost doc.
And it doesn't matter where I put this extra parameter when constructing the grid.

### What should be happening:

I'm not expecting this error message

### Minimal example code to reproduce

```R

library(caret)
library(xgboost)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# split train/test
set.seed(1)
testDataBinaryClass  <- twoClassSim(100)
intrain <- createDataPartition(y = testDataBinaryClass$Class, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
training <- testDataBinaryClass[intrain,]
testing <- testDataBinaryClass[-intrain,]

######################### hyper-parameter grid search
xgb_grid_1 = expand.grid(
    nrounds = 1000,
    # scale_pos_weight = 0.32, # uncommenting this line leads to the error
    eta = c(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3),
    max_depth = c(2, 4, 6, 8),
    gamma = c(1, 2, 3), 
    subsample = c(0.5, 0.75, 1),
    min_child_weight = c(1, 2, 3), 
    colsample_bytree = 1
)

xgb_trcontrol_1 = trainControl(
    method = "cv",
    number = 5,
    verboseIter = TRUE,
    returnData = FALSE,
    returnResamp = "all",
    classProbs = TRUE,
    allowParallel = TRUE
)

set.seed(1)

xgb_train_1 = train(
    x = as.matrix(training %>% select(-Class)),
    y = factor(training$Class, labels = c("TP", "FP")),
    trControl = xgb_trcontrol_1,
    tuneGrid = xgb_grid_1,
    method = "xgbTree"
)


```

title: Difference between formula and "x=, y=" in train()
description:
Hi,
I thought it was equivalent to express the input data in `train()` either as a formula (`y ~ x, data=`) or as `y=y, x=x` but I just found a difference when retrieving importances for the `rf` method. 

* If `train()` is expressed as a formula, then the importances will be given by factors' levels of the categorical variable. 
*  If `train()` is NOT expressed as formula, then the importances will be given for the whole factor variable, as expected.

The package `randomForest`, from which `train()` is based for this method, does not allow to express as a formula and only give the overall importances.

Where does this difference come from ? 

``` r
library(tidyverse)
data("chickwts")
# Add a numeric predictor in the data
dt <- data.frame(chickwts, xx = rnorm(length(chickwts$feed)))

rfCARET <- caret::train(
  y          = dt$weight,
  x          = dt %>% select(-weight),
  method     = "rf",
  importance = T
)
caret::varImp(rfCARET$finalModel)
#>         Overall
#> feed 46.4034574
#> xx   -0.4728728

rfCARET_form <- caret::train(
  weight ~ .,
  data       = dt,
  method     = "rf",
  importance = T
)
caret::varImp(rfCARET_form$finalModel)
#>                  Overall
#> feedhorsebean 29.3780596
#> feedlinseed   18.8974110
#> feedmeatmeal   1.8305809
#> feedsoybean   11.5654634
#> feedsunflower 13.5071325
#> xx            -0.6113386



## Try with RandomForest package. 

library(randomForest)
rf <- randomForest(x = dt %>% select(-weight),
                   y = dt$weight)
importance(rf)
#>      IncNodePurity
#> feed      213583.0
#> xx        129131.1
```

title: FeaturePlot tibble dependence

Feature plot sometimes returns a coercion error and sometimes does not, depending on how the data frame is input.

- [ X] Start a new R session

- [X ] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)

#### Minimal dataset:
```{R}
library(caret)
library(tidyverse)
# create dataset and base model
data_set <- diamonds %>%
  filter(row_number() <= 1000) %>%
  select(carat, depth)
```

featurePlot(x = as.data.frame(data_set[,-1]), y = as.data.frame(data_set[,1]))

title: Formula vs non-formula interface with train()
description:
Hello,

First, I cannot thank you enough for all your tremendous contributions with packages and book/seminars/webinars/courses. I am new to caret, and learning a lot everyday. I have the following issue that I [reported elsewhere](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47705991/formula-vs-non-formula-interface-in-train), and can see that others have had similar problems too, but haven't found a solution yet. The issue is that I can get`glmnet, ranger`and`xgbTree`working with formula interface for both classification and regression problem, but they all fail with non-formula interface. Judging by the consistency with which I am facing this issue, it could be either a feature of the models/methods that I am yet to understand, or perhaps something is wrong with my own setup. The only thing I know (?) is that the formula interface causes `train()`to convert each categorical variable into indicator variables, but not sure if that could be the source of this difference. All my datasets have multiple categorical predictors, so could not test with one that does not.

I could use my own codes/datasets here, but thought a better illustration could be with one of your example codes pasted below (taken from DataCamp course). The formula/non-formula interface and method can be chosen by uncommenting  appropriately. The error I get with this code is different from [what I get with my own code](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47705991/formula-vs-non-formula-interface-in-train), but the pattern of failure seems similar. I am using RStudio v1.1.382, R v3.4.3_x64, caret v6.0-78 (devtools version).

Thanks again,
Manojit

```
library(caret)
library(C50)
library(glmnet)
library(mlbench)
library(xgboost)

data(churn)

set.seed(42)
myFolds <- createFolds(churnTrain$churn, k = 5)

myControl <- trainControl(
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
  classProbs = T,
  savePredictions = T,
  index = myFolds,
  allowParallel = F
)

churnTrain$churn <- factor(churnTrain$churn, levels = c("no", "yes"))
X <- churnTrain[, !(names(churnTrain) %in% "churn")]
Y <- churnTrain$churn
fit <- train(
#  x = X, y = Y,                 # non-formula
  churn ~ ., churnTrain,         # formula
  metric = "ROC",
#  method = "glmnet",
  method = "ranger",
#  method = "xgbTree",
  trControl = myControl
)

print(plot(fit))

title: Seeds with Parallel Training
description:
Hello,

I have been training some models with different datasets and I noticed an issue that may be of concern when creating reproducible models with parallel training. I am using `doParallel` with `caret::train`. The problem I'm seeing is that even though I supply seeds, the model performance changes, usually for the better, after a repeat run of the model with the same data. After the first repeat, every subsequent repeat run produces the same performance. 

In short, the first run for any particular dataset always produces an irreproducible result, but subsequent runs with the same data and seeds always provide the same results. This is not a problem with a small dataset where multiple runs are easily doable but with a large dataset the computing expense to get a reproducible result increases very quickly. 

I am wondering if there's some way to get the reproducible result on the first run or if I am doing something wrong here. A short example follows:
```
library(caret)
require(doParallel)
data(iris)
cl<-makeCluster(detectCores())
registerDoParallel(cl)
svmradred_grid<-expand.grid(sigma = 0.015625, C =  64) #sigma = c(.125^(-3:4)), C = c(.125^(-3:4))
svmradredfit<-caret::train(Species ~ ., data=iris, 
                           method ="svmRadial", 
                           tuneGrid = svmradred_grid,
                           metric = "Kappa", 
                           preProcess = c("scale","center"),
                           trControl = trainControl(allowParallel = T, 
                                                    method = "cv",
                                                    number= 5,
                                                    savePredictions = T, 
                                                    seeds = list(837, 692, 246, 34, 132, 886)
                                                    )

svmradredfit

title: Possible bug in learnings_curve_dat()
description:
I think there is a bug in the ```caret::learing_curve_dat ()``` function (#278). The performance calculation for the test set is done on the model predictions of both, the test and train data set (line 36 of the function). 

Here is my minimal example. I added a few prints to the ```caret::learing_curve_dat ()``` function, to show the true performance compared to the one which is currently used.

Additionally, the typo in the function name was not fixed, mentioned in #278.

## Minimal, reproducible example:

``` r
require(plyr)
require(caret)
data(mtcars)

learing_curve_dat <- function(dat, 
                              outcome = NULL,
                              proportion = (1:10)/10, 
                              test_prop = 0, 
                              verbose = TRUE, ...) {
  if(is.null(outcome))
    stop("Please give a character stirng for the outcome column name")
  proportion <- sort(unique(proportion))
  n_size <- length(proportion)
  
  if(test_prop > 0) {
    for_model <- createDataPartition(dat[, outcome], p = 1 - test_prop, list = FALSE)
  } else for_model <- 1:nrow(dat)
  
  
  n <- length(for_model)
  
  resampled <- vector(mode = "list", length = n_size)
  tested <- if(test_prop > 0) resampled else NULL
  apparent <- resampled
  for(i in seq(along = proportion)) {
    if(verbose) cat("\nTraining for ", round(proportion[i]*100, 1), 
                    "% (n = ", floor(n*proportion[i]), ")\n", sep = "")
    in_mod <- if(proportion[i] < 1) sample(for_model, size = floor(n*proportion[i])) else for_model
    mod <- train(x = dat[in_mod, colnames(dat) != outcome, drop = FALSE],
                 y = dat[in_mod, outcome],
                 ...)
    
    
    if(i == 1) perf_names <- mod$perfNames
    resampled[[i]] <- merge(mod$resample, mod$bestTune)
    resampled[[i]]$Training_Size <- length(in_mod)
    
    if(test_prop > 0) {
      if(!mod$control$classProbs) {
        test_preds <- extractPrediction(list(model = mod), 
                                        testX = dat[-for_model, colnames(dat) != outcome, drop = FALSE],
                                        testY = dat[-for_model, outcome])
      } else {
        test_preds <- extractProb(list(model = mod), 
                                  testX = dat[-for_model, colnames(dat) != outcome, drop = FALSE],
                                  testY = dat[-for_model, outcome])
      }
      true_perf = plyr::ddply(test_preds, .(dataType), 
                              function(x) mod$control$summaryFunction(x, lev = mod$finalModel$obsLevels))
      test_perf <- mod$control$summaryFunction(test_preds, lev = mod$finalModel$obsLevels)
      print(rbind(data.frame(dataType="Total", 
                             RMSE=test_perf[1], 
                             Rsquared=test_perf[2], 
                             MAE=test_perf[3], row.names = 0), 
                  true_perf))
      test_perf <- as.data.frame(t(test_perf))
      test_perf$Training_Size <- length(in_mod)
      tested[[i]] <- test_perf
      try(rm(test_preds, test_perf), silent = TRUE)
    }
    
    if(!mod$control$classProbs) {
      app_preds <- extractPrediction(list(model = mod), 
                                     testX = dat[in_mod, colnames(dat) != outcome, drop = FALSE],
                                     testY = dat[in_mod, outcome])
    } else {
      app_preds <- extractProb(list(model = mod), 
                               testX = dat[in_mod, colnames(dat) != outcome, drop = FALSE],
                               testY = dat[in_mod, outcome])
    }
    app_perf <- mod$control$summaryFunction(app_preds, lev = mod$finalModel$obsLevels)
    app_perf <- as.data.frame(t(app_perf))
    app_perf$Training_Size <- length(in_mod)    
    apparent[[i]] <- app_perf
    
    try(rm(mod, in_mod, app_preds, app_perf), silent = TRUE)
  }
  
  resampled <- do.call("rbind", resampled)
  resampled <- resampled[, c(perf_names, "Training_Size")]
  resampled$Data <- "Resampling"
  apparent <- do.call("rbind", apparent)
  apparent <- apparent[, c(perf_names, "Training_Size")]
  apparent$Data <- "Training"
  out <- rbind(resampled, apparent)
  if(test_prop > 0) {
    tested <- do.call("rbind", tested)
    tested <- tested[, c(perf_names, "Training_Size")]
    tested$Data <- "Testing"
    out <- rbind(out, tested)
  }
  out
}
dmy = learing_curve_dat(dat=mtcars, outcome = "disp", test_prop = .2, proportion=(1:3)/3)

title: Machine Learning Workflow with Feature Selection
description:
Hello,
at the moment I try to build a machine learning workflow with caret. In the process I struggle with my general understanding of how to intergrate feature selection into the workflow. 

My previous workflow, which is inspired by the `train` Function looks like this: 

  Resampling
  Define sets of model parameter values to evaluate
  **for each** parameter set **do**
    **for each** resampling iteration **do**
      Hold out specific samples
      Preprocess data
      Fit the model
      Predict the hold out samples
    **end**
  Calculate average performance across hold-outs predictions
  **end**
  Determine the optimal parameter set 
  Fit the final model
  Predict the hold-out samples
  Calculate performance of hold-outs prediction

Now I would like to integrate feature selection into this workflow. My first guess was to do a filter selection after the preprocessing step. But after I read some other issues #503, #487, #439 I guessed, that this is not the way to do. I think the reason for that is that a further evaluation of the feature selection is needed. In my understanding the algorithm described in the issues is:

  Resampling
  **for each** resampling iteration **do**
    Features Selection
    Define sets of model parameter values to evaluate
    **for each** parameter set **do**
      **for each** resampling iteration **do**
        Hold out specific samples
        Preprocess data
        Fit the model
        Predict the hold out samples
      **end**
    Calculate average performance across hold-outs predictions for selected features
    **end**
    Determine the optimal parameter set of selected features
    Fit best model for selected features
    Predict the hold out samples
  **end**
  Determine the optimal selected Features
  Fit the final model
  Predict the hold-out samples
  Calculate performance of hold-outs prediction

I am a bit confused, so my first question is if I understood things right. If it is right I am struggeling with the outer resampling evaluation, because feature selection is performed on training and testset of the inner resampling. Isn't there a bias problem? 

Because of my confusion and because I am a beginner with machine learning it would be nice if you can post an algorithm like the one for the `train` function and maybe explain it a bit or give me a hint where I can find a good machine learning workflow which I can adopt.

Greetings, 
Louise

title: R caret: rfe nnet “undefined columns selected”
description:
As reported on SO (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/39418075/r-caret-rfe-nnet-undefined-columns-selected):

I am running into problems when applying recursive feature selection to nnet models with caret::rfe; I get the following error message:

> ```
> Error in { : task 1 failed - "undefined columns selected"
> ```

The actual task is more complex than the following example, but I am confident that this is a similar problem:

```
library(caret)

rfe(x = iris[,1:3],
         y = iris[,4]/max(iris[,4]),
         sizes = c(2), 
         method="nnet",
         rfeControl = rfeControl(functions = caretFuncs) 
         )
```

I know this error can occur when trying to select more features than there are available in x (e.g. see http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/18362/odd-error-with-caret-function-rfe), but this does not seem to be the problem here. I also ran very similar calls in earlier versions of caret, without this problem occurring.

I use R 3.3.1 and caret 6.0.71.

Thank you very much for your help.

EDIT: I went through the archived versions of caret and found that the example code is working in caret versions <= 6.0.62.

title: Documentation of recall wrong?
description:
To my mind there might be a mistake in the documentation for `recall`. It reads:

```
The recall (aka specificity) is defined as the proportion of relevant results out of the number of samples which were actually relevant.
```

Is is indeed the definition of recall, but not of specificity. Recall = Sensitivity. Specificity, in your example, would be D/(B+D)

title: How to limit the number of sub-processes created by caret::train ?
description:
I am having a hard time to train gradient boost with a large regression matrix that takes about 2 GB of memory. I initially thought it was an issue with the `doParallel` package [failing to restrict the number of "cores" available to the `train` function](https://stackoverflow.com/q/49852556/2066215). However, I have tried it with other parallelisation packages and the result is always the same: the number of back end sub-process is always a multiple of the CPUs available in the workstation, inevitably leading to memory exhaustion and the consequent crash.

Therefore I now suspect that these sub-process are being created by the `train` function itself. Could this be the case? if yes, how can restrict its number to, say, 8?

title: Error when training univariate recipes with sampling
description:
When using `train` on an object of class `recipe` that has only one predictor variable, along with a sampling method specified in `trainControl()`, an error is thrown:

```{R}
Error in `[.data.frame`(training, , x$var_info$variable, drop = FALSE) : 
  undefined columns selected
```

#### Minimal dataset:
```{R}
library(caret)
library(recipes)
set.seed(1)
dat <- twoClassSim(100)
a <- dat[,5]
y <- dat[["Class"]]
df <- data.frame(a,y)
rec <- recipe(y ~ .,data = df)
```

#### Minimal, runnable code:
```{R}
rec <- recipe(y ~ .,data = df)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                     repeats = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
                     sampling = "smote",
                     verboseIter = TRUE)

fit <- train(rec,data=df,method = "glm",family = "binomial",trControl = ctrl)

>Error in `[.data.frame`(training, , x$var_info$variable, drop = FALSE) : 
  undefined columns selected
```

It looks like this is due to lines in the `rec_model()` function.

#### Error when `sampling$first == TRUE`
For cases where sub-sampling occurs before preprocessing, `sampling$first == TRUE`, the error occurs here:
```{R}
other_dat <- dat[, other_cols]
tmp <- sampling$func(other_dat, y)
orig_dat <- dat
dat <- tmp$x

trained_rec <- prep(rec, training = dat, fresh = TRUE,
                        verbose = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = TRUE,
                        retain = TRUE)

>Error in `[.data.frame`(training, , x$var_info$variable, drop = FALSE) : 
  undefined columns selected
```
If there is only one value for `other_cols` (i.e. one non-outcome column), the result `other_dat` will be a vector rather than a `data.frame` or `tbl`. When this occurs, `sampling$func(other_dat, y)` assigns an arbitrary name to the column in `tmp$x` dataframe, also called `x`. When the frame `dat` is later passed to `prep()`, the predictor name in `dat`, now set to `x`, no longer matches the predictor name in `rec`, which is set to `a` in this example. This causes `prep`() to throw an error, because it cannot find the predictor column.

#### Error when `sampling$first == FALSE`
For cases where sub-sampling occurs after preprocessing, `sampling$first == FALSE`, the error occurs here:
```{R}
if(!is.null(sampling) && !sampling$first) {
      tmp <- sampling$func(x, y)
      x <- tmp$x
      y <- tmp$y
      rm(tmp)
    }

>Error in matrix(if (is.null(value)) logical() else value, nrow = nr, dimnames = list(rn,  : 
  length of 'dimnames' [2] not equal to array extent
>Called from: matrix(if (is.null(value)) logical() else value, nrow = nr, dimnames = list(rn, 
    cn))
```
`x` is a `tbl`, and when it has only one column, `sampling$func` treats it like a vector, causing the function to throw an error (I have tested for `up`, `rose`, and `smote`).

#### Example without error
Because of the `if` statement at the top of `rec_model` that checks for a sampling method, this problem only occurs if a sampling method is specified. 

```{R}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                     repeats = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,
                     #sampling = "smote",
                     verboseIter = TRUE)

fit <- train(rec,data=df,method = "glm",family = "binomial",trControl = ctrl)
```

#### Possible fix
I believe the way to fix it would be to change `other_dat <- dat[, other_cols]` to `other_dat <- dat[, other_cols,drop =FALSE]` when `sampling$first == TRUE` and to add `x <- as.data.frame(x)` prior to `tmp <- sampling$func(x, y)` when `sampling$first == FALSE`. I have tested these changes and they were successful. I can submit a pull request with these changes.

        ## In case no predictors are selected:

        out <- train(x[,ind], y, method = "qda",

title: Training using awtan method fails with error Error : 'lpawnb' is not an exported object from 'namespace:bnclassify'
description:
When trying to train a model using the awtan method, `caret::train()` fails with the following error(s):

    model fit failed for Resample04: score=bic, smooth=1 Error : 'lpawnb' is not an exported object from 'namespace:bnclassify'

See [my question on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48306658/awtan-method-in-carettrain-fails-with-error-lpawnb-is-not-an-exported-objects) for a reproducible example. 

Based on the [release notes](https://github.com/bmihaljevic/bnclassify/releases) for bnclassify v0.3.2, it appears that bnclassify has replaced `lpawnb()` with `lp()`. 

Currently `getModelInfo('awtan') defines $awtan$fit as:

    function (x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) 
    {
        dat <- if (is.data.frame(x)) 
            x
        else as.data.frame(x)
        dat$.outcome <- y
        struct <- bnclassify::tan_cl(class = ".outcome", dataset = dat, 
            score = as.character(param$score))
        bnclassify::lpawnb(struct, dat, smooth = param$smooth, trees = 10, 
            bootstrap_size = 0.5, ...)
    }

title: mlpML tuneGrid checking implementation flawed
description:
The mlpML model treats a nn size definition of c(5,0,7) as the same as (5), ignoring anything following an empty layer, but not producing an error. The mlpML caret implementation has checking to avoid this in line 28 of mlpML.R, however, the logic is incorrectly implemented.
`if(param$layer2 == 0 & param$layer2 > 0) stop("the second layer must have at least one hidden unit if a third layer is specified")`
should be 
`if(param$layer2 == 0 & param$layer3 > 0) stop("the second layer must have at least one hidden unit if a third layer is specified")`

#### Minimal, runnable code:
```{R}
library(caret)
set.seed(1)
dat <- twoClassSim(100)
X <- dat[,1:5]
y <- dat[["Class"]]

mlpMLGrid <- data.frame(layer1=5,
                        layer2=0,
                        layer3=7)

model_class <- train(X, y, method='mlpML', tuneGrid=mlpMLGrid)
print(model_class$finalModel$archParams)
```

### Session Info:
```{R}
sessionInfo()
```

Thanks!

description:
Hello!

After starting a new R session and installing the latest version... I couldn't get the plotting to work so I'm asking for help.

I suppose the plotting is not working because I've set up a new method. Here is the minimal example

```{R}
# load mtcars data as example
data("mtcars")

# create our custom method to have minsplit added to the cross validation 
rpart_ck <- getModelInfo("rpart", regex = FALSE)[[1]]

# add minsplit parameter
rpart_ck$parameters <- data.frame(parameter = c("cp", "minsplit"),
                                  class = rep("numeric",2),
                                  label = c("Complexity","MinimumSplit"))

# modify grid function
rpart_ck$grid <- function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
  library(rpart)
  
  dat <- if(is.data.frame(x)) x else as.data.frame(x)
  dat$.outcome <- y
  
  initialFit <- rpart::rpart(.outcome ~ .,
                             data = dat,
                             control = rpart::rpart.control(cp = 0,
                                                            minsplit = 1))$cptable
  initialFit <- initialFit[order(-initialFit[,"CP"]), , drop = FALSE]
  if(search == "grid") {
    if(nrow(initialFit) < len) {
      tuneSeq <- expand.grid(cp = seq(min(initialFit[, "CP"]),
                                      max(initialFit[, "CP"]),
                                      length = len),
                             minsplit = seq(1,
                                            nrow(dat)/2,
                                            length = len))
    } else tuneSeq <-  expand.grid(cp = initialFit[1:len,"CP"],
                                   minsplit = seq(1:nrow(dat), length = len))
    colnames(tuneSeq) <- c("cp","minsplit")
  } else {
    tuneSeq <- expand.grid(cp = unique(sample(initialFit[, "CP"], size = len, replace = TRUE)),
                           minsplit = unique(sample(nrow(dat)/2, size = len, replace = TRUE)))
  }
  
  tuneSeq
}

rpart_ck$fit <- function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
  cpValue <- if(!last) param$cp else 0
  minsplitValue <- if(!last) param$minsplit else 0
  theDots <- list(...)
  if(any(names(theDots) == "control"))
  {
    theDots$control$cp <- cpValue
    theDots$control$minsplit <- minsplitValue
    theDots$control$xval <- 0
    ctl <- theDots$control
    theDots$control <- NULL
  } else ctl <- rpart::rpart.control(cp = cpValue, minsplit = minsplitValue, xval = 0)
  
  ## check to see if weights were passed in (and availible)
  if(!is.null(wts)) theDots$weights <- wts
  
  modelArgs <- c(list(formula = as.formula(".outcome ~ ."),
                      data = if(is.data.frame(x)) x else as.data.frame(x),
                      control = ctl),
                 theDots)
  modelArgs$data$.outcome <- y
  
  out <- do.call(rpart::rpart, modelArgs)
  
  if(last) out <- rpart::prune.rpart(out, cp = param$cp)
  out
}

set.seed(123)
cvCtrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                       # 5-cv...
                       number = 3,
                       # repeat 2 times
                       repeats = 3,
                       summaryFunction = twoClassSummary
                       ,
                       classProbs = TRUE,
                       sampling = "up"
)

tuneGrid <- expand.grid(cp = seq(0, 0.1, length.out = 10),
                        minsplit = seq(10, 50, by = 10))

# change am variable to character
mtcars$am <- ifelse(mtcars$am == 1, "Man", "AM")

rpart_ck_prof <- caret::train(am ~ ., data = mtcars,
                              method = rpart_ck,
                              #tuneLength = 10,

                              tuneGrid = tuneGrid,
                              metric = 'ROC',

### session info
sessionInfo()

title: extractProb Incorrect dimensions when X Has One Column
description:
When using the `extractProb` function on a model that was trained with only one column in `X`, the following error is thrown:
```
Error in newdata[, object$method$center, drop = FALSE] : 
  incorrect number of dimensions
```

The problem seems to be caused by this [line](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/0e6aa496bf9f01b478ceca596c0d5a1a21f1497f/pkg/caret/R/extractProb.R#L23) when the `data.frame` is turned into a `vector`.

Minimum reproducible example:
```
library(caret)
TrainData <- data.frame(x = runif(100))
TrainClasses <- sample(c("Y", "N"), 100, TRUE)
fit <- train(TrainData, TrainClasses,
             method = "glm",
             preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
             trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", classProbs = TRUE))
extractProb(list(fit))
```

I would suggest adding the argument `drop = FALSE` like the `extractPrediction` function has in this [line](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/0e6aa496bf9f01b478ceca596c0d5a1a21f1497f/pkg/caret/R/extractPrediction.R#L15)

Then use e.g. `dput()` to give us something that can be put in R immediately, e.g. `dput(head(iris,4))`

If you must use `dput(head())`, please first remove an columns from your dataset that are not necessary to reproduce the error.

If your data frame has a factor with many levels, the `dput` output can be unwieldy because it will still list all the possible factor levels even if they aren't present in the the subset of your data. description:
Hey everyone,

Trying to install the library(caret) package to use the preProcess function but doesn't seem to be working. Code and error message are the following:

> library(caret)
Loading required package: ggplot2

title: feature suggestion: highlight classification models that allow class probabilities
description:
Firstly, thank you for the superb documentation here: 
https://topepo.github.io/caret/train-models-by-tag.html

I really appreciate the effort put into creating such a ready-to-use manual instead of a simple vignette. There is one feature missing for me, although, I don't who else is running into this. 

I often evaluate numerous models for time series predictions. I usually work with classification models, where I use the class probabilities instead of the actual classification result as a performance measure. As you know, not all models support this and finding out by trial-and-error is cumbersome with 100+ models. 

I suggest adding a qualifier like "This model supports class probabilities." in the model description page (link above), just like you indicate the availability of varImport ("A model-specific variable importance metric is available.")

title: Questions over preProcOptions list and preProcess functions
description:
Hello,
1)Does preProcOptions override preProcess options if both are applied in the same train instance?
2)In preProcOptions of trainControl there is a list element ICAcomp, on preProcess of the train we have pcaComp and ICAcomp seems to be missing. (ICAcomp is not an execution parameter of fastICA). Are they equivalents or merge at any point?
3)(Meta-question)Why are the preProcOptions set in the train control?(I see it more as the defining object for sampling, cv, etc..)
Ty for your amazing package, 
André

title: Help adding new metrics for output in regression tasks
description:
Hello, 
I've read issue #657 and wondered if there is a way to add new metrics.
I'm not sure adding random metrics is desired for everyone for the caret package, but I wondered if it is possible to add metrics functions on my own.

Example: is it possible to override postResample ? : 
"    me <- mean(pred - obs)
      mse <- mean((pred - obs)^2)
      mae <- mean(abs(pred - obs))
      out <- c(sqrt(mse), resamplCor^2, mae, me)
    }
    names(out) <- c("RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE", "ME")
  }"

The code above was successful while using train() function, but when I use a function from another package that imports caret, postResample, it uses the OLD postResample function.

I guess it has the function already imported. Is there a way to re-import that function? make the other package import the new postResample?

Thank you.

title: Feature request: metric = "deviance" when running logistic regression via glmnet
description:
The title says it all: I would really appreciate the implementation of deviance as a metric for logistic regression, i.e. I would like to be able to say:

train(y ~., data = training2,
                             method = "glmnet",
                             family = "binomial",
                             metric = "deviance",
                             trControl = caretTraining,
                             tuneGrid = toyGrid,
                             standardize = TRUE)

Thank you for your hard work!

title: custom performance metric
description:
I have a question about the consequences of using a custom performance metric (via "metric" in train and "summaryFunction" in trainControl). 

I can see that the custom metric has an effect on the performance metric for parameter tuning. however, when caret is "Fitting final model on full training set" I see that the custom metric is ignored (i.e. I get the same results for the final model (and fitted/predicted values) as if I had used the standard (RMSE) metric. 

Am I right/wrong? Is that intended? Is there a way of forcing the custom metric to be used in fitting the final model on the full training set? 

An R-script with an example can be found here: [https://www.dropbox.com/s/yuqjd24v0x39hpe/caret-xgboost-custom-metric-icecream-data.R?dl=0](https://www.dropbox.com/s/yuqjd24v0x39hpe/caret-xgboost-custom-metric-icecream-data.R?dl=0) 
At the very end I compare metrics of four different versions; (1) xgboost-standard, (2) xgboost-custom, (3) caret-xgboost-standard, (4) caret-xgboost-custom; all four versions are based on models fitted to the entire training set. I expected (2)=(4), however, (1)=(3)=(4). 

Thanks! 

Igor

title: time series models in train
description:
Quite a few people have asked to include these models in the package so that they can tune models with `train`. 

Right now, the only time-series related features are [rolling forecast origin resampling](http://topepo.github.io/caret/splitting.html#time) but this is general purpose. 

Here is what I see as the issues for including time series models:
1. I assume that most data sets will be class `ts` (please invalidate this if it is not the case). Right now, you could use `train` by having a data frame with a column for the time variable and another for the outcome. I would think that maintaining the original class would be important instead of reconstructing it inside `train` especially since some of the original data will be used as the holdout. We can make `train.ts` as a new class but that might take some work. 
2. `train` wouldn't do a great job on forecasting. For example, the `predict` function only returns a single scalar result per data point. It would not be able to produce forecast errors unless you predict from the original model object (which can be dicey)

Max

title: Error when training a ranger model with factor variables (with solution)
description:
I've been trying to train a model with `method="ranger"` and was getting the following error:

```
fit <- train(fmla, mydata, method = "ranger", trControl = ctrl1, tuneLength = 3, metric = "ROC")
Error in `[.data.frame`(data, , independent_vars, drop = FALSE) : 
  undefined columns selected
```

Took me awhile to figure out, but I found the cause (and solution), which I wanted to share. The error was related to some of the factor variables in my data. There were two issues that had to be fixed with the factor variables:

1. I had some factor variables that had levels with counts of 0. I had to make sure to drop those levels from the factor.
2. Some of the levels of my factor had characters that were not alpha-numeric, which were causing problems. I'm not sure exactly what characters were causing the problems, it might have just been white space. But when I stripped the factor levels of all non-alphanumeric characters with the following code, everything worked:

```
levels(x) <- gsub(pattern = "[^A-Z,a-z,0-9]", replacement = "", levels(x))
```

I was not getting the error when I fit the model directly using `ranger()`, so it must be somewhere in the pre-processing. I also was not getting the error when I ran some other models, including `rf`, so it seems specific to `ranger`.

Of the two issues above, the first is not as important... that's probably on me for providing bad data. However, it's notable that this only causes a problem when using `ranger` through `train`, so perhaps it should be fixed. The second one I think is more essential to be fixed.

Sorry for not posting a MRE, but since I have a solution, this is more of a "feature request" than a "bug report". Let me know if you have problems reproducing the error on your end.

title: Something is wrong; all the Dist metric values are missing:
description:
Hi, this code is straight from the manual gives an error. Great package though, thanks.

http://topepo.github.io/caret/using-your-own-model-in-train.html#Illustration5

### Minimal, reproducible example:

```{R}
library(caret)

set.seed(442)
trainingSet <- twoClassSim(n = 500, intercept = -16)
testingSet  <- twoClassSim(n = 500, intercept = -16)

## Class frequencies
table(trainingSet$Class)

set.seed(949)
mod0 <- train(Class ~ ., data = trainingSet,
              method = "rf",
              metric = "ROC",
              tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = 3),
              ntree = 1000,
              trControl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                                       repeats = 5,
                                       classProbs = TRUE,
                                       summaryFunction = twoClassSummary))
getTrainPerf(mod0)

## Get the model code for the original random forest method:

thresh_code <- getModelInfo("rf", regex = FALSE)[[1]]
thresh_code$type <- c("Classification")
## Add the threshold as another tuning parameter
thresh_code$parameters <- data.frame(parameter = c("mtry", "threshold"),
                                     class = c("numeric", "numeric"),
                                     label = c("#Randomly Selected Predictors",
                                               "Probability Cutoff"))
## The default tuning grid code:
thresh_code$grid <- function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
  p <- ncol(x)
  if(search == "grid") {
    grid <- expand.grid(mtry = floor(sqrt(p)), 
                        threshold = seq(.01, .99, length = len))
  } else {
    grid <- expand.grid(mtry = sample(1:p, size = len),
                        threshold = runif(1, 0, size = len))
  }
  grid
}

## Here we fit a single random forest model (with a fixed mtry)
## and loop over the threshold values to get predictions from the same
## randomForest model.
thresh_code$loop = function(grid) {   
  library(plyr)
  loop <- ddply(grid, c("mtry"),
                function(x) c(threshold = max(x$threshold)))
  submodels <- vector(mode = "list", length = nrow(loop))
  for(i in seq(along = loop$threshold)) {
    index <- which(grid$mtry == loop$mtry[i])
    cuts <- grid[index, "threshold"] 
    submodels[[i]] <- data.frame(threshold = cuts[cuts != loop$threshold[i]])
  }    
  list(loop = loop, submodels = submodels)
}

## Fit the model independent of the threshold parameter
thresh_code$fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) { 
  if(length(levels(y)) != 2)
    stop("This works only for 2-class problems")
  randomForest(x, y, mtry = param$mtry, ...)
}

## Now get a probability prediction and use different thresholds to
## get the predicted class
thresh_code$predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
  class1Prob <- predict(modelFit, 
                        newdata, 
                        type = "prob")[, modelFit$obsLevels[1]]
  ## Raise the threshold for class #1 and a higher level of
  ## evidence is needed to call it class 1 so it should 
  ## decrease sensitivity and increase specificity
  out <- ifelse(class1Prob >= modelFit$tuneValue$threshold,
                modelFit$obsLevels[1], 
                modelFit$obsLevels[2])
  if(!is.null(submodels)) {
    tmp2 <- out
    out <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(submodels$threshold))
    out[[1]] <- tmp2
    for(i in seq(along = submodels$threshold)) {
      out[[i+1]] <- ifelse(class1Prob >= submodels$threshold[[i]],
                           modelFit$obsLevels[1], 
                           modelFit$obsLevels[2])
    }
  } 
  out  
}

## The probabilities are always the same but we have to create
## mulitple versions of the probs to evaluate the data across
## thresholds
thresh_code$prob = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
  out <- as.data.frame(predict(modelFit, newdata, type = "prob"))
  if(!is.null(submodels)) {
    probs <- out
    out <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(submodels$threshold)+1)
    out <- lapply(out, function(x) probs)
  } 
  out 
}

fourStats <- function (data, lev = levels(data$obs), model = NULL) {
  ## This code will get use the area under the ROC curve and the
  ## sensitivity and specificity values using the current candidate
  ## value of the probability threshold.
  out <- c(twoClassSummary(data, lev = levels(data$obs), model = NULL))
  
  ## The best possible model has sensitivity of 1 and specificity of 1. 
  ## How far are we from that value?
  coords <- matrix(c(1, 1, out["Spec"], out["Sens"]), 
                   ncol = 2, 
                   byrow = TRUE)
  colnames(coords) <- c("Spec", "Sens")
  rownames(coords) <- c("Best", "Current")
  c(out, Dist = dist(coords)[1])
}

set.seed(949)
mod1 <- train(Class ~ ., data = trainingSet,
              method = thresh_code,
              ## Minimize the distance to the perfect model
              metric = "Dist",
              maximize = FALSE,
              tuneLength = 20,
              ntree = 1000,
              trControl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                                       repeats = 5,
                                       classProbs = TRUE,
                                       summaryFunction = fourStats))
