title: Caret Training Time Inconsistencies for Different Methods
description:
I have been training a few different models, and it seems that different methods take wildly different training times depending upon the training function used. For example, training an `svmRadial` model using train with 5 x 20 fold repeated cross validation with `DoParallel` takes about 14 seconds. Doing the same with `rbf` takes around 25 seconds. 

With `gafs`, 5 fold internal and external cross validation, as well as `DoParallel`, `svmRadial` took 2.5 hours, which can be expected when comparing 5x20=400 models completed by `train` with the population size and iterations for `gafs`. But `rbf` took 2 days and 7 hours with `gafs`, which is much much more than expected compared to `train`. Similarly, with a custom implementation of particle swarm optimization that uses `caret::train` for training the models, `svmRadial` took 50 minutes (again, as could be expected from the PSO parameter space), but `rbf` has been running for more than 30 hours and still hasn't completed. 

Can anyone provide pointers on how to optimize training speeds or whether some methods work better than others within these training methods. My setup, data type and code have been provided here: https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/805.

Thanks,
Murtaza

library(caret)

                 method = "ranger",
                 preProcess = c("center", "scale"),

                 tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = 1:3,
                                        splitrule = c("gini"),

title: Issues training with gbm
description:
Hi,

I conducted a simulation study back in September 2017 that used `caret` for automatic tuning with `gbm`. I revisited my code recently and train no longer works. 

I toyed around with the Boston Housing data from `MASS` package and encountered a similar error. I used code that I had previously implemented for a teaching lecture over the summer, but the model fitting no longer works. It appears there is some error when computing `gbm` predictions within the CV folds.

This code produces my error:

```{R}
library(MASS)
library(caret)
library(gbm)

attach(Boston)

gbmGrid <-  expand.grid(interaction.depth = c(1:2),
                         n.trees = (1:5)*100,
                         shrinkage = c(.01,.005),
                         n.minobsinnode = c(5, 10))

tune.gbm <- train(medv~., 
                  data=Boston, 
                  method="gbm", 
                  verbose=F,
                  tuneGrid=gbmGrid, trControl=trainControl(
                  verboseIter=F, method="cv", number = 5))
```

This gives me the error:
```
Something is wrong; all the RMSE metric values are missing:
```

RMSE is not computed in any of tuning conditions or CV folds, and in each fold/tune grid condition there is the following warning:

```
40: predictions failed for Fold5: 
shrinkage=0.010, interaction.depth=2, 
n.minobsinnode=10, n.trees=500 
Error in predict.GBMFit(modelFit, newdata, 
type = "response", n.trees = 
modelFit$tuneValue$n.trees) : 
newdata must be provided as a data frame
```

I also tried `method = "boot"` and received the same error. If it helps, I received an additional error when re-running the code in my original simulation script: 
```
Error in { : 
  task 1 failed - "arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 0"

title: ["models" help inconsistent]: xgboost required parameters for the new caret version (6.0-62)
description:
Hi,
In the new _caret_ version (6.0-62) there is an enhancement for  _xgboost_. According to _models_ (_train_model_list_) help, it is required to specify a new control parameter: _gamma_ :

``` r
eXtreme Gradient Boosting (method = 'xgbTree')

For classification and regression using packages xgboost and plyr with tuning parameters:

Number of Boosting Iterations (nrounds, numeric)

Max Tree Depth (max_depth, numeric)

Shrinkage (eta, numeric)

Minimum loss reduction *(gamma, numeric)*
```

But when running a model with just this parameter:

``` r iris
library(caret)

bootControl <- trainControl(number=5, verboseIter=TRUE)

xgbGrid <- expand.grid(
  eta = 0.12,
  max_depth = 10,
  nrounds = 400,
  gamma = 0                  #default=0
)


modFitxgb <-  train(
  Species ~ .,
  data = iris,
  trControl = bootControl,
  metric = "Accuracy",
  method = "xgbTree",
  tuneGrid = xgbGrid,
  verbose = 1,
  num_class = 3
)
modFitxgb
```

It produces this error message:

``` r
Loading required package: plyr
Error in train.default(x, y, weights = w, ...) : 
  The tuning parameter grid should have columns nrounds, max_depth, eta, gamma, colsample_bytree, min_child_weight
```

While by specifying the three required parameters it runs smoothly:

``` r

library(caret)

bootControl <- trainControl(number=5, verboseIter=TRUE)

xgbGrid <- expand.grid(
  eta = 0.12,
  max_depth = 10,
  nrounds = 400,
  gamma = 0,               #default=0
  colsample_bytree = 1,    #default=1
  min_child_weight = 1     #default=1
)


modFitxgb <-  train(
  Species ~ .,
  data = iris,
  trControl = bootControl,
  metric = "Accuracy",
  method = "xgbTree",
  tuneGrid = xgbGrid,
  verbose = 1,
  num_class = 3
)
modFitxgb
```

Results:

title: Issue with factors for filterVarImp
description:
From what I could gather, when a column in the `x` argument of the `filterVarImp` is a factor, it gets
converted into a numeric via `as.numeric` as in:

```{R}
asNumeric <- function(data){
  fc <- sapply(data, is.factor)
  modifyList(data, lapply(data[, fc], as.numeric))
}

filterVarImp <- function(x, y, nonpara = FALSE, ...){
  # converting factors to numeric
  notNumber <- sapply(x, function(x) !is.numeric(x))
  x = asNumeric(x)
```

The issue that I'm seeing is that `as.numeric` uses alphabetical ordering, which can cause some misleading results.

Below is an example:

```{R}
library(caret)

df_example <-
  data.frame(
    x1 = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 54, 12, 11, 1, 19), 
    x2 = c("l", "a", "l", "l", "a", "c", "z", "c", "z", "c"), 
    x3 = c("a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "l", "x", "g", "m", "x"),
    y1 = c("y", "y", "y", "y", "y", "n", "n", "n", "n", "n")
  )

filterVarImp(x = df_example[, -4], y = df_example$y1)
```

This yields:

|      |    n  |    y   |
| --- | ---- | ----- |
| x1  | 0.84 | 0.84 |
| x2  | 0.64 | 0.64 |
| x3  | 1.00 | 1.00 |

even though `x2` perfectly classifies `y1` (all `l`s and `a`s are `y` and all `c`s and `z`s are `n`).

I'm not sure how this issue can be addressed.

description:
R version 3.4.2 (2017-09-28) -- "Short Summer"

Hi Max, one year ago I had a script that modelled radial SVMs, among other models. Recently I re-ran the code and found that the radial SVM results were not reproduced - Acc/Kappa were systematically constant (Kappa specifically was null) across a wide range of independent prediction problems.

```{R}
library(caret)
X <- matrix(rnorm(251*272), 251, 272)
colnames(X) <- 1:272
Y <- sample(c("A","B","C","D","E"), 251, replace = T)
stratFolds <- createMultiFolds(Y, k = 3, times = 5)
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", index = stratFolds)
svmFit <- train(x = X, y = Y,
                      method = "svmRadial",
                      metric = "Kappa",
                      trControl = ctrl,
                      tuneLength = 15)
```
No matter what the seed is, the output is always the same - constant accuracy and Kappa. Maybe something to do with memory or max iterations from `kernlab`? Cheers

title: Adding the possibility to plot the confusion matrix
description:
Hi,
I've been searching a way to plot the confusion matrix of a trained model (especially in the multi-class case). I wasn't able to find a good answer (in my opinion), so I decided to write my own function.
If someone is interested here you have the code:
```r
plotConfusionMatrix <- function(model, norm = "none"){
  
  cm <- confusionMatrix(model, norm = norm)
  
  conf_matrix <- matrix(cm$table, ncol = length(unique(model$trainingData$.outcome)))
  
  nr <- nrow(conf_matrix)

  M <- t(conf_matrix)[, nr:1]
  Mv <- as.vector(M)
  colnames(M) <- colnames(cm$table)[nr:1]
  rownames(M) <- colnames(cm$table)
  
  g <- ggplot2::ggplot(reshape2::melt(M), ggplot2::aes_string(x='Var1', y='Var2', fill='value')) + ggplot2::geom_raster() +
       ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low='blue', high='red') + ggplot2::xlab("True") + ggplot2::ylab("Predicted") +
       ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x=ggplot2::element_text(angle=45,hjust=1,vjust=1)) + 
       ggplot2::geom_text(aes(label = round(Mv,2)), vjust = 1)  

  return(g)
  
}
```
Hope someone find it useful.
Best,
Simon

title: naive_bayes method - Laplace Correction
description:
Hello,

First of all, thank you for including [`naivebayes`](https://github.com/majkamichal/naivebayes) package into your excellent `caret` package!

The parameter responsible for `Laplace Correction` in [`naivebayes::naive_bayes`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/naivebayes/naivebayes.pdf) function is called `laplace`:

```
## Default S3 method:
naive_bayes(x, y, prior = NULL, laplace = 0, usekernel = FALSE, ...)
```

However,  in the [`caret/models/files/naive_bayes.R`](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/28a1dca9c5062043058d403e83837a96a428bf59/models/files/naive_bayes.R).  a (wrong) parameter `fL` is consistently used:

```
...
parameters = data.frame(parameter = c('fL', 'usekernel', "adjust"),
                                          class = c('numeric', 'logical', "numeric"),
                                          label = c('Laplace Correction', 'Distribution Type', "Bandwidth Adjustment")),
                  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") 
                    expand.grid(usekernel = c(TRUE, FALSE), fL = 0, adjust = 1),
                  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
                   if(param$usekernel) {
                          out <- naivebayes::naive_bayes(x, y, usekernel = TRUE,  fL = param$fL, adjust = param$adjust, ...)
                   } else out <- naivebayes::naive_bayes(x, y, usekernel = FALSE, fL = param$fL, ...)
                   out
                  },
...
```

---------------------

Below you can find a modified version of [`caret/models/files/naive_bayes.R`](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/28a1dca9c5062043058d403e83837a96a428bf59/models/files/naive_bayes.R) where `fL` is changed to`laplace`:
```
modelInfo <- list(label = "Naive Bayes",
                  library = "naivebayes",
                  loop = NULL,
                  type = c('Classification'),
                  parameters = data.frame(parameter = c('laplace', 'usekernel', "adjust"),
                                          class = c('numeric', 'logical', "numeric"),
                                          label = c('Laplace Correction', 'Distribution Type', "Bandwidth Adjustment")),
                  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") 
                    expand.grid(usekernel = c(TRUE, FALSE), laplace = 0, adjust = 1),
                  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
                   if(param$usekernel) {
                          out <- naivebayes::naive_bayes(x, y, usekernel = TRUE,  laplace = param$laplace, adjust = param$adjust, ...)
                   } else out <- naivebayes::naive_bayes(x, y, usekernel = FALSE, laplace = param$laplace, ...)
                   out
                  },
                  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
                    if(!is.data.frame(newdata)) newdata <- as.data.frame(newdata)
                    predict(modelFit , newdata)
                  },
                  prob = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
                    if(!is.data.frame(newdata)) newdata <- as.data.frame(newdata)
                    as.data.frame(predict(modelFit, newdata, type = "prob"))
                    },
                  predictors = function(x, ...) if(hasTerms(x)) predictors(x$terms) else names(x$tables),
                  tags = c("Bayesian Model"),
                  levels = function(x) x$levels,
                  sort = function(x) x[order(x[,1]),])
```

as well as modified/corrected version of [`pkg/caret/man/models.Rd`](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/99beaa87a8a425b70783661bf4b9c383bac2d40c/pkg/caret/man/models.Rd) where `fL` is also changed to `laplace`


```

\strong{Naive Bayes} (\code{method = 'naive_bayes'})
For classification using package \pkg{naivebayes} with tuning parameters:
\itemize{
\item Laplace Correction (\code{laplace}, numeric)
\item Distribution Type (\code{usekernel}, logical)
\item Bandwidth Adjustment (\code{adjust}, numeric)
}
```

Regards,
Michal

title: Imputing NAs inside train function
description:
I want to train a model with cross-validation and impute some NAs in my training data with the preProcess option of caret's train function. 

 This is a minimal code example that shows my problem. It works with different resampling techniques and models:

```{R}
library(caret)

t <- data.frame(1:20, 1:20, 1:20)
for (i in 1:20) {
  if (i %% 2 == 1) t[i,1] <- NA; 
  if (i %% 2 == 0) t[i,2] <- NA 
}

names(t) <- c('X1', 'X2', 'Y')

train(Y ~ X1 + X2,
      data = t,
      method = "pls",
      metric = "RMSE",
      preProcess = "medianImpute",
      na.action = na.pass)
```

 2 predictor

  1.724075  0.919367  1.328847

Tuning parameter 'ncomp' was held constant at a value of 1

But, I want to impute the NAs in order to have 20 samples. This confirms the stored training data inside the fit object (fit$trainingData). title: createDataPartition and create Functions Inconsistent Documentation
description:
If using `?createResample`, the `createDataPartition` help page is loaded. However, the Usage section does not specify the format of the function. It should be `(y, times = 10, list = TRUE)`. There's an example of it in the Examples section so I think the function should be formally defined in the Usage section.

Also, Section 5.3 of the documentation website states 

> By default, simple bootstrap resampling is used for line 3 in the algorithm above, which is `inTraining <- createDataPartition(Sonar$Class, p = .75, list = FALSE)`.

I find this to not be true, as every selection by `createDataPartition` has unique selections rather than what would be expected by resampling with replacement.

```
library(mlbench)
data(Sonar)

anyDuplicates <- sapply(1:1000, function(iteration)
{
  inTraining <- createDataPartition(Sonar$Class, p = 0.50, list = FALSE)
  any(table(inTraining) > 1)
})

> table(anyDuplicates)
anyDuplicates
FALSE 
 1000
```

It seems like there was some incomplete refactoring in the past. It's unclear how these two functions should be used by the end-user.

title: Possible memory leak in doc example?
description:
Hi, I wrote some code based on this here:

https://topepo.github.io/caret/using-your-own-model-in-train.html#illustrative-example-2-something-more-complicated---logitboost

particularly 

```
lbPred <- function(modelFit, newdata, preProc = NULL, submodels = NULL) {
  ## This model was fit with the maximum value of nIter
  out <- caTools::predict.LogitBoost(modelFit, newdata, type="class")
  
  ## In this case, 'submodels' is a data frame with the other values of
  ## nIter. We loop over these to get the other predictions.
  if(!is.null(submodels)) {
    ## Save _all_ the predictions in a list
    tmp <- out
    out <- vector(mode = "list", length = nrow(submodels) + 1)
    out[[1]] <- tmp
    
    for(j in seq(along = submodels$nIter)) {
      out[[j+1]] <- caTools::predict.LogitBoost(modelFit,
                                                newdata,
                                                nIter = submodels$nIter[j])
    }
  }
  out                   
}
```

The particular code in my implementation is here:-

https://github.com/AgileVentures/CommunityMaintenanceSupport/blob/tune_model_ab/ada_boost_double_cv.R#L69

This was leaking memory like crazy on my data set, but as soon as I added 

tmp <- NULL

it seemed to clear up most of that.

title: PCA as a preProcess option with time slicing
description:
Hi topepo, 

I am using PCA as a preProcess option in combination with the time slicing method as follows:

```{R}
set.seed(123)
seeds <- vector(mode = "list", length = 108)
for(i in 1:108) seeds[[i]] <- sample.int(1000, 5)
seeds[[109]] <- sample.int(1000, 1)

myTimeControl <- trainControl(method = "timeslice",
                                  initialWindow = 108,
                                  horizon = 1,
                                  fixedWindow = FALSE,
                                  allowParallel = FALSE,
                                  verboseIter = TRUE,
                                  seeds = seeds,
                                  preProcOptions = list(thresh = 0.85))

tuneLength.num <- 5

glmnet <- train(target ~ .,
                data = df_model,
                method = "lm",
                trControl = myTimeControl,
                preProcess = c("pca"),
                na.remove = TRUE,
                tuneLength = tuneLength.num)
```
My question is how the PCA works together with time slicing. Is it the case that:

(a) a PCA is applied to each resampling step individually; or 
(b) there is only one PCA applied to the full data set?

Thank you very much for your help and your great package.
Lukas

title: Inactive unit tests
description:
Some unit test files in [caret/pkg/caret/tests/testthat](https://github.com/topepo/caret/tree/master/pkg/caret/tests/testthat) have names without `test_` prefixes which are [required](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/tests.html) by `testthat` framework:

> Test structure
> A test file lives in tests/testthat/. Its name must start with test.

As a consequence, such files (e.g. [preProcess_methods.R](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/master/pkg/caret/tests/testthat/preProcess_methods.R)) are skipped when running the test suite with `devtools::test`.

Hi,

There is a typo in pkg/caret/R/resamples.R and I first saw the problem when I switch from R.3.3.x to R.3.4.2. Here is the fix (I believe the typos are self-explanatory e.g. "time" -> "times"). Producing a test-case would be quite cumbersome but I can do if required. 

$ git diff HEAD^^ HEAD pkg/caret/R/resamples.R
diff --git a/pkg/caret/R/resamples.R b/pkg/caret/R/resamples.R
index 691be39..7f4108c 100644
--- a/pkg/caret/R/resamples.R
+++ b/pkg/caret/R/resamples.R
@@ -129,9 +129,9 @@ resamples.default <- function(x, modelNames = names(x), ...) {
   getTimes <- function(x){
     out <- rep(NA, 3)
     if(all(names(x) != "times")) return(out)
-    if(any(names(x$times) == "everything")) out[1] <- x$time$everything[3]
-    if(any(names(x$times) == "final")) out[2] <- x$time$final[3]
-    if(any(names(x$times) == "prediction")) out[3] <- x$time$prediction[3]
+    if(any(names(x$times) == "everything")) out[1] <- x$times$everything[3]
+    if(any(names(x$times) == "final")) out[2] <- x$times$final[3]
+    if(any(names(x$times) == "prediction")) out[3] <- x$times$prediction[3]
     out
   }

require(data.table)

title: Document Advice for nominalTrainWorkflow Warning
description:
How to handle such a warning as an end-user? Here is a minimal trigger:

```
classifyData <- data.frame(measure = rnorm(1000), group = sample(LETTERS[1:2], 1000, replace = TRUE),
                           outcome = sample(rep(c('Y', 'Z', c(800, 200)))))

CVparams <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 5, sampling = "up")
crossValidated <- train(x = classifyData[, -match("outcome", colnames(classifyData))],
                        y = classifyData[, "outcome"], "glmStepAIC", direction = "forward",
                        trControl = CVparams, trace = FALSE)
```

You should then see

> Warning in nominalTrainWorkflow(x = x, y = y, wts = weights, info = trainInfo,  :
  There were missing values in resampled performance measures.
Something is wrong; all the Accuracy metric values are missing:

The nominalTrainWorkflow warning also appears in issue #719 

It's not exported from the package for end-user usage, so I guess this problem is not expected to occur.

```
> nominalTrainWorkflow()
Error in nominalTrainWorkflow() : 
  could not find function "nominalTrainWorkflow"
```

title: Error in varImp[, "%IncMSE"] on RFE rfFuncs regression subset fit
description:
varImp on the final regression fit of an RFE with rfFuncs gives an error. It comes from rfFuncs$fit.
It can be fixed modifying rfFuncs$fit, see example below.

```R
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
set.seed(123)

# Simulate data
x <- matrix(rnorm(1e3), ncol = 10)  # Feature matrix
colnames(x) <- paste0('x', seq_len(10))
y_cont <- runif(1e2)                            # Continuous response
ctrl <- rfeControl(functions = rfFuncs, method = 'cv'
fit_cont <- rfe(x, y_cont, sizes = seq_len(3), rfeControl = ctrl)

varImp(fit_cont$fit)

# adding importance computation for selected model
rfFuncs$fit <- function (x, y, first, last, ...) 
{
  loadNamespace("randomForest")
  randomForest::randomForest(x, y, importance = (first|last), ...)
}

ctrl <- rfeControl(functions = rfFuncs, method = 'cv')
fit_cont <- rfe(x, y_cont, sizes = seq_len(3), rfeControl = ctrl)
varImp(fit_cont$fit)
```

description:
On the help page of `train`, the parameter `summaryFunction` makes reference to a function `defaultSummary` and the link goes to a help page of `postResample` however the function specification of `defaultSummary` is not in the Usage section and there's only one sentence about it in Details section, so the user does not know the function's [prototype](https://www.pcmag.com/encyclopedia/term/43583/function-prototype).

Perhaps also adding an example using a custom summary function, of which there currently are none, to the Examples section of `train` help would be useful for readers, with a simple example such as a function for [balanced error rate](http://www.modelselect.inf.ethz.ch/evaluation.php).

title: Extremely randomised trees in caret using ranger
description:
Hello,

Since version `0.6.4` the package `ranger` supports [Extremely randomised trees](http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10994-006-6226-1). Strictly-speaking the only "new thing" would be to actually change the argument `splitrule = "extratrees"`, nevertheless I have the feeling that people would miss out using extr. random trees if they are not careful. There is a package, which is included in `caret` already, `extraTrees` that implements the same algorithm. That implementation though does not do multi-core computation out-of-the-box (and its code-base hasn't change in the last 2 years either, which worries me too) so I think there is a case to use `ranger` directly. 

Should one:
1. Let things as is and hope/trust the user to find the e.r.t. functionality themselves or
2. Add a method like: `rangerExtreme` so users can directly invoke extremely randomise trees?

Let me note that `0.6.4` is *not* available on CRAN, so you might want to nap the issue of adding the e.r.t. functionality until it is included in the CRAN release?

All best,
Pantelis

title: Forward Selection Logistic Regression Fails Because of Space in Factor Level
description:
Backward selection completes successfully but forward selection does not. It is caused by a space in a factor level. Consider the minimal example:

```
dataTable <- data.frame(recovery = rep(c("No", "Yes"), each = 3),
                        treatment = rep(c("None", "PD1 Inhibitor"), each = 3))
train(recovery ~ ., data = dataTable, "glmStepAIC", direction = "forward",
      trControl = trainControl("LOOCV"))   
Error in { : task 1 failed - "<text>:1:23: unexpected symbol
1: .outcome~treatmentPD1 Inhibitor
                          ^"
```

There's no such problem with backward selection, though.

```
train(recovery ~ ., data = dataTable, "glmStepAIC", direction = "backward",
      trControl = trainControl("LOOCV"))
...        ...
                           Df Deviance    AIC
<none>                          0.0000 4.0000
- `treatmentPD1 Inhibitor`  1   6.7301 8.7301
...        ...
Resampling results:

  Accuracy  Kappa
  1         1
```

Note that PD1 Inhibitor is automatically enclosed in backticks for the backward selection.

title: Possible bug in the calculation of mnLogLoss
description:
Hello, 

I suspect that the value returned by `mnLogLoss` is wrong. As first commented on the commit 4c9cd0eb8c1a44cd22222169883d0f9eeed5adac it appears that `caret` casts a factor vector to a numeric vector. This results in a numeric vector containing values `1`and `2` instead of `0` and `1`. These values are what is used for `y` for the calculation of the log-Loss by `ModelMetrics::logLoss` while by definition `y` is supposed to be zero or one.
In the issue https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/107 @zachmayer  appears to correctly use something like: `obs  <- ifelse(data[,  "obs"] == class, 1, 0)` before using `Model::logLoss` but this is not present in the current release. (I use/refer at the latest (~01:30, 22 April 2017 (BST)) Github version following commit d0849e9104a8b98d855d06804e816e02dffe11bb.)

The following code snippet showcases this behaviour: 

```{R}
rm(list=ls())
devtools::load_all('git_projects/original-caret/pkg/caret/');
set.seed(1); N = 100
datTr <- twoClassSim(N)
X <- datTr[,1:(ncol(datTr)-1)]
y <- datTr[["Class"]]

datTst <- twoClassSim(N)
XTst <- datTst[,1:(ncol(datTst)-1)]
yTst <- datTst[["Class"]]

set.seed(3)
mod  <- train(X, y,
  trControl=trainControl( method="cv", number=5, 
  classProbs=TRUE, summaryFunction=mnLogLoss, savePredictions="final"))
test_pred <- predict(mod, XTst, type = "prob")
test_pred$obs <- yTst
test_pred$pred <- predict(mod, XTst)

mnLogLoss(test_pred, lev = levels(test_pred$obs)) # 0.4129...

# Reproducing outside mnLogLoss/postResample 
ModelMetrics::logLoss(predicted = test_pred$Class1, 
                         actual =  as.numeric(test_pred$obs) ) # 0.4129...

obs  <- ifelse(test_pred$obs == 'Class1', 1, 0)
ModelMetrics::logLoss(predicted = test_pred$Class1, actual =  obs ) # 0.5738...
```

title: Running BINDA with bagImpute preProcess method failing.
Ambigious error when the user specifies the data twice
description:
Just a pointer for other users and perhaps for the maintainers of the package. Usually caret very diligently points out the mistake the user did by specifying the same argument twice, however this is not the case for the data argument specifically. 
This error could be produced when the user supplies both the "data" argument as well as the x and y arguments: In adaptiveWorkflow(x = x, y = y, wts = weights, info = trainInfo,  :   There were missing values in resampled performance measures.

Some methods can overcome this (e.g., rf), but the majority crash with the aforementioned error. 

Through debugging the error is actually: "formal argument "data" matched by multiple actual arguments".

The obvious fix from the user side is to specifiy only either of the arguments.

title: Submodel trick in glmnet
description:
I looked to other threads about this but I could not understand exactly if and eventually how the train function exploit the submodel trick. Sorry in advance if it is just me that I could not understand it properly.

Using "glmnet" as methods, it is mandatory do provide both "alpha" and "lambda" as hyper-parameters:

1) if the submodel trick is actually applied, what is "lambda" for? Shouldn't a range for "lambda" be better asked instead?
2) also, it seems to me that the cv performance it returns is the one obtained with the level of "lambda" as provided and not the one who achieved the the best cv performance trying several of them (I see that there is a parameter in glmnet to decide how many should be tried along the regularization path).

Thanks!

description:
Hello,

There is a new model (just for `regression`) that predicts based on graph proximity.

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/kinn/index.html

_A graph based regression model from flat unstructured dataset. Each line in the input data set is treated as a node from which an edge to another line (node) can be formed. In the training process, a model is created which contains sparse graph adjacency matrix. This model is then used for prediction by taking a predictor and the model as inputs and outputs a prediction which is an average of the most similar node and its neighbours in the model graph._

It looks like you can give [irace](http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/irace/index.html) an upper and lower bound for each of your parameters, and it will automatically (and iteratively) search that space for good parameter sets.  It seems to support both qualitative (e.g. gbm$distribution must be in "gaussian", "bernoulli", etc) and quanitiative (e.g. gbm$n.trees must be between 1 and 100) parameters.

In particular, the [mlr package](https://github.com/berndbischl/mlr) uses irace, and in my testing it seems to work really well. (Although it's not yet aware of the "sub model" trick and can waste a lot of time fitting models it doesn't need).

title: Make theDots available in summaryFunction
description:
Hi all,

while working on survival type analyses I came across the following issue: theDots is not available in the summaryFunction

Background: The reformulation of a survival problem to a regression problem may require the inclusion of an offset (cf. http://data.princeton.edu/wws509/notes/c7.pdf for details). For example. one may use a Poisson GLM (with or without regularisation) with the log-exposure as an offset. In this case the correct loss function is the deviance (RMSE or R2 are missleading). For example, glmnet also uses the deviance as a performance measure. In order to compute the deviance, one needs to know the offset, which is not available
in summaryFunction; only data, lev and model are. Hence my idea to add theDots to the argument list.

Current Workaround: I'm using weights to hand over the offset. However, this means I have to "customize" each model because an offset is treated differently than a weight.

title: Discussion: LeaveOneGroupOut CrossValidation with caret
description:
In Social psychology we are working on a project where we try to predict relationship quality (outcome) by personality (features). Main goal is to contribute to better match people with have higher chances to have a happy long lasting romantic relationship. I would be very grateful if you could help me with this by answering the following question:

At the moment, in R the k-fold-cv randomly sorts rows of data/people into the folds. A couple is represented by two rows in the dataset (partner 1 and partner 2) which are of course not always equally happy in the relationship they have with each other. But nevertheless the relationship quality of partner 1 and partner 2 correlate, which means the cases are somehow dependent. How can I sort partners of one couple to the same fold (but still as two cases), so that the test sample is always completely independent to the trainings sample? How can I write a Leave One Group Out CS - command in R, as it exists in Python (which I unfortunately cannot perform with)?

Couples are identified by the same number in the row paarID.

Here is the processing part of the code in R from the situation:

```
library(caret)
outcome <- "RQ_continuaryScale"
variables <- colnames(dat)[use_covar_i]
model <- paste(variables, collapse=" + ")
model <- paste(outcome, '~', model, collapse=' ')
training_config <- trainControl(method="cv", number=5, repeats = 100)
fit <- train(as.formula(model), data=dat_nomiss, "glmnet", trControl = training_config)
```

Thanks for your help!!

title: performance metric evaluation code to be less random
description:
When `train` starts it creates an initial random data set to mimic what comes out of the prediction code. It evaluates this to make sure that the evaluation code works and also to get the names of the performance measures.

`evalSummaryFunction` takes a random sample of the data:
```r
obs_samp <- factor(sample(levels(y), min(10, n), replace = TRUE), levels = lev)
```
but this can lead to samples with only one unique value of `obs_samp`. It would use something like 
```r
rep_len(levels(y), min(10, n))
```
instead.

title: [suggestion] Tutorial/Handbook addition repeadedcv
description:
Can you please clarify whether it makes sense or not to use nested cv? 

He is confused, and I am too:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/189364/caret-repeated-k-fold-cross-validation-vs-nested-k-fold-cross-validation-repe

You say no:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/125843/outer-crossvalidation-cycle-in-caret-package-r

He says it's an alternative to split your data into test and training, which would be a HUGE benefit (comment):
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/225949/do-we-need-a-test-set-when-using-k-fold-cross-validation

He says you don't need test and training dataset at all and just can go along with cross validation:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/148688/cross-validation-with-test-data-set
He agrees:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/261643/do-i-need-a-global-test-set-when-using-k-fold-cross-validation-and-a-small-n-n?noredirect=1&lq=1

He says to never use your test data for model parameters:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/152907/how-do-you-use-test-data-set-after-cross-validation

Much confusion going on!

I think just adding one or two lines in the documentary would elimate a lot of these questions. Something like:
If your dataset iss too small using (nested?) repeatedcv will deliver sufficient power to make your model statistically sound and not a balloon filled with hot air. You lose power by not splitting into a testing and training set, but it is okay.
or:
Ever ever ever use a training and testing set, or you can flush your model down the toilet.

title: createFolds does not return equally sized folds or even requested number of folds
description:
If you are making a feature request or starting a discussion, you can ignore everything below and go wild =D

If you are filing a bug, make sure these boxes are checked before submitting your issue— thank you!

- [x ] Start a new R session
- [x ] Install the latest version of caret: `update.packages(oldPkgs="caret", ask=FALSE)`
- [ x] [Write a minimal reproducible example](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)
- [ x] run `sessionInfo()`

### Minimal, reproducible example:

``` r
set.seed(3)
library(caret)
#> Warning: package 'caret' was built under R version 3.3.3
#> Loading required package: lattice
#> Loading required package: ggplot2
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 3.3.3
subjects <- paste0("SUBJECT", 1:17)
createFolds(subjects, k=10)
#> $Fold1
#> [1]  8 14
#> 
#> $Fold2
#> [1] 15
#> 
#> $Fold3
#> [1] 10 11
#> 
#> $Fold4
#> [1]  2  3  4  5 16
#> 
#> $Fold5
#> [1] 12 13 17
#> 
#> $Fold6
#> [1] 9
#> 
#> $Fold7
#> [1] 1 6 7
```

As you can see - instead of the requested 10 folds, only 7 are being returned. In addtion, the number of elements per fold is not the same (or only different by 1 as necessary to distribute all items across folds). Instead, Fold4 has 5 items, while Fold2 only has 1. This is counter-intuitive to my understanding of Cross-Validation, where folds are intended to be of equal size (or as close to equal as possible if you can't divide the number of samples by the number of folds without remainder).

title: RFE: custom preProcessing
description:
Please extend preProcessing to accept "unknown" preprocessing methods. (Or better document how to do it with current caret.)

As a motivational example, I'd like to have a preprocessing step where factors with large numbers of values would be replaced by a new column: The median value of the response for the train data for the subset of the train data with the same factor level. This will depend on the training data, and when using a basic train/validation split with createDataPartition, the median would be calculated on just the train subset. But when using caret's cross validation, it's currently impossible to make this preprocessing happen on the right data subsets.

Suggested interface:

Add a new function in caret to define a custom preProcessing step. User would provide a pair of functions (processing on the train, and application of the resulting obj on the used data), and would get back something they could name in the environment --- a list-as-object or something snazzier.

Enhance the current preProcess code to search the parent environment(s) for any unrecognized method names, to be run after all current preprocessing steps (*).

As a final enhancement, extend the current preProcesss to take an method_order variable that specifies the order to attempt things, with the default value matching the current preProcess code, and all unknown values happening subsequently. This would allow someone to center or rescale the output of a custom preProcessor.

The way the mlr package handles this (https://mlr-org.github.io/mlr-tutorial/devel/html/preproc/index.html) might also be worth a look.

title: timeslice conserving a grouping variable (id)
description:
Hello,

First things first - amazing package! Big fan.

We have recently switched from survival analysis to logistic regression in order to better deal with time-varying covariates in our data using ML (so we don't really have ts data but seems like this is not an issue). The problematic nature of using regular CV methods with TVCs led us to the timeslice option in `trainControl`. However, our data is also grouped by an id variable, which needs to preserved in addition to the progression of time. An example would be 8 rows/years for England, followed by 5 years for Germany etc. - we don't want the CV method to use partial durations, cutting any spell in the middle.

Given the arguments for timeslice (initialWindow and horizon) accepts numeric values, is there a way around this? Basically, what we need is a dynamic horizon function if possible at all - we can set up the initialWindow manually. However, horizon would take different lengths at each iteration, so any thoughts on that is appreciated.

Cheers,

Gokhan

title: train with plr and ROC error: Error in .subset(x, j) : invalid subscript type 'list'
description:
I get an error when running `train` with `method = "plr"` and `metric = "ROC"`: `Error in .subset(x, j) : invalid subscript type 'list'`.

When I run `step.plr` directly with `step.plr(d[,c("bar", "baz")], d$foo, cp = "bic")`, it runs fine (although it selects the null model given these fake data).

#### Minimal, runnable code:
```{R}
library(caret)
#> Loading required package: lattice
#> Loading required package: ggplot2
set.seed(1024)
d <- data.frame(
  foo = c(rep(TRUE, 10), rep(FALSE, 10)),
  bar = sample(letters[1:4], 20, replace = TRUE),
  baz = sample(letters[5:8], 20, replace = TRUE)
)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv",
                     repeats = 3,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)

plr_grid <- expand.grid(
  cp = c("aic", "bic"),
  lambda = c(1e-4)
)

fit <- train(foo ~ .,
             data = d,
             method = "plr",
             tuneGrid = plr_grid,
             trControl = ctrl,
             metric = "ROC")
#> Loading required package: stepPlr
#> Error in .subset(x, j): invalid subscript type 'list'
```

#### Minimal, runnable code:
MCC_func <- function(data, lev = NULL, model = NULL){
	pred <- data$pred
	obs <- data$obs
	
	cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, obs, positive = "1")
	A <- cm$table[1]
	B <- cm$table[2]
	C <- cm$table[3]
	D <- cm$table[4]
	
	MCC <- (A*D-C*B)/sqrt((A+B)*(A+C)*(D+B)*(D+C))
	list <- list("MCC" = MCC)
	return(list)
}

title: Proposal: use of requireNamespace(QuietStop) instead of require to avoid search path pollution
description:
Dear all,

I really like the _caret_ package and teach it as the _right way_ to do learn and predict in R. I'm however always annoyed by the fact that so many packages are attached along the way, polluting the search path. I was always wondering whether something can be done in such a complex meta-package setting... and I may have a solution.

Roughly speaking, it seems that using __requireNamespace__ and explicit package name scheme (::) in _caret_ is (almost) sufficient to get rid of this issue. I've made a fork [lepennec/caret](https://github.com/lepennec/caret) that replace all instances of __require__ by __requireNamespace__ in the package and modify a few packages (the ones required to run the tests and the 6 llast ones in alphabetic order). The only drawback, and it's a big one, is that _foreach_ and _doParallel_ have been made to use __library__ and not __requireNamespace__... so that the previous modifications are not sufficient. I've made a fork of _foreach_ [lepennec/foreach](https://github.com/lepennec/foreach) that add a new parameter .namespaces which plays the same role than .packages but use __requireNamespace__ instead of __library__. I've used it with success in the fork. Note that the same modification can easily be done in _doParallel_. 

To summarize, it seems that the search path pollution issue can be solved with the help of __requireNamespace__ but that it requires some modifications of _foreach_ and _doParallel_... If you are interested I can keep on the work..

Yours,

Erwan

If you are filing a bug, make sure these boxes are checked before submitting your issue— thank you!

- [ ] Start a new R session
- [ ] Install the latest version of caret: `update.packages(oldPkgs="caret", ask=FALSE)`

### Minimal, reproducible example:

__Please read this page__: [reprex = {repr}oducible {ex}ample](https://github.com/jennybc/reprex#what-is-a-reprex) 

Text and example code modified from [the R FAQ on stackoverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)

#### Minimal dataset:
```{R}
library(caret)
set.seed(1)
dat <- twoClassSim(100)
X <- dat[,1:5]
y <- dat[["Class"]]

```
If you have some data that would be too difficult to construct using `caret::twoClassSim` or `caret::SLC14_1`, then you can always make a subset of your original data, using e.g. `head()`, `subset()` or the indices. Then use e.g. `dput()` to give us something that can be put in R immediately, e.g. `dput(head(iris,4))`

If you must use `dput(head())`, please first remove an columns from your dataset that are not necessary to reproduce the error.

If your data frame has a factor with many levels, the `dput` output can be unwieldy because it will still list all the possible factor levels even if they aren't present in the the subset of your data. To solve this issue, you can use the `droplevels()` function. Notice below how species is a factor with only one level: `dput(droplevels(head(iris, 4)))`

model_class <- train(

title: `predict` fails if formula method is used with deleted variables
description:
In a multi-class classification problem, trying to get the class probabilities from a model object trained with the formula method with deleted variables (i.e. `-variable`) fails with `predict` when `newdata` is not specified. 

Reproducible example:
```
fit.lda <- train(Species ~ . -Petal.Length, 
  data = iris, 
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"), 
  trControl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", 
    number = 10, 
    repeats = 3, 
    classProbs = TRUE, 
    savePredictions = "final", 
    selectionFunction = "best", 
    summaryFunction = multiClassSummary), 
  method = "lda", 
  metric = "Mean_F1")
```
then

`predict(fit.lda, type = "prob")`

fails with:

> Error in predict.lda(modelFit, newdata) : wrong number of variables

If the `-Petal.Length` is omitted in the `train` formula, there is no error. 

This error occurs for some models (`lda`, `knn`, `svmRadial`, `mlpML`) but not others (`nnet`, `rf`, `xgbTree`).

=====

**Workaround** 

If `newdata` is specified with the training data, it seems to succeed in retrieving the class probabilities. Is this the correct way of doing it? 

In the documentation for `predict`: 

> `newdata`: an optional set of data to predict on. If NULL, then the original training data are used

In the past, I always omitted `newdata` for obtaining information from the trained model, and included the parameter when using on new testing data.

pacman::p_load(R.utils, caret, doParallel)

cl <- makeCluster(8, outfile="")
registerDoParallel(cl)

set.seed(2)
dat <- twoClassSim(48842)
fit_on <-  list(rs1 = 1:1300, rs2 = 4:1600,         rs3 = 7:9000)
pred_on <- list(rs1 = 4:9, rs2 = c(1:3, 7:9), rs3 = 1:6)
indexFinal = 1:1000

fitControl <- trainControl(method = "boot632",number=1,repeats=1
                           , classProbs = TRUE,summaryFunction = twoClassSummary,

title: TimeSlice feature request
description:
hi,

Regarding timeslice cross-validation : I think it would be useful to have an option NOT to fit a 'final' model on the full dataset. The whole point of timeslice crossvalidation in many contexts is to reflect the temporal context with non-stationarity. We fit a model only using X days of lookback and test on the next Y days - partly to determine if that X-Y paradigm is effective. In this case I'd rather not waste cycles training the model on the full data set because at the end i'm only interested in the most recent fit and the hyperparameters.

best, Jason

title: Changed default grid specification for xbgTree
Setting index in trainControl invalidates repeats/numbers arguments.
description:
Hello,

I am uncertain that this is "truly" a bug but it is somewhat unexpected behaviour nevertheless. If one sets the `index` argument to `trainControl` the additional arguments to `repeats` and or `number` are ignored. This can be misleading if you want to have a short simulation. For example in the following script `train` will attempt to do as many resamples as the length of the list of training indexes provided instead of  `repeats` * `number`.

```R
set.seed(123)
library(caret)
N = 1000;
myDF <- data.frame(predVal =as.factor(
                     sapply( 1:N, function(u) paste0(collapse = '', 'target', sample(10,1)))),
                   x1 = runif(N), x2 = runif(N), x3 = runif(N), x4 = runif(N), x5 = runif(N), 
                   x6 = runif(N), x7 = runif(N), x8 = runif(N), x9 = runif(N), x10 = runif(N), 
                   userID = as.factor(
                     sapply(1:N, function(u) paste0(collapse = '', 'user', sample(100,1)))))
                   
Nusers = length(unique(myDF$userID))
userIDs = lapply(unique(myDF$userID), function(u) which(myDF$userID == u))

kOfFolds = 5; propForTest = 0.3

Ntest = round(propForTest * Nusers)

testUserIDs = unlist(userIDs[1:Ntest])
trainUserIDs = unlist(userIDs[(1+Ntest):Nusers])

indexForCT = sapply(simplify = FALSE, 1:35, function(u){
  set.seed(1+u); 
  unlist(userIDs[sample((1+Ntest):Nusers, round((1-(1/kOfFolds))*(Nusers-Ntest)))]) })

ctrl2 = trainControl(method='repeatedcv', verboseIter = TRUE, repeats = 4, number= 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE, index = indexForCT)

set.seed(1);
mod2 = train(myDF$predVal, x= myDF[,2:11], method= 'knn', trControl = ctrl2)
```
The behaviour is similar when using simply `cv`. If we use `adaptive_cv`, `train` will do the adaptive search  check but it will ignore the `repeats` / `number` arguments nevertheless. 
 
```R
ctrl2 = trainControl(method='adaptive_cv', verboseIter = TRUE, repeats = 4, number= 5,
                     adaptive = list(min=12, alpha=0.02, method='gls', complete=FALSE),
                     classProbs = TRUE, index = indexForCT)
```

 This behaviour is the same on the CRAN binary as well as the github master-branch. Maybe a warning message should be issued that  `repeats` / `number` args are overridden? (Or at least some mention of this in `trainControl`'s documentation?) Thank you for checking this!

All best,
Pantelis

Text and example code modified from [the R FAQ on stackoverflow](http://stackoverflow.com/a/5963610)

X <- dat[,1:5]
y <- dat[["Class"]]

```
If you have some data that would be too difficult to construct using `caret::twoClassSim` or `caret::SLC14_1`, then you can always make a subset of your original data, using e.g. `head()`, `subset()` or the indices. Then use e.g. `dput()` to give us something that can be put in R immediately, e.g. `dput(head(iris,4))`

If you must use `dput(head())`, please first remove an columns from your dataset that are not necessary to reproduce the error.

If your data frame has a factor with many levels, the `dput` output can be unwieldy because it will still list all the possible factor levels even if they aren't present in the the subset of your data. To solve this issue, you can use the `droplevels()` function. Notice below how species is a factor with only one level: `dput(droplevels(head(iris, 4)))`

title: Example were `findLinearCombos` does not find linear dependencies
description:
I am attempting  to port the code that identifies linear dependent columns to Java/Scala. More specifically I am coding the function `internalEnumLC` found in [findLinearCombos.R](https://github.com/topepo/caret/blob/master/pkg/caret/R/findLinearCombos.R). To test this I created a matrix with one column being the linear combination of another 3. More specifically I have: 

    v3 = (v1 * 56.03) + (v2 * 89.309) + (v5 * 0.9077)
 
I then executed my code that did indeed find these columns, but surprisingly Caret's implementation did not find the solution. I suspect it may be a case of numeric stability due to the QR decomposition algorithm used. I am using the [Java matrix toolkits](https://github.com/fommil/matrix-toolkits-java). This library uses the [Java netlib API](https://github.com/fommil/netlib-java) that calls the LAPACK/BLAS functions in [NetLib](http://netlib.org/). Initially I attempted to use the [Apache Math Commons library](http://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-math/apidocs/org/apache/commons/math4/linear/QRDecomp), but its implementation of the QR decomposition algorithm failed with the simple example shown in [Caret's documentation](http://topepo.github.io/caret/pre-processing.html#lindep]) - rank was incorrectly determined.

### Minimal, reproducible example:

As per the instruction I checked for the latest update used a new session.
  
#### Minimal dataset:
```{R}
library("caret")

deps = matrix(
  c(1.01,  0.03,  119.61,  1.00,  66.06,
    10.01,  0.04,  654.65,  0.00,  98.90,
    20.02,  0.02,  1221.51,  0.00,  107.71,
    300.03,  0.03,  16913.50,  1.00,  110.01,
    5.06,  0.04,  348.42,  0.00,  67.08,
    6.06,  0.06,  425.57,  0.00,  88.87), 6, 5, byrow = TRUE)
deps
```
which shows:

```{R}
       [,1] [,2]     [,3] [,4]   [,5]
[1,]   1.01 0.03   119.61    1  66.06
[2,]  10.01 0.04   654.65    0  98.90
[3,]  20.02 0.02  1221.51    0 107.71
[4,] 300.03 0.03 16913.50    1 110.01
[5,]   5.06 0.04   348.42    0  67.08
[6,]   6.06 0.06   425.57    0  88.87
```

#### Minimal, runnable code:

Note that column 3 is a linear combination of columns 1,2 and 5. So I think that at least one of the  following two calls should yield the expected result.  

```{R}
findLinearCombos(deps)
findLinearCombos(deps[,c(1,2,5)])
```
but I get 

``` {R}
$linearCombos
list()

$remove
NULL
```
To show that in fact we have a linear combination we calculate the values of column 3:

``` {R}
coeffs = matrix(c(56.03, 89.309, 0.9077), 3, 1)
deps[,c(1,2,5)] %*% coeffs
```
which gives us:

``` {R}
          [,1]
[1,]   119.2322
[2,]   654.2042
[3,]  1221.2751
[4,] 16913.2162
[5,]   347.9727
[6,]   425.5676
```

Not exactly the values we expect, but they seem quite close. To check how close I did:

``` {R}
deps[,3] - (deps[,c(1,2,5)] %*% coeffs)
```
and got:

``` {R}
         [,1]
[1,] 0.377768
[2,] 0.445810
[3,] 0.234853
[4,] 0.283753
[5,] 0.447324
[6,] 0.002361
```
### Session Info:
```{R}

So I have the following (related) questions:

1. Given the matrix I created can we expect to find the collinear columns (albeit with some error in reconstruction) as shown? Note that in my implementation I use is the LAPACK `dgeqp3` function and test for equality with an _eps_ of 1e-12.

2. In the Caret code we have:
```  
b <- qr.coef(b, Y)                # get regression coefficients of
# the dependent columns
```
Assuming the columns are correctly identified, do each of the `b` columns represent the coefficients of the linear combinations? I have done some test on simple matrices and it seems so, but for this case I get coefficients: 

```
 0,01

-0,63
``` 

which is nothing like the values I used. Calculating the linear combination with these coefficients also does not yield the expected values (I check this in my code and it unexpectedly it passes - must be a bug on my side but cannot find it).  

3. Finally, is there any reference to an article or book that explains the algorithm used by Caret?
 
TIA

description:
I recently asked and answered a question on Stack Overflow about an error I ran into with the _caret_ package, possibly as a result of the _lazyeval_ package. I haven't been able to specifically verify that my explanation for the issue is correct, but I did find a solution that may help to track down the reason, at least. This error arose when I attempted to train any model whatsoever, but I do provide a reproducible example, as well as my session info before and after, on the Stack Overflow question here:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/41558992/r-caret-package-running-into-compile-environment-error/41579786

My best guess is that perhaps a function from _lazyeval_ is being used in the _caret_ package without specifying it as a dependency, and thus older versions of _ggplot2_ run into a problem. Caret loads _ggplot2_, and the newest version of _ggplot2_ loads _lazyeval_, but older versions do not.

I could be off base, as it was a very strange error I had to track down, but I think you may be able to resolve this either by specifying lazyeval as a dependency, or specifying ggplot2 >= 2.2.

title: Two-parameter Box-Cox for zero values?
description:
This is a question and not an issue but I though I'd rather drop you an issue than an email.
In your book and in carret it seems you're doing the one-parameter box-cox transformation. That doesn't work for zero values. I was wondering if you have any advice on what a good default strategy is for zero values and if you think the two-parameter box-cox transformation is a good way to deal with them.

I'm mostly asking for designing the box-cox transformation for scikit-learn (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/6781) and I'd welcome your advice. Needing non-zero values will likely tempt users to add an epsilon, and I'm not sure if that's a good solution.

description:
Dear Max, 

I trained a series of regression models with the same settings using caret. 
For some (__glmnet, lasso, gbm__), I always got the same error:

#### Minimal, runnable error code:
This:
```{R error=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
library(caret)

# Lasso
set.seed(1)
fit <- train(mpg~.
             , data= mtcars
             , method = 'lasso'
             , importance = TRUE
)

```
produces this error:
``` Something is wrong; all the RMSE metric values are missing:
      RMSE        Rsquared  
 Min.   : NA   Min.   : NA  
 1st Qu.: NA   1st Qu.: NA  
 Median : NA   Median : NA  
 Mean   :NaN   Mean   :NaN

 NA's   :3     NA's   :3    
Error in train.default(x, y, weights = w, ...) : Stopping
In addition: There were 26 warnings (use warnings() to see them)```


After a while of playing around I found that this is due to the option: `importance = TRUE`  I had set in the train function.

This
```{R error=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
library(caret)

# Lasso
set.seed(1)

title: Crash in `multiClassSummary`.
description:
Hello,

I think there is a bug related with `multiClassSummary` (`caret_6.0-73`). An `NA` is introduced within `train` when getting the names of the metrics, (`perfNames <- names(testSummary)`). This a problem because within `adaptiveWorkflow`/`nominalTrainWorkflow` the command: 
`resamples <- rbind.fill(result[names(result) == "resamples"])` will immediately err. 

More specifically: The `NA` is introduced by  `multiClassSummary` when trying to get the `logLoss`. Because the output of `mnLogLoss(data = data, lev = lev, model = model)` within `multiClassSummary` is already a named element and the line `c(CM$overall, logLoss = lloss, ROC = roc_stats)` results in a vector with a named element `logLoss.logLoss`. Therefore the last line: `stats <- stats[c(stat_list)]` fails to find `logLoss` and the final `stats` object has an `NA`. This is probably a byproduct of issue [514](https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/514) / commit: [9d1c56b](https://github.com/topepo/caret/commit/9d1c56bdc72355dd73f5f5835ea4db577c9d3793).

Immediate fix:
Replace line: 
`c(CM$overall, logLoss = lloss, ROC = roc_stats)`
with
`c(CM$overall, logLoss = as.numeric(lloss), ROC = roc_stats)`. This appears to fix the problem in my local copy. 

All best,
Pantelis

title: predict does not produce the probability for glmboost
description:
This may not be an issue of caret, but I just want to bring it to your attention. In short, `predict(train_object, type='prob')` actually does not produce the probability for `glmboost` (and probably for `gamboost` in the `mboost` package as well).

According to the [`mboost` paper](http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00180-012-0382-5),
"For reasons of computational efficiency, the binary response y ∈ {0, 1} is converted into ˜y = 2y − 1 where ˜y ∈ {−1, 1}. ... Note that the transformation ˜y = 2y − 1 changes the interpretation of the effect estimates because now we get the half of the log-odds ratio. One implication is that the coef() output is half the estimations that result from glm(). **This means that the user has to double the coefficients manually in order to get the final standard estimates of a logistic regression model**. ... However, mboost automatically doubles the logits prior to the reverse probability transformation. This means that calling `predict(fit, newdata, type ="response")` produces the final probability estimates."

Let X be the predictor matrix, b the coefficients extracted by 'coef()'. Unlike `predict(fit, newdata, type ="response")`, `predict(fit, newdata, type ="link")` would only give `Xb` while the correct value is `2Xb`. It seems that `caret` does something as `predict(fit, newdata, type ="link")`. i.e., without doubling `Xb`, and then takes the inverse logit transformation to calculate the probability.

Below is an example of the relationship among
`predict(train_object$finalModel, newdata, type ="link")` 
`predict(train_object$finalModel, newdata, type ="response")`
`predict(train_object, newdata, type='prob')`

title: multiClassSummary
description:
Prototype here: https://gist.github.com/zachmayer/3061272

``` R
multiClassSummary <- function (data, lev = NULL, model = NULL){

  #Load Libraries
  require(Metrics)
  require(caret)

  #Check data
  if (!all(levels(data[, "pred"]) == levels(data[, "obs"]))) 
    stop("levels of observed and predicted data do not match")

  #Calculate custom one-vs-all stats for each class
  prob_stats <- lapply(levels(data[, "pred"]), function(class){

    #Grab one-vs-all data for the class
    pred <- ifelse(data[, "pred"] == class, 1, 0)
    obs  <- ifelse(data[,  "obs"] == class, 1, 0)
    prob <- data[,class]

    #Calculate one-vs-all AUC and logLoss and return
    cap_prob <- pmin(pmax(prob, .000001), .999999)
    prob_stats <- c(auc(obs, prob), logLoss(obs, cap_prob))
    names(prob_stats) <- c('ROC', 'logLoss')
    return(prob_stats) 
  })
  prob_stats <- do.call(rbind, prob_stats)
  rownames(prob_stats) <- paste('Class:', levels(data[, "pred"]))

  #Calculate confusion matrix-based statistics
  CM <- confusionMatrix(data[, "pred"], data[, "obs"])

  #Aggregate and average class-wise stats
  #Todo: add weights
  class_stats <- cbind(CM$byClass, prob_stats)
  class_stats <- colMeans(class_stats)

  #Aggregate overall stats
  overall_stats <- c(CM$overall)

  #Combine overall with class-wise stats and remove some stats we don't want 
  stats <- c(overall_stats, class_stats)
  stats <- stats[! names(stats) %in% c('AccuracyNull', 
    'Prevalence', 'Detection Prevalence')]

  #Clean names and return
  names(stats) <- gsub('[[:blank:]]+', '_', names(stats))
  return(stats)

}
```

xgbFitOK2 <- train( Class ~ ., data = trainData, objective = "binary:logitraw",
                   method = "xgbTree", tuneLength = 2, trControl =  trCntlList) 
```

The error occurs within the `foreach` loop of `nominalTrainWorkflow`. In particular around Line # ~203 during the call to the `probFunction`. `probFunction` errs because the argument `modelFit$param$objective` is NULL. To that respect, `modelFit` does not have a `param` field to begin with.  That is somewhat surprising but that it can be explained by the fact that `createModel` never appended a `param` field. This is expected as `createModel` is fully agnostic about the objective function used. It should have a point where it creates a `params` field to the `modelFit` returned.

I can tell that this error was introduced with `ed79d6d` as I back-tracked it; the code runs "fine" at the `5cc19a5` commit. (well, not totally fine, the probabilities are wrong as show in  [511](https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/511)  but at least it works when `objective = "binary:logistic"`). title: Documentation Request: explicit example passing parameters to model.
description:
The `train()` function has an explicit `method` parameter that specifies a model.  However, models like `polr` exist that also have a `method` parameter.  Normally,  you can pass parameters to the underlying functions in the `dots` parameter, but you cannot when you have a parameter name clash.  The solution seems to be to feed it as a column of the `tuneGrid` parameter data frame.  I got the answer here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/41230809/passing-parameters-to-dots-that-conflict-with-explicit-parameters/41258583#41258583 .

I suggest that this behavior be documented somehow, somewhere, with an example.  Perhaps in the documentation that refers to `polr` in the "available models" listings.  Thank you.

title: caret seems to be really slow
description:
I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong, but it seems that training a model using randomForest is much much faster if I just use the `randomForest()` function rather than `train()` I'm using R version 3.1.2 and the latest version of caret available on CRAN. Here is a reproducible example, taken from some of the Johns Hopkins Data Science specialization track on Coursera.

```
if (!file.exists("pml-training.csv")) {
  download.file("https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-training.csv", "pml-training.csv", method="curl")
}
if (!file.exists("pml-testing.csv")) {
  download.file("https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-testing.csv", "pml-testing.csv", method="curl")
}
set.seed(75681)

library(caret)
library("randomForest")
training <- read.csv("pml-training.csv")
testing <- read.csv("pml-testing.csv")

# Remmove the times and user_name
training <- training[,-c(1,2,3,4,5)]
testing <- testing[,-c(1,2,3,4,5)]

# remove the columsn with near zero variance. I remove the same columns from the testing set as were taken from the training set to
# ensure that the two data sets are consistent
nzv <- nearZeroVar(training)
training <- training[,-nzv]
testing <- testing[,-nzv]

# There are a lot of columns that are NA for every value. Let's just remove them since most
# machine learning algorithms don't like NA values anyway.
mostly_na <- apply(training, 2, function(x) { sum(is.na(x)) } )
training <- training[,which(mostly_na==0)]
testing <- testing[,which(mostly_na==0)]

# Since I'm slashing columns out left and right, why not take out any 
# highly correlated variables
muchCor <- findCorrelation(cor(training[, 1:dim(training)[2]-1]), cutoff=0.8)
training <- training[,-muchCor]
testing <- testing[,-muchCor]

# Finally, we will only keep the complete cases from the two data sets
# instead of removing these cases we might have to do some of that impugning data.
training <- training[complete.cases(training),]
testing <- testing[complete.cases(testing),]

# Now divide the training set up into modelTraining and modelTesting
randomSelection <- createDataPartition(training$classe, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
modelTraining <- training[randomSelection, ]
modelTesting <- training[-randomSelection, ]

###
### Now it's time to train some models and see how they perform ###
start <- Sys.time()
rfModel <- randomForest(modelTraining[,1:ncol(modelTraining)-1], modelTraining[,ncol(modelTraining)])
Sys.time() - start
```

That last line returned 30.19 seconds of wall time to finish training the model. Then I ran this

```
start <- Sys.time()
rfModel <- train(classe ~ ., data=modelTraining, method="rf", verbose=FALSE)
Sys.time() - start
```

I finally stopped running it after 12 minutes had passed. I don't know how long it would have gone on for. Obviously this is a really big different in run time and I'm wondering if I'm doing something wrong in the way I'm calling `train()` or if there is an actual bug somewhere?

description:
Hi,

I am trying to use a custom performance metric called "mapk",
while training an xgb model and getting the following error:

**Error in ctrl$summaryFunction(testOutput, lev, method) : 
  unused arguments (lev, method)**

Thanks,
Ronen

Here in the training code:

```

and the function that implement the mapk metric:

```
fn_MAPK <- function (data, lev = c("No","Yes")) {
  data$obs <- factor(data$obs, levels=c(0,1), labels=c("No", "Yes"))
  data$pred <- factor(data$pred, levels=c(0,1), labels=c("No", "Yes"))
  eval_result <- data.frame(display_id=numeric(), score=numeric())
  for (i in unique(data$display_id)){
    df <- data %>% 
          filter(display_id == i)
    k <- nrow(df)
    actual <- df$obs
    predicted <- df$pred
    score <- mapk(k,actual,predicted)
    d <- c(i, score)
    eval_result <- rbind(eval_result, d) }
  out <- mean(eval_result[,2])
  names(out) <- "mapk"
  out}

apk <- function(k, actual, predicted)
 { score <- 0.0
   cnt <- 0.0
   for (i in 1:min(k,length(predicted)))
   { if (predicted[i] %in% actual && !(predicted[i] %in% predicted[0:(i-1)]))
     { cnt <- cnt + 1
       score <- score + cnt/i  }}
   score <- score / min(length(actual), k)
   score }  
  
 mapk <- function (k, actual, predicted)
 {if( length(actual)==0 || length(predicted)==0 ) 
   {return(0.0)}
    scores <- rep(0, length(actual))
   for (i in 1:length(scores))
   { scores[i] <- apk(k, actual[[i]], predicted[[i]]) }
   score <- mean(scores)
   score }
```

title: xgboost class probabilities inaccurate if `objective = "binary:logitraw"`
description:
Hello,

This may be a bug when using `xgbTree` when attempting to return probabilities using `classProbs = TRUE` and `predict`. In particular, if one defines `objective = "binary:logitraw"` the returned probabilities are not true probabilities (they do sum up to 1 though if that is any consolation! :D )

``` R

rm(list=ls())
library(caret)
set.seed(42)  
trainData <- twoClassSim(500)    
testData <- twoClassSim(500)  

trCntlList <- trainControl(method = "boot", number = 6, classProbs = TRUE) 

set.seed(55)  
xgbFitOK<- train(  Class ~ ., data = trainData,  objective = "binary:logistic", 
                   method = "xgbTree", tuneLength = 2, trControl =  trCntlList)
set.seed(55)  
xgbFitNotOK <- train( Class ~ ., data = trainData, objective = "binary:logitraw",
                   method = "xgbTree", tuneLength = 2, trControl =  trCntlList) 
```

where the resulting probabilities are:

``` R

head(predict(xgbFitOK, testData, type='prob')) # Seems legit
      Class1       Class2
1 0.04302632 9.569737e-01
2 0.63181454 3.681855e-01
3 0.99995232 4.768372e-05
4 0.98860931 1.139069e-02
5 0.06293963 9.370604e-01
6 0.99990976 9.024143e-05
head(predict(xgbFitNotOK, testData, type='prob')) # Nope.
      Class1     Class2
1 -1.5372999  2.5372999
2  0.6052027  0.3947973
3  7.0601740 -6.0601740
4  3.3764718 -2.3764718
5 -3.3586116  4.3586116
6  7.5873170 -6.5873170
```

Yes, sure these are the output scores before the logistic transformation but they are not probabilities as suggested by `trainControl`. Actually one needs to be a careful because even simply taking something like:

title: Unnamed vector returned by mnLogLoss breaks model selection in training
description:
The latest CRAN version 6.0-72 has a bug in the summary function `mnLogLoss` that prevents `logLoss` from being used as a metric in training resampling. 

The previous version (6.0-71) returned a named vector where the computed logloss values are assigned the name `logLoss`. 

The new version in 6.0-72 that uses `ModelMetrics::mlogLoss` returns an unnamed vector. 

In addition to that, `train.default` is not robust to all of the non-parameter columns in `performance` being unnamed. Since the column for logLoss is unnamed, it trips up when trying to extract that column from `performance` and triggers the 

    cat(paste("Something is wrong; all the", metric, 
        "metric values are missing:\n"))
        
error.

title: 'skip' in createTimeSlices()
description:
Minor request here.

1) The 'skip' arg for createTimeSlices is not available when passing trainControl(method = "timeslice"...) to train(), which means a user must create the time slices themselves if they need to reduce the sample space. That's a very common need for timeseries analysis. For example, if doing a timeseries analysis with 1 minute data over a one month period, you can easily end up with thousands of train/test samples... 

2) The 'skip' parameter itself is not that useful, as a user has to do some math to figure out just how many samples will be generated when creating the slices. It might be more useful to specify the total numer of test samples (n_samples), and randomly select them without replacement from the possible samples.

i.e. replace line 25 in createTimeSlices.R:
`x[seq(1, n, by = skip)]`
with 
`sample(x, n_samples, replace = FALSE)`

Hello,

Every fuzzy method I've tried has thrown lots of the following warning: `There are your newdata which are out of the specified range`. [By chance I found a day-old stackexchange post about this problem](http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/237139/warning-messages-in-model-with-caret). args$range.data <- apply(x, 2, extendrange)

title: Bug: train with rlm only works with factors or characters if all levels would be legal as column names
description:
Took me a while to pin this done but the discipline of making a MRE pinned it for me.  Using `method="rlm"` in `train()` causes problems with categorical explanatory variables unless each distinct value of the categorical variable would be legal as a column name.  This problem doesn't happen when using `rlm()` itself, and doesn't happen with other methods (eg `lm`) in `train`.  It's presumably something to do with the one hot encoding at some point in `train()`.

Here's the minimal reproducible example:

``` R
library(caret)
# make some test data including an explanatory variable with
# levels that would be illegal as column names:
n <- 100
testdata <- data.frame(
   x1 = rnorm(n),
   x2 = sample(c("dog", "cat's mother", "bear"), n, replace = TRUE)
)
testdata$y <- with(testdata,
                   0.5 + x1 * 0.2 + (x2 == "bear") * 0.3 - (x2 =="dog") * 0.2 +
                      rnorm(n)
                   )

# make a variant of x2 that *would* be legal as column names
testdata$x3 <- make.names(testdata$x2)

#---------------fit models-------------
cv_control <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 5)

# doesn't work, because x2 contains levels that are illegal as column names
mod_rlm <- train(y ~ x1 + x2, data = testdata, method = "rlm", trControl = cv_control)

# does work:
mod_rlm <- train(y ~ x1 + x3, data = testdata, method = "rlm", trControl = cv_control)

# so far I've only found this a problem with rlm.  eg this works ok
mod_lm <- train(y ~ x1 + x2, data = testdata, method = "lm", trControl = cv_control)

# problem doesn't happen with rlm used directly
rlm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = testdata)
```

title: sbf() returns anomalous results with factors
description:
#### Problem description

I am not sure if this is more of a bug or a feature request, but I have had some difficulty with the `sbf()` function.  When I use the function on a dataframe containing factors there appears to be some strange data type conversion that occurs resulting in inappropriate results for the `lmSBF` functions (it ignores any non-factor variables).  Here is my best guess at the source of the error.  The error seems to occur somewhere between the call

`scores <- apply(x, 2, sbfControl$functions$score, y = y)`

in `sbfIter()` and when it is received by the `score` function of the `sbfControl` parameter.  In `sbfIter()` all the variables have their original datatypes, however when it is received by the `score` function all of the variables are converted to type `character`.  This happens with both the `lmSBF` functions and the `rfSBF` functions, however `rfSBF` still works and `lmSBF` does not.  I believe this is because `rfSBF$score()` calls either `anovaScores(x, y)` or `gamScores(x,y)` where as `lmSBF$score()` calls `anovaScores(y, x)` (y and x are reversed).  Either way, a number of warnings are thrown.  For `rfSBF` it is:

`In model.response(mf, "numeric") : NAs introduced by coercion`

and for `lmSBF` it is:

`In anova.lm(object) :`
`ANOVA F-tests on an essentially perfect fit are unreliable`

Bellow is an example to reproduce the result.  Note that if the `sbf()` function is run with `x` instead of `xfact` in either of the examples below everything runs just fine and the same variables (`Var04 (14%)` and `Var02 (10%)`) are returned for both models.
#### Minimal dataset:

``` R
library(caret)
set.seed(1)
dat <- caret::SLC14_1(100)
x <- dat[, 1:5]
x <- as.data.frame(x) #lmSBF requires x to be a dataframe
y <- dat$y
set.seed(10)
xfact <- x
xfact[["bogusLetters"]] <- LETTERS[sample(1:2, nrow(xfact), replace = TRUE)]
```
#### Minimal, runnable code:

``` R
filterCtrl <- sbfControl(functions = rfSBF, method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 5)
set.seed(10)
rfWithFilterFact <- sbf(xfact, y, sbfControl = filterCtrl)
rfWithFilterFact

filterCtrl <- sbfControl(functions = lmSBF, method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 5)
set.seed(10)
lmWithFilterFact <- sbf(xfact, y, sbfControl = filterCtrl)
lmWithFilterFact

title: Reproducibility of createFolds()

the result of createFolds() can depend on the system locale:

library(caret)

> Something is wrong; all the RMSE metric values are missing

I don't seem to be able to get to the root of it. It is preventing me from using many available models.

Below, I am reporting 2 examples.

**Example 1**
In this example, I am using a simple dataset with random NAs added to make it more realistic.

```
library(ISLR); library(ggplot2); library(caret);

data(Wage)
Wage <- subset(Wage, select=-c(logwage))

# adding some random NAs
n <- nrow(Wage)
Wage[,-11] <- do.call(cbind.data.frame, lapply(Wage[,-11], 
                    function(x) {x[sample(c(1:n),floor(n/10))]<-NA
                    x}))

set.seed(1234)
inTrain <- createDataPartition(y=Wage$wage, p=0.7, list=FALSE)
training <- Wage[inTrain,]
testing <- Wage[-inTrain,]

# Create dummy variables (necessary to use preProcess)
dummies <- dummyVars(wage ~ age + jobclass + education, data = training)
dummy_tr <- as.data.frame(predict(dummies, training))
dummy_tr$wage <- training$wage

modFit <- train(wage ~ ., method="treebag", 
                preProc = c("medianImpute"),    
                na.action = na.pass,
                data=dummy_tr)
```

**Example 2**

title: RWeka classifier hyperparameters
description:
Is there a reason that some of the `RWeka` classifiers only have one specified hyperparameter?  The LMT model has multiple available values for hyperparemeters for grid/random search while others do not. For example, J48 has `C = 0.25`, PART has `threshold = 0.25` and `pruned = "yes"`, and JRip has `NumOpt = 1:len`.

```
library(caret)
data(iris)
library(RWeka)

# No other hyperparameter values, no random search
getModelInfo("J48")

# No other hyperparameter values, no random search
getModelInfo("PART")

# This needs sampling for random search
getModelInfo("JRip")
# Also it appears NumOpt it now named O in RWeka
RWeka::WOW("JRip")

# Other values of these hyperparameters run when called directly through RWeka

# J48 called through RWeka
j48c1 <- J48(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(C = 0.2))
j48c2 <- J48(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(C = 0.25))

# JRip called through RWeka
jripc1 <- JRip(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(O = 3))
jripc2 <- JRip(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(O = 100))

# PART called through RWeka
partc1 <- PART(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(threshold = 0.25, pruned = "yes"))
partc2 <- PART(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(threshold = 0.2, pruned = "no"))
partc3 <- PART(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(threshold = 0.25, pruned = "yes"))
partc4 <- PART(Species ~ ., data = iris, control = Weka_control(threshold = 0.2, pruned = "no"))
```

I can do some testing on what are decent values for these hyperparameters and put together a PR if necessary.
